en: These are all characters formed by the same strokes and dots; yet when a person with discerning insight seizes upon them, they can—like a painter adding the "eye" to a portrait—cause the character to overflow with life, such that one facing it cannot help but exclaim in wonder.
It is as if each person were given a mirror to behold their own face, making everything perfectly clear. The staff of Deshan and the shout of Linji seem even more so.
This is more exhilarating than anything else. It is a collection from the ocean of various poisons; the verses and hymns of the ancient sages are all of this nature.
These are the true writings of a genuine man of the Way. Within the Zen school, one resorts to words only out of necessity; it must be like this before they may be used.

I have often said that if members of our monastic community do not disclose the truth from their own fundamental ground, but instead race about with cleverness and dazzle others with their wit—[this is a grave error].

To dazzle with phrasing and sentences, vying with literary men and scholars for skillful artistry, boasting of abundance, and contending for elegance—how is this any different from what the Master of Mount Ni (Confucius) called "the gentleman departing from benevolence"?
If one were made to wander through such a sea of poison, I know they would surely be left in a state of utter dismay.
This collection, following its revision and expansion by the two venerable masters Shuzhong and Meigou, is compared to that of Longshan.
This undertaking has achieved a truly grand vision. However, because the woodblocks for the Southern editions were not widely circulated, scholars in the North rarely had the opportunity to see them.
Therefore, I have re-engraved this work, supplementing it with one or two additions. I have followed the precedent set by Master Mei and combined these elements as he suggested;
I do not dare to act out of favoritism. Long ago, the World-Honored One himself described his state while still on the path of causes.
At that time, having obtained half a verse, he inscribed it everywhere upon forest leaves and stone walls to transmit it to the people of the land.
My current endeavor to carve this supplement is not intended to vie for merit with those who came before; it is merely to relieve the labor of copying upon leaves and walls.
Preface by the Śramaṇa Xingyin of Gulin Temple, in the sixth month of summer, the Jiawu year of the Kangxi era.

Formerly, when the Great Patriarch Miaoxi resided at Yangyu Hermitage, whenever he gave discourses or teachings, the attendant monk, the Head Seat Hong, recorded them all and titled the collection *The Sea of Mixed Poisons*.
This was likely because the Patriarch had said that those who fail to attain realization through Zen meditation...

These are mostly words in which various poisons have entered the mind. Therefore, later scholars, whenever they encountered the verses, hymns, or accounts of Buddhist services by their former teachers or eminent virtuous ones, would transcribe them by hand into volumes, yet they also labeled them with the title "The Sea of Miscellaneous Poisons.
This practice has long existed. One day, Zen Master Zhongyou of Longshan reviewed these records and, weary of their errors and corruptions, proceeded to edit them.
Its contents were so voluminous and redundant that he extracted the essential points and categorized them into fascicles, beginning their publication.
His intention was, above all, not to辜负 (disappoint) the author’s own intent, and to establish it as an enduring and elegant model for future students. Some may say:
"The Master’s dedication is certainly praiseworthy, but what of his contravening the instructions of Miaoxi? However, regarding words and language, non-attachment is held as the highest priority.
For example, if ordinary people drink the venom of the *hen* bird, they die; yet when Cao Meng drank it, he suffered no harm.
It depends entirely on the scholar’s capacity for discernment and selection. Thus, the circulation of this compilation will not fail to be of benefit to the Dharma-gate.
Therefore, I have written this preface. Recorded by Wuyun of Mafeng in the seventeenth year of the Hongwu era.

Master Shuzhong said: "What our school calls 'verses' (gāthās) borrow phenomena to manifest principle, awakening the human mind-ground so that phenomena and principle are blended and unified, pure and without admixture.

Like the flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) or the fragrance of the *campaka* flower, they cause one’s nose and tongue to experience them briefly, yet they penetrate the heart and pervade the body, bringing about a state of refreshing clarity."

It is further said that during the late Song and early Yuan dynasties, whenever the various venerable masters (zunsu) composed verses for parting when departing from their lodgings, or for chanting as titles for their works, they invariably followed the four-line verse form (gāthā).
Their compositions were of such exquisite refinement that even if the titles were removed, the meaning would remain clearly manifest.

This was possible because they had not only realized the profound and subtle truth through meditative verification but were also thoroughly conversant with the classical canons; thus, they could draw freely from these sources.
The aforementioned Fengyuan was one whose every action accorded with the Way; yet he was unable to rely upon this [work] to chant and expound the ultimate purport.
I have often said to my disciples: "This composition of hymns and gāthās is an unalterable established doctrine; it is a golden needle that opens the eyes of men.
This book has circulated within the Dharma community for a long time. By the beginning of the Hongwu era, Longshan...
Master Lian compiled this by pruning the redundant and extracting the essential, categorizing it into a collection that was first published for circulation within the monastic community.

Venerable Shu Zhong then composed a preface for it. I observe that Master Lian’s intent in re-compiling this work accords perfectly with what Master Shu discussed, and Master Shu’s intent in writing the preface likewise shares the same spirit as Master Lian’s selection and editing. Therefore, I have emulated...

The two masters [Wu]ping browsed extensively through the "pearls left behind" by ancient predecessors and gathered the "complete jewels" of recent times. They categorized and added to them, re-circulating them within the monastic community.
The original collection comprised seven hundred and thirty-two verses; now, more than eight hundred and seventy have been added.

As for indiscriminately adopting [accounts] from Āśmarathya, how could I dare? Should there be anything in my observations or learning that is meager or erroneous, I pray only that those of lofty wisdom will instruct me.
Recorded by Xing Yue of Nanjian in the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era.

Re-edited by the monk Shingon, successor in the lineage at Kōtoku-ji in Kyoto:
The Buddha’s birth was devoid of artifice within the womb; he displayed his elegance in the Lumbinī Garden. Year after year, the foul waters are difficult to turn back.
Avoidance. All afflictions arise because one forces oneself out of the head (Shushan Rui).
From the beginning, a wealthy family produces a pampered child; as soon as it emerges from the womb, it begins to strike about wildly.
Only when its skills are exhausted beneath the twin trees does it finally realize that for forty-nine years it has been in error (Lan’an Shu).
Never having entered the womb of Māyā, with both hands knowing not where he was placed;
emerging from her right side, a demonic realm appeared—fit only for lamentation, unfit to behold. (Tianmu’s Veneration)
Pointing to heaven, pointing to earth, brandishing halberds and spears; even until this very day, the battle has not ceased.
Even if all living beings were slaughtered to extinction, one body would still have its own sorrows. (Gao Feng Miao)
Today Māyā gave birth to an infant; she descended from the celestial palace of the Pure Abode. It was not a phoenix’s egg born from a hen’s nest;
clearly, an elephant cub emerged from a donkey’s womb. (Qianyan Chang)
When the Eye was struck out from Gautama upon his attainment of the Way, there was but a single branch of plum blossoms amidst the snow. Now, thorns grow everywhere;
one can only laugh at the spring wind that blows so disorderly. (Huìtáng Xīn)
Six years on the snowy peaks, the Way was finally perfected; he struck out the eyes of the ghosts from long ago.
With his face full of shame and no place to hide, to this day he is terrified at the sight of the morning star (Jingsou Jue).

When entering the mountains, what did you intend? When emerging from the mountains, for what purpose have you come? Had you known of today’s affairs beforehand, you would regret not having been more cautious at the outset. (Wu Zhunfan)
Raising his head, he saw the stars and suddenly awakened to the Way. On Mount Huangni, mugwort and grass grew wild;
Old Lady Li made her own old-fashioned clothes—she did not cut the crimson, she cut the fragrant soap (Yutang Yi).
On the eighth day of the twelfth month two thousand years ago, the yellow-faced Gautama’s eyes were alive.
Having consumed much salt over incalculable eons, his six years of asceticism only served to increase his thirst. (Yuejiang Yin)
This morning is precisely the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month. Śākyamuni, the Old Man, has gone blind. Under the bright sun and clear sky, he is bewitched by demons;
at night, facing the morning star, he scrapes out his eyes. (Chaozong Ren)
Leaving the mountains, he could not endure the hunger and cold for six years; filled with shame, he sought to re-enter the human world.
Had he known from the start that his skill was merely this, why did he not simply stay out of the mountains in the first place? (Wuquán Fàn)
Tangled hair flows down through the emerald peaks; frozen clouds and lingering snow cling to his *kāṣāya*. There is no need to further inquire about matters within the mountains;
by observing his countenance, one shall know at once. (Shiwu Hong)
Hunger and cold are hard to endure, and the Way is difficult to seek; yet he goes among men to sell mere words.
If his face does not turn yellow as wax, how can he conceal such shame? (Qianyan Chang)
Not remaining in the royal palace, this foolish fellow; leaping over the city wall at midnight is truly strange. Who would have cared for your six years of asceticism?
When his resources were exhausted, he had no choice but to come forth from the mountains. (Wuji Guan)
The *ge-teng* tree atop Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Nirvāṇa sends forth vines and twigs that grow everywhere across the earth.
Were it not for the power of Pāpīyān to topple it, there would still be no path for people to travel today. (Fóxīguāng)
At the moment of death, one should rest, yet they refuse to rest; once the two soles of the feet emerge, it is difficult to withdraw them again.
To this day, the bones and joints, along with every pore, are exposed upon the tips of the hundred grasses in the spring breeze (Xutang Yu).
In the groves of Amitābha, the True Dharma is discussed day after day; by the waters and birds, Right Contemplation is reflected upon from time to time.
It is only because the minds of sentient beings have not yet glimpsed this that you must labor so diligently to extend your hand down from the edge of the clouds (Huisi Ming).
In this Sahā world today, suffering and sorrow abound; the land is vast and people are few—what can be done?
If one were to load all beings onto a single ship, it would surely cause wind and waves to rise from level ground. (Zhuan’an Cheng)

Mañjuśrī is vaguely present amidst the wind and waves of the fisherman; he is faintly discernible among the mist and smoke of the cowherd boy. When will these ghost-like sentient beings come to an end?
Look, look—Wutai Mountain is being left to waste away (Xisongshou).
Avalokiteśvara seeks out voices to save from suffering in great haste; mud and water soak his entire body in layers of sweat.
Though ten thousand people are difficult to transform, he constantly keeps them recorded within his belly (the great river that saves ten thousand people by virtue of his internal organs).
The White Flower Rock is not the reality; at the Dragon Flower Assembly, his entire body appears. Such a person is truly clever;
within his belly, he constantly accommodates ten thousand people. (Duanya Yi: Ten Thousand People’s Karmic Conditions)
Her graceful form and tilted tresses entice the young man to recite the Lotus Sutra;
once her skeleton is carried away, one knows not under whose roof the bright moon shall fall. (Yinshan Can)
A crescent moon slants across the solitary sea-gate; chasing waves and following currents is no mark of a true man.
When both hands are held out to others, one uses fish-eyes to trade for bright pearls. (Boat at a Separate Bay)
The youth has not yet returned from his southern journey; beneath the White Flower Rock, I have gazed for a long time.
On a cloudless night across ten thousand miles of vast sky, the moon speaks from the heart of the waves—to whom? (Shiwu Hong)
A blue center with a brocade tail has no apparent cause; fearing it will rot, one often sells it at the market head. One must know that the wealthy loathe poverty and do not love it;
how can this compare to casting it aside and forgetting all sorrow? (Daiweng Yue-er)
The vow to lift up all sentient beings is vast; the vow is only fulfilled when every being has been delivered.
Yet, one does not know that the realm of sentient beings can never be exhausted—where, then, would you set your basket once it is empty?
I prostrate to the Honored One of Perfect Penetration and Sovereign Freedom. Do not lightly regard the thought of saving beings from suffering.
Now, in every place, Avalokiteśvara manifests; even the ears can serve as eyes. (Yuan Yu Jiao)
Vimalakīrti, the old Vimalakīrti within the city of Vaiśālī—his single silence and wordlessness are full of guile.
How it will be when thirty-two thousand lion thrones are overturned all at once! (Wu-yung’s entire verse).
The profound discourse on non-duality transcends all views and knowledge; in silence, one has long since entered the realm of fragmentation.
Had you encountered my own house at that time, upon any hesitation, I would have struck your face with my fist—[the lineage of Wuji].
Feigning illness has been incurable from the start; Mañjuśrī specifically applied his needle and awl. The matter was stripped away, leaving a mouth three feet long;
when questioned, it remains as before, like a drum mallet. (Wunian Fan)
Manifesting illness in the chamber of Vimalakīrti, even Mañjuśrī found it difficult to approach his side. Looking at him, there was no medicine that could cure him;
abstaining from food was the only supreme remedy. (Xiyuan Hui)
The wrinkled brows of a woman are knit tight; who knows these ailments? Mañjuśrī draws out the needle from the Gao-huang acupoint;
it is already like treating a dead horse with medicine. (Zhongxuan Fu)
Sudhana’s fifty-three people are strung together on a single thread; though the child is small, his courage is like heaven’s.
Amidst the vast, boundless mists and waters beyond counting, he has purchased the splendor of the scenery for no price at all. (Beijian Jian)
Throughout his life he carried a wooden board and displayed his cleverness; having finished his practice and returned home, what was the matter? He traveled through all one hundred and ten cities;
where one knows many people, there are many disputes. (Xiaowen Kan).
Having traveled through many clouds and mists in the south, he has gathered rare treasures that fill his ship;
with a mere snap of the fingers, the wind-driven sails reach the shore, all at once transformed into great coins of light (Wuquán Fàn).
The old woman by the eastern city wall sits upon a lotus pedestal; the true eye of all sentient beings in the great earth is opened.
Born together with the Buddha, she yet detests seeing him; one body cannot become two Tathāgatas. (Xutang Yu)
The old woman had Gautama in her eyes; thus she was able to see clearly the tip of the finger.
If one says she never wished to see him for her entire life, then believing such a thing surely means one has been deceived by him.
When the butcher Guang'e laid down his meat cleaver, he could not be turned back even by a blow of the staff. Clouds drift toward the imperial capital;
waters flow back to the Yangtze and Han rivers. (Tuan’an Xiu)
What "attainment" or "non-attainment" could there be for this Buddha? Fools speak of dreams and believe them to be real.
One must know that once you have personally laid down the blade, every subsequent stroke will reveal the blood of life. (Daiweng Yue)
The Arhat tears up empty space to patch empty space; He startles the golden crow to emerge from the eastern sea.
To call this "the matter beneath the patched robe" Shows you have never yet mastered the thread of the path. (Beijian Jian)
Where the golden needle pierces through, one is liberated from all patterns; letting go and gathering back, one attains spontaneous mastery.
Having snapped the red thread from one’s hand, Zhaozhou hangs his gourd upon the eastern wall (Miaofeng Shan).
Horizontal and vertical pieces haphazardly joined; long and short needles linked as they please. One merely sees the sun rising from the eastern side;
one knows not what year it is in this dusty world. (Wuzhun Shanfeng)
Tattered and frayed, a broken old relic; one hole patched, then another.
As three poles of red sun pierce through the fence, look at it—how could it weigh less than seven catties? (Xueyan Qin)
These are things needed urgently during the cold season; seize the warmth to do some needlework.
Suddenly, when the twelfth lunar month arrives, you will avoid falling into a state of frantic confusion. (No gate to open, part two.)
Having just caught a glimpse of a fragment of light, one seeks to resolve the final chapter. If this were the "fist with no opening," I would not strike such a dull-witted fellow.

Shouldering and back-to-back, we board a single reed raft; for one who gazes upon the ocean, it is difficult to regard it as mere water. As for the Dragon Kings competing in wealth, I compete with them.
Poor; without spending a single coin, he can command ghosts (Tianru Ze).
A tattered robe held up before the sun—whose eyes possess pupils? Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all contained within the point of a single needle (Huiweng Ming).
Seizing the mist and grasping the clouds, he vainly acts in madness; suddenly, upon level ground, the waves overturn like a river. From what venerable one has he come, and from where?
Within the sound of a finger-snap, he immediately surrenders. (Liaonan Yu)
Neither dwelling in the human realm nor in the heavens, he mostly stays by mountains and by waters. With a single snap of his fingers, dragons and tigers submit;
at his heels, he does not even spend a cent on straw sandals. (Weian Ran)
Before the tongue has even moved, the literary brilliance is revealed; the five thousand scrolls are completed all at once.
If one says they must wait for the moon to open the volume again, I dare guarantee that by the time of their donkey years, they will still not have reached the end. (Zhuyan Yin)
Master Zhigong let out one cry, searching all over the ground. His heart for benefiting beings was like the hollow of a carpenter’s square.
On the lofty winds of Mount Zhongfu, atop a withered tree, the hungry eagle no longer attempts to repair its precarious nest. (End of the lineage root)
Fenggan mounted the tiger;
once on its back, he could not dismount. Was it perhaps a mistaken deliberation at that time? Sentient beings look up to you for guidance, like children holding lotus flowers;
tell me, with what will you provide the decisive direction? (Zhiguanhui)
Master Fu did not lodge this body in the Twin Trees; instead, he stirred up dust and grime in the land of Liang.
Had it not been for the Elder Zhigong at that time, he too would have departed as a sorrowful man of the land. (Xuedou Xian)
Clad in tattered rags, as cold as a fragment of drifting cloud; feet in morning sandals, head crowned with a cap.
To make the three houses return to a single track—though one may knead sand, it will never form a ball. (Xiaowen Kan).
Neither Confucian, nor Daoist, nor yet Chan; his fabricated practice is truly pitiable.
He has wasted a lifetime with three matters unresolved, even now more than eight hundred years have passed. (One-Nap Jie)
The Baguī of Chángtīng is a madman on the wind-swept heights; dragging his staff, he turns his head—waiting for whom? He says, "That person has been here all along;
you must know there is a time to turn back" (Tiānmù Lǐ).
Patting his back and begging for money is a leakage; turning one's head and twisting one's brain is to obscure the true mechanism.
Alas, in the bustling marketplace no one recognizes him; he returns alone, carrying his cloth bag upon his shoulder. (Zhu’an Guang)
Carrying a black-lacquered staff and a cloth bag, he turns around and forgets the Suddhavasa Heaven;
heedless of the heavy burden on his shoulder, he still seeks a single coin from those he meets. (Zhongfeng Edition)
Leaning on his cloth bag, he smiles faintly; half like one who is dull-witted, half like one who is mad.
Seeing you in such a state, with no coming or going, when will you attain Buddhahood? Wait for the year of the donkey (Qianyan Chang).
On a single sandbar, the autumn moon vanishes into the mist; on both banks, cold forests hang with moss and vines.
Day after day, Maitreya Buddha descends to be born; he alone deceives Jiang Mahā (the Han River).
A cloth bag slung across his shoulders, a staff held at the head; bare-chested and barefoot, he knows no shame.
Piteously, forgetting his way back to the inner court, he wanders instead among men into the lower streams. (Yue-weng Jiu)
Lowering his flower crown, he departs from Tuṣita; with a smiling face, he meets everyone everywhere with earnest kindness.
Even the cloth bag must be cast aside entirely; traveling alone, one becomes light and carefree. (Master Yunmen)

Carrying a staff and a cloth bag, he wanders through the dust of the mortal world. How could one ever perceive the reality of this matter? Consciousness of karma is vast and boundless, lacking any foundation;
unaware, one does not know whom to laugh at when opening one's mouth. (The Cause of the Great Dream)
A single coin to beg for—whose poverty would it save? Amidst the vast expanse of dust, who is truly kin? Your own stingy purse you cannot let go;
yet you open your mouth again to laugh at whom? (Ji’ān Dà)
The indolent Ran-can knows only that the yam is sweet over a fire of dung; he does not recognize the fresh purple-clay seal of the silver hook.
Having no remaining strength to wipe away cold tears, how could he have the leisure to face worldly people? (Hong Juefan)
Hanshan and Shide sweep away the moonlight of a thousand autumns before the altar; beneath the pines, they finish their five-character verses.
All failures and shortcomings are completely encompassed; the moon over Mount Wutai shines upon Mount Emei (and Shaoshi).
A single smile as the two brothers gaze at one another; their faces are like tigers, their hair is matted with dust. Who knows who can harmonize with these startling words?
Sing them for the ten thousand phenomena of the universe to hear. (Liaoyan Yu)
A single phrase cannot be written. The paper is dragged down and the brush is gripped fast. I now lend you strength at the wrist;
move it and the clear sky will instantly burst into wind and rain. (Qianyan Changsi)
Holding a single broom in one's hand, the dust of the great earth arises day after day; the more one sweeps, the more there is, and one never ceases.
Let it go, and naturally the universe is pure.
Meeting face-to-face, the smile has not yet been realized; this ready-made phrase rests upon the tip of the brush. In every word written here, past and present are ground together;
I only fear that the *bānyǎo* plant cannot endure the autumn.

The sands within the oceans of the worlds of the ten directions; the flowers in the eyes of all Buddhas and sentient beings—how can a single bamboo tube, so small in size, contain such a multitude of dregs?
"A single bald broomstick so large! To an onlooker, it cannot help but become a subject of ridicule. I urge you not to waste your energy;
let go of all worldly dust and return home. (Daiweng Yue)
Four sleepers pick up [the staff] and Hanshan laughs without ceasing; Fenggan rides a tiger to pursue Lüqiu. Now, as before, they form a group;
were it not for karmic debts, they would not gather under one roof (Xiaoweng Kan).
Fenggan, Shide, and Hanshanzi—these three have toppled the great hairless beast. Joining their fires and joining their heads, they dream together;
unaware that the bright moon has ascended the high peak (Xutang Yu).
The First Patriarch steered his solitary boat ten thousand miles across raging waves; his long pole was intended to haul in the golden tortoise.
He cast two lines in succession with no news at all; in vain he came and struck out once—how regrettable! (Tianmu Li).
A powerful general does not know how to whistle with his lips or gnash his teeth; how could barbarian speech ever confuse the Chinese?
If King Liang’s skin still possessed blood, he surely would have driven them away across the shifting sands.
An old *gǔzhā* tree coming ten thousand li from the West, He did not follow the rules of conduct as he crossed the shifting sands.
Struck by another, his front teeth were knocked out; The mute man clearly experienced the bitter sting. (Oran’s Verse)
The treasures stored above the Han-yuan Hall are beyond reckoning; sitting before the peaks of Shaoshi, there is a cause for this.
Had he met with a murderous hand at that time, he would not have burdened ordinary people for a thousand ages (Fuan).

The thief’s body has not yet been revealed, yet his crimes are fully manifest. He has stirred up the Western Region (India) until it boils like hot soup. With an iron cangue upon his neck, there is no way to escape;
he has come instead to the land of the East to divide the plunder. (No door opens.)
Traveling east and west until the skin of one's feet is worn through—how could there ever have been a separate transmission outside the teachings? Let you have it:
though a single flower may bloom into five petals, a fine son never spends his father’s money. (Yuan’an Yu)
The Second Patriarch pondered: "What is the use of seeking peace of mind? To find peace of mind is to make the body suffer.
At the place where he stood amidst three feet of deep snow, who can be said to be the man within the snow? (Foguo Bai)
Seeking the mind, there is no place to rest; one must chew to pieces a glowing mass of iron.
Even if you were to open your eyes with prideful spirit, how could it compare to not being deceived by the Old Barbarian? (Dahui Zonggao)
On level ground, a heap of bones rises from nowhere; one carries this living body to be buried in the snow.
Even if you were to exhaust both skin and marrow, bring me back my mother-born arm! (Yinshan Can)

The Third Patriarch’s whole body was itchy, so he asked someone to scratch him. Though they scratched deep into his bones until his body grew weary, with one stroke the person hit the mark, and all the places that had been itchy throughout his life vanished at once. (Shui-an) 1.
To realize that the nature of sin is originally non-existent—once severed, how could it ever revive again? It was originally but a chronic ailment from before;
it was forcibly plastered over by having one's arm cut off (Chijue Chong).
The entire body is but illness, bone adhering to skin; throughout the world, no one recognizes him.
Even if one were to fully repent for all roots of transgression, one would still have lost both eyebrows.
The Fourth Patriarch explained the deep pit to attain freedom; carrying it alone and playing with it, he displayed his elegance. Unwarrantedly, he implicated the old man who planted pine trees;
his karmic consciousness remains vast and boundless, refusing to rest. (Nu’an Zhao)
Lay down the dull mattock for planting pines; with hands clasped at the chest, what do you seek? Originally there is not a single dharma worthy of transmission;
in vain you have forged a mortal enmity at Huangmei (Tianmu Li).
Purple clouds fly from the peak of Pòtóu; having thrice declined the heavenly decree, he grows old in the emerald mists.
Although this surplus stock has no further use, it should not be handed over to a small child (Mù of Shàoshì).

The Fifth Patriarch, with his hair turning white, descended from the green mountains; after seven years of return, he had exchanged his former appearance. While the man has grown young, the pine has grown old;
from this point on, right and wrong shall fall upon the world of men (Foguo Bai).
Having planted seeds across a thousand mountains with no empty space left, a single branch still hangs from the side of the mattock.
Had it not been for the deception of Zhou’s daughter, how could the robe and bowl have reached you to be transmitted? (Zhongfeng Ben)
For many years his livelihood has been by the pickaxe; ten thousand pines lock in the emerald mist. The dream is shattered at Caoxi—the world is vast;
returning again, he is not worth half a coin. (Shaoshi Mu)
I planted several hundred pine trees with my own hands; when hungry I eat, when thirsty I drink, remaining as I am.
Without cause, I borrowed a path to meet you again, yet I have been made out to be part of the lineage chart of the Patriarchs (Ret’ung-hyu).
The Sixth Patriarch at Huangmei made a mistaken transmission in the middle of the night; as soon as he caught a glimpse of a star, he began to act recklessly.
At the head of Dayu Ridge, he left behind a great heap of filth, which has brought defilement upon his descendants for generations. (Muan Yong)
The seven hundred eminent monks gathered for the Chan assembly; their eyes emptied the four seas, their noses reaching toward heaven.
If Huangmei had been without partiality or crookedness, what robe or bowl would there have been for you to transmit? (Chijue Chong)
Carrying a bundle of firewood, the eyes are empty before them; entering the road of Huangmei, one’s skill is already exhausted.
Having sold off the branches and leaves of the forest, there is no ground left in Lingnan to plant the spring breeze (Zhongfeng Ben).
Bosuṅ was originally a man from Lingnan; though called with the ten characters, nine were not true. Having stolen his robes and bowl, he fled through the night;
even now there is nowhere for him to lay his whole body down. (T’aean Hyŏng)
Lanrong sits atop the Oxhead Peak, locked within heavy clouds; sitting alone in vast stillness, he entrusts his body to this state. A hundred birds do not come as spring passes by again;
one knows not who is the person who reaches the hermitage. (By Mingjue Xian)
Purple qi mingles and permeates the white clouds; having met the Master of the School, the path from delusion was pointed out. The hundred birds carrying flowers are left in vain lamentation;
they do not see the former master within the hermitage (Yang Woei).

Flowers fall and flowers bloom as the hundred birds lament; the things before the hermitage remain, yet the master is no more. Though the Peach Blossom Spring is but a few feet away, there is no place to find it;
with a single oar and a fisherman’s cloak, he returns in solitude. (Zhang Wujin)
Catching the horse by its bridle, he rides away; empty-handed, he returns on foot. Before the path to the silent hermitage, the flower-bearer bird does not fly.
(Tieshan Ren). Pao-tuo of the Broken Oven.
Calamity and fortune, majesty and severity do not manifest their own spiritual power. To whom are these leftover cups and cold roast meats offered?
Since you departed, there has been no news; yet the village elder still beats the sacrificial drum. (Fuyan Yuan)

Relying on the hearth as a spirit, yet it is not self-enlightened; where the traces of the spirit are severed, there is but a heap of dust. The village elder does not come to beat the sacrificial drum;
striking the right cause while departing from the heterodox is a different kind of spring. (Fodeng Xun)
On a clear night at Mount Meng, he received the robe of Old Lu; I hate to death that old, ancient wraith of Huangmei. He said, "When chasing someone, do not chase them so hard.
Indeed, he fell from his rank once and returned home. (Xuexi Jie)
The bird’s nest blows away the feathers; the red sun is high at midday. Because King Zhao was fond of swords, the people of the entire state wore blades. (Zhenjing Wen)
There is something of the Buddha-dharma; within words, the net is cast. Where the cloth-hair is blown up, it remains as before, not leaving its nest (Wuzhun Fan).
Reaching old age and forgetting artifice is the bird’s nest;
atop the West Lake, misty vines drape the shore. When the cloth-hair is blown up, there is not much more to it.
Son, with iron eyes and copper pupils, what can be done?
(Baofeng Qian) There has never been a trace of axe or hatchet; let him remain a man of his own kind, a mountain dweller.
Those who pointlessly sprout branches outside the joints invite calamity from out of the blue to fall upon their own door. (Xiaoru Yuan)
Mazu’s “This very mind is Buddha” was mere idle chatter; “Neither mind nor Buddha” became even more unbearable.
With eighty-four men each having their own distinct gateways, when has there ever been a single one who was a true fellow-student? (Chu-shih Qi)
Thank you, O graceful lady before me; you well might disturb the dream of King Xiangwang.
My Zen mind has already become like a willow catkin soaked in mud, following the eastern wind as it drifts wildly up and down. (Lü yu jiao)

Baizhang once took an ancient mirror and polished it again; only after wiping it clean did he realize that the "cracking" and the "pecking" were simultaneous. After one shout, the sound in his ears lasted for three days;
until now, he sits alone atop Mount Daxiong. (Fóxìng Tái)
The wild duck flies high and alights upon the distant marsh; it deceives people until their noses ache from twisting them.
When one reflects on such a thing, there is no flavor to be found; one cannot laugh, yet one cannot cry. (Chu Shi Qi)
Master Pang has exhausted his worldly life and sells a bamboo sieve; he seeks advantage among those who snatch by stealth.
Look at his skill—such as this—and yet he says, "With an empty mind, I have passed the imperial examination and returned" (Biefeng Yin).
Zhaozhou, for no reason at all, brought up the seven-pound robe. How many practitioners of Chan have applied their minds to investigate it?
They all make their nests in Qingzhou, unaware that the spring colors lie in Jiangnan.
Puhua presented the truth mistakenly within the assembly at Panshan; turning a somersault, he makes people laugh to death.
He further joins forces with the "white-handed thief"—a blind donkey whose eyes truly lack any sinews. (Tianmu Li)
Shaking the wooden gong and ringing the bell, he willfully sells his eccentricities; at the Hall of Great Compassion, he attends a village feast. Let the wooden pagoda of Heyang be left unaltered;
what does it matter to him as a pair of worn-out straw sandals on the street? (Xiaowen Kan).
The Boatman’s single stroke across the mouth [of the boat] fully embodies both killing and giving life; nodding three times, he then reaches for the heavens.
To this day, his elegance endures through the ages—whom can it be said that he capsized his boat at Huating? (Fozhao Guang)
Three inches away from the hook, he snaps the oar once; a hundred thousand pores shiver with cold.
Although it was entrusted by his own two hands, it must be for him to nod his head himself (the lineage of Wuji).
For over thirty years at Yaoshan, how could the livelihood of a ghost-household ever be transmitted?
Had it not been for Old Jia Shan at that time, you would have had to patiently endure until the boat was torn asunder (Qingxi Che).
Linji and Huangbo paid no heed at all to the blows from their staffs; on the rapids of Gaoyuan, they mistakenly engaged in deliberation. Endlessly they planted thorns everywhere;
the Buddha-dharma originally lacks even a single inch of length. (Fozhao Guang)
Calamity and fortune have no gate; one summons them from within oneself. Three times he suffered the painful blows of a staff upon his donkey-waist.
Alas for this resentment that ruins nations and destroys families—through ten thousand ages, the spring breeze shall not blow it away. (Tianmu Li)
Prime Minister Pei supplemented the seasoning of the soup, with every ingredient prepared first. This ancient Buddha has passed through many years;
since Huangbo bestowed his name upon him, his nostrils have, for no reason, lost one half. (Tianmu Li)
Deshan went personally to Longtan and did not see the dragon; the paper lamp was blown out, and before his eyes all was empty.
With a single white staff that overturns heaven and earth, he extinguished the Dharma lineage of the West-coming Bodhidharma. (Fozhao Guang)
In Dongshan’s Phoenix Pavilion, the incense has grown cold; the moonlight is intimate. In the ancient temple of lapis lazuli, his entire body appears.
Vast and boundless is the universe with its countless people, yet one who can transmit this blue-and-white lineage has not yet been seen. (Xiaoweng Kan)

At Stone Creek (Shishuang), the moon sets in the third watch and the two mountains shine bright. The ancient path stretches far, covered in growing moss. When the golden lock shakes, no hand can intrude;
within the heart of the blue waves, the jade hare constantly moves. (Touzi Qing)
Touzi’s waters flow from Kunlun, their waves continuous; heaven is high and the earth vast, with exquisite forests and peaks. As the meditation seat slightly lowers, clouds and mountains vanish;
both mundane and sagely traces are gone, as seas and mountains turn cold.
Jiashan disperses the assembly and wanders far to the edge of the sea; A series of painful blows, both parties are wrong. Father south, son north—where can they be found?
The moon is cold as the fisherman’s song falls upon the fishing pier. (Tianmu Li)
The "One Jewel of Zhongyuan" from Xinghua has its origins. It pressed the King until he drew back his head-covering.
Had there been no "blue and white eyes" at this point, who would have dared to offer a light response when the opportunity arose? (Xuexi Yi)

At Mount Cao, the golden casket’s incense has faded and the night-watchmen’s clepsydra drags on. Deep within the jade palace, purple moss grows. The high heavens hold a moon that illuminates a thousand gates;
upon the Great Way, no one is there, and I walk alone. (Shifan Xing)
Nine peaks capped with horns, a body of beastly fur; cold ashes and withered wood, dust in the eyes. He laughs at those who lack hands to scale the dragon’s scales;
they possess nothing but one intimate move at the moment of departure (Danxia Zhen).
The reason Xuefeng went to Dongshan nine times; why he still hesitated upon his three ascents of Touzi.
Since the snow covered Mount Aoshan, the single peak of Xianggu has remained green to this day. (Huian Guang)
Yuan Sha’s dripping drops are all over his body as festering pus. On the fishing boat, he manifests his family style. People of the time look only at the fishing line;
they do not see the reeds facing the red smartweed. (Tianyi Hui)

Fenyang sets out cups and wine to offer sacrifice to his ancestors; there is nothing further of primordial mystery to transmit to others. The ten wisdoms of the same reality distinguish beauty from ugliness;
though the face remains, the skull is pierced through (the lineage of Wuji).
Yangqi’s house is old and its four walls are dilapidated; snowflakes leap upon the bed. Yet he still possesses a leisurely spirit, laughing aloud at the white clouds (Dachuan Ji).
Celestial robes flutter as the tide turns; the moon shines bright upon the cold shore. The lives of father and son follow divergent paths. Only one who can break his home can truly make a living;
why worry about letting a whole boat of fish slip away? (Yuedang Chang)
The Five Patriarchs, Yuan, Yangqi, Lüzzi, and Baiyun Guan—kicking and stomping clearly, yet all so casual. A destitute ghost of one hundred and twenty catties carries it on his back;
with one shoulder he bears it to Dongshan (Xiaoweng Kan).
Furong Kai:
Incense from the imperial burner within the hibiscus curtains; the twelve towers divide the coolness of the forbidden gardens. When night falls at the Water Palace, wind and moon are still;
by the shores of Kunming Lake, mandarin ducks dance. (Lingtíng Tǐng)
Yuanwu recognized the sound of "Little Yu" being called out repeatedly; in a hurry he opened his eyes, and the cock had already crowed.
From this point on, Dongshan’s secret signal was extinguished; the lineage has now become as cold as ice (Xiaowen Kan).
The authentic pulse of Ying’an and Yangqi was a single, precarious thread; at Yangyu Hermitage, he specially bestowed the robe. In the end, Huqiu became father and son;
in the final reckoning, uncle and nephew did not carry on the lineage. (Dongshi bows twice.)
The methods of our late master, Miam, were enough to bite through pigs and dogs; how could one ever repay him for his observance of the precepts? That broken sand pot is the True Dharma Eye;
it does not hinder one from painting a cat after the model.
The Dragon Pond Traveler’s Diagram:
The lamp-flower bursts and severs the iron ox’s hoof; treading across Jambudvīpa, he enters Mount Wutai. The peach blossoms bloom on the warm waves of Xiaoyan;
with a single straw hat, he goes and returns (Tianli Zhen).
At Tiantong, for a thousand years, bare white bones lie exposed within a copper coffin. Even Buddhas and Patriarchs can hardly look upon it with a direct eye.
A chilling wind of raw stench blows across the great earth; to casually touch it makes one’s hair stand on end (Hongjue Man).
His belly full of ignorance, he has no outlet for his anger; whenever he meets someone, he wishes he could kill them.
Those who recognize what is beneficial and harmful should look closely: is this truly a Bodhisattva, or is it a rākṣasa? (Daiweng Yue)
Qingshan scrapes the marrow from empty space and seizes the embryo of the pillar. Weyin ate the staff; he was destined to suffer calamity.
Striking at the third watch by day, the true lamp illuminates the world as the clouds part. (Tianli Zhen)

Yunmen Cheng takes up the straw stalks; they surpass the sharp blade of a spirit. Killing or giving life according to the occasion, he never relaxes his grip. He turns the Mount Qin upside down and returns home;
the fragrance of the jade plum wafts through the wind of the Ye River. (Position within the rank, the tally.)
At Nanjian, the staff-head falls like rain and the shout like thunder; Linji’s collapsing banner is alone revived.
With an iron heart and liver and a smiling face—how many can truly capture this master in a portrait? (Daoweng Yue)
"Master Lou, since you have no mind, I shall leave it at that. This body has neither joy nor sorrow; when hungry, one eats, and when weary, one sleeps.
Let the falling flowers follow the water as it flows. (Upādhyāya Fu)
How pitiable is the little mussel amidst the piles of spirit-money paper! As soon as its foul mouth opens, it creates a tangle of complications.
It has squandered the meager livelihood of the ghostly realm; even now, no one travels to the ancient temple (Dongshan Yuan).
Picking shrimp and crayfish by the river, the river wind blows cold against my face. I do not understand the meaning of that which comes from the West;
I push out the wine table and tray. (Yin Shangzi)
The Nirvana of the Venerable Fu, its partiality and correctness, and its circulation—these do not escape the single laugh of a Zen practitioner.
For a thousand ages, the path beneath Pingshan Hall remains as it was, where cold horns stir the mournful wind. (Xiaoweng Kan)

The clear waves flow beneath the Yellow Ox Bridge day and night; at the bridgehead, the spring scenery turns ever more serene and secluded. How marvelous! What matter is there that cannot be protected?
Why must one ride an ox while still seeking another ox? (Muzhou of Shaoshi)
Master Yushan:
At the top of a hundred-foot pole, he tramples the bridge through. Where the void bulges, the water and sky are concave. Since antiquity, countless people have suffered this fall;
it is not only you, O Kalyāṇamitra, who have met with this mishap. (Beijian Jian)

When Marshal Li saw Weishan’s dilapidated wall and the mud he was applying himself, he did not realize that an official was approaching behind him. Observe how he turned his ceremonial tablet to pass it on;
it was enough to make the void laugh until its cheeks were full (Liaoyuan Yu).
Huyin Jisong, following sounds and chasing forms at will, roams freely. He simply wants people to recognize him and then leave it at that. Having received his alms-money, where does he go?
With a grand air, he goes straight up to the wine shop on the tower. (By Tianmu Li)
Master Lingzhao sank his livelihood into the Xiang River; he left you to toil on the street selling ladles.
It was not that poverty brought suffering upon his son; how many can truly understand this heart? (Wuji Pai)
Unwilling to remain within the inner chambers, he enters the marketplace with his person. There is no place to sell the colander;
one can only weep to the blue heavens (Wunian Fan).
Grasping it in hand and carrying it on his shoulder into the market, who will buy this colander to scoop up the wind? It is better to smear red earth upon an ox.
Milk. Turning his steps home, he coaxed his grandfather (Grandfather Dai Yue).
Ling Xingpo, young in her conduct, leaned alone against the tower; daughters from a hundred households sought her hand, yet she refused to board the floating cup.
The eye. Looking into a mirror, one sees that the hair has turned entirely white (Laughing Old Man Kan).
A pig’s head is held up by a pig’s head; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot reach it. If someone asks what this is like: fat enters through the mouth (Gulin Maoer).
The shrimp is dredged from the water; it is brought forth in the open light. The three realms are vast and boundless;
for the sake of the shrimp’s offspring, Zhang Guolao rides his donkey backward.
How many people are there in all the world? None can equal this old fellow. It is not that he rides backward on a donkey; it is simply that he loves to look back over his shoulder. Self-praise:
His appearance is ancient and his form is sparse as he leans upon a cane staff. He is clearly depicted as Subhūti. Having mastered emptiness, he does not permit himself to depart from sound.
Colors: Like hearing foxes and monkeys wailing under the moon (Cheng-gong Zheng).
Rain washes the tender, pale-red peach blossoms; wind shakes the light, pale-green willow filaments. Within the shadows of white clouds, strange rocks are revealed;
amidst the luster of green waters, ancient trees appear new (Chan-ti Zhao).
Seated, he cuts off the foremost peak of Nanmin; the host of demons lose heart and the tigers hide their tracks.
Sometimes a single shout stirs the spring thunder, capable of forcing a living snake to transform into a live dragon. (Changling and Zhuo)
His face is rugged and his ears hang down to his cheeks; when he is at ease, it is like the Buddha’s smile.
Do not let him touch the bag of ignorance, or hundreds of monsters and thousands of demons will all come forth.
The congee is too thin when sitting for the midday meal; the bed is narrow when lying down first. Deaf, he loves loud voices; with blurred vision, he requires large characters.

(Yùquán Hào) For many years I have searched through the dusty world, yet among a hundred arts, I possess not even one skill. Since ancient times, the Jiangnan region has been a nest of mountains and waters;
how could it give birth to such a monk? (Zhūān Guī)
There is no awakening in Zen meditation. One’s literacy has its limits. His eyes are triangular, like those of a sorrowful foreigner from Mount Yen-shan;
his face is wrinkled in a hundred folds, like an old woman of Chao drinking vinegar. With a single stroke he rises far above all quarters; I dare say that rice is made from grain. (Cang-sou Zhen)

The primordial barrier of the ancients was not broken, yet the primordial barrier broke of itself; the hollow mortar of the present moment was not shattered, yet the hollow mortar shattered of itself.
The robe of Vulture Peak has rotted away, and the discourse of West Hill has left no transmission. (Dachuan Ji)
One kills a person with a blade, yet the human mind does not die. One kills a person with bare hands, yet the human mind does not die.
When all skillful means are exhausted, the human mind dies of its own accord (Hyōnggwam Gung).
A spoon cannot lift this rustic fellow; there is not a single speck of literary refinement in his breast.
He once pried open the very bones of empty space, and his ill repute has won him a full measure across the rivers and lakes (Wuyongquan).
A stubborn nature has never been compliant with worldly sentiments; when have I ever fabricated wonders to fish for empty fame?
Holding aloft a single string of one hundred and eight wood nut beads, I have exchanged the eyes of thousands of great men. (From *Jianxin fu*)
Intoxicated and arrogant, his wild ways never cease; with the bright moon upon his staff, he reigns supreme in the southern region.
Who can understand his shifting turns and steps? Snow covers the reeds amidst the twelve towers. (Jidian)

Throughout my life, I have sought only to speak of the Zen of sheer blindness. How can one dig into the earth and hope to find the sky? Dwelling in the mountains in these three places, my poverty has reached the very marrow of my bones;
I have nothing at all—neither robe nor bowl—to pass on to others. (Dai’an)
*Zadu hai*, Scroll One;
*Zadu hai*, Scroll Two.
Re-edited by the Berlin-based successor to the Patriarchs, the Śramaṇa Xingyin, in the Capital.
When Li Zu-xiang asked Huan-zhong, "What is the essence of prajñā?
he answered according to the form and following the sound; after his words, there was not even a needle’s point of opening for further inquiry.
On the ground, beneath the eaves, red rain falls as fallen blossoms drift down.
Outside the Faji Gate, ranks upon ranks of the army of blades approach. The Master has not yet fully extinguished his breath; had he been beheaded into three pieces at that time—
Segment. How could one obtain to be buried alive once again? (Xiangtan Yong).
Yunmen and Muzhou exerted all the strength in their arms; to betray righteousness and forget kindness is utterly perverse. If you wish for excellence, do not have covered it from the start.
Covered. Following the teaching, for a thousand ages the corpses remain exposed (Zhe-weng Yan).

With a single word, Changqing cut off all paths; Beidu-tuo remains so for ten thousand ages, the green of Mount Zhi never wearing thin. I dare ask: regarding that year when the curtain was not [drawn]—
Rolling it up, one does not know what affairs in the world are like (Stone Creek Moon).
One does not understand what the Three Augusts and Five Emperors truly are. Having endured twenty years of hardship, even the entire Great Canon of Teachings cannot contain it.
Attained. To this day it lies in disarray before the Milk Peak (Xiangtan Yong).
The sun sinks into the wild waters, the treasury of radiance; orchids bloom on the spring mountains, the heart-mind of the ancient Buddha.
There is no need to bow your head in bitter searching; every joint and bone is pure gold (Mozongben).
Celestial robes and the Vairambha winds blow down the tangled vines and stakes; they raise high the great Dharma banner of Shao Yang. It cannot be hidden before the Yellow Crane Tower;
how many times do the shadows of wild geese fall upon the cold river? (Ji Shí Péng)
Asaṅga gazes longingly at Mount Wutai, his thoughts lingering; under the bright sun and clear sky, he is bewitched by ghosts.
There is one most painful aspect that is difficult to comprehend: when drinking tea from a glass cup (Xiangtan Yong).
When Bao Ning took his vow before Lubaofeng, once a word has been uttered, it is as hard to recall as a galloping horse.
Buried alive three feet deep in the soil of Jinling, the Way did not pass through him, and indeed he did not return. (By Mingji Jun)

The teachings of Mingjiao were as his words and as his practice, brilliant as the sun and stars; he stood like a solitary pillar turning back the surging waves. By the lake, how could one find a rock to polish?
I shall simply carve this "Eulogy for the Venerable Monk" as an inscription. (By Penglai Jishi)
The Great Awakened One is locked in cold mist deep within the ivy-clad vines; a single stupa towers loftily before the myriad phenomena. Though fire be set, it cannot consume the dragon-brain bowl;
Mount Mao’s peak soars high, yet does not reach the blue heavens. (By Boting Wen)
The great wisdom bamboo pointer, three feet long—how hard it is to repay its debt. Blood splatters the empty mountains as the grasses and trees turn autumnal.
This is not merely one's own kin and bone; one ought to flee a thousand miles away to a mountain state (Penglai). (Jieshi Peng)
The true sound of Hongzhi does not resound from the peak of Mount Wutai; the events before Mount Yangguang are truly lamentable.
An old cypress lies prostrate in the waves as its cold shadow stirs—whom can it call its companion? Who says it cannot come alone? (By Mingji Jun)

Sti-tian takes advantage of the clear weather to come harvest the rice in the fields. He circumambulates three times the stūpa at the edge of the clouds. The bamboo draws in the pure breeze, and the pines bear the dew.
Though his form and countenance are slight, his speech is abundant (the extreme of folly is supreme wisdom).
Dried-up meditation by the ancient stream before Mount Qingfeng; above the eaves of the house, there is no more sky.
Now, reflecting with a cold heart, I tear the spring clouds apart to make paper money. (Yugu Zhi)
He paid homage at the Patriarch’s Stupa,
the Avataṃsaka Stupa,
the Horse Stable before the mountain, the Puguang Hall, the ox pen outside the gate, and the Site of Perfect Enlightenment. On this same day, fifty-three people [performed the same rites].
The burial. As Shanzai ran, his feet grew sores (Ying’an Hua).
He paid homage at the true stupa of the Sixth Patriarch;
at Caoxi, a single drop of water is itself the spiritual source. It flows into the vast ocean where waves splash the heavens. How many fish and dragons vie to undergo transformation!
Transformation. The single stream at its source remains refreshingly clear (Han-shan Qing).
Sending off Master Xin to pay homage at the ancestral stupa of Da Mei:
"Mind is Buddha" is a tiger leaping from a cliff; "Neither mind nor Buddha" is a bird caught in a net. Do not treat this cooking cloth with indifference.
Unfurl [the mat]. Beneath the knees of a man lies gold (Shuzhong Yun).
Accompanying the Venerable Fuku to pay homage at the Patriarch’s Stupa:
the Patriarch’s Stupa is made of *hulun* bricks; it stands only by the mountains and by the waters. Circumambulate and pay homage to each one from beginning to end.
Pervasive. The straw sandals remain as before; he personally returns the money (Shiwu Yong).

Paying respects at the ancestral pagodas of the various patriarchs of Shuanghua, ten thousand years pass in a single thought, while dust arises from his mouth. Like withered wood and cold ashes, he lives yet remains buried. Eight hundred eminent men cannot support him.
Arising, yet to this day there is no plan for emerging (Lingxi Yu).
Paying respects at the ancestral stupa of Shishuang Yuan, the Lion of Xihe has no den.
Treading through my straw sandals, he has deceived me into coming; there is only the Frost Flower Pond.
The moon’s cold light shines upon the desolate terrace through the ages.
At Mingzhao’s stupa, the stiff wind-head has long been perverse; returning once more to the warm chamber, he buries himself alive, causing his traces to endure for a thousand ages.
Traces. You have come in vain to eat the white rice of Luoshan (Pengl).
Deep vines and short creepers, with pagodas piled one upon another; the Dragon known as "The One-Eyed" is likely he.
Setting down the earthenware tray and standing with hands clasped—back then, you mistakenly killed the short *śrāmaṇera* (Guzhizhe Er).

The skull of the one who honored the Way of Xian was originally possessed of its own numinous light. What has Xuedou ever done but emptied his bowels? He has cut off the three-inch tongue of the old woman;
to this day, the two swords lean against the heavens, long and vast.
Traveling to visit the stupa of Chan Master Gushan, I have traversed ten li of pines along the western slopes of Xiang. Arriving at the gate, I stand still and gaze upon the various peaks;
there is no place to find traces of Master Chong’s deeds, yet in the spring mud beneath the courtyard, the tracks of a tiger are visible. (Hong Juefan)
I pay homage at the Stone House Pagoda of the Southern Patriarch Huanglong, where steep layers cover the heap of bones. As the three folds of his robe are unfurled, his smiling countenance opens.
Lightly wishing to strike the horn of Huanglong, suddenly the mountain torrents overflow and the peaks topple over (Gumei You).
Visiting the Stupa of Chan Master Zhun:
Born of the same lineage, yet dying of different lineages; revealing the full mechanism, who is first and who is last? This one phrase, muddled and indistinct, is difficult to split apart;
I bestow it all at once for my descendants to transmit. (Hong Juefan)
Seeing Off Master Yuan on His Pilgrimage to Pay Homage at the Stupa of Patriarch Wuzhun:
He is a descendant of Yuanzhao; from afar he has come to pay his respects and sweep away the dust from the stupa.
In days past, the fire for smelting gold was tempered with both gentle and fierce flames; even now, its warmth remains like spring. (Yuejiang Yin)
I pay my respects at the stupa of the Patriarch Huqiu Long;
from ancient times to the present, the atmosphere of Yunyan has been majestic. Smoke and fire rise from a thousand households, and the morning pounding of grain resounds.
Who would have known that the "Sleeping Tiger" of those days claimed this foremost peak of Eastern Wu for himself? (By Yanwen of Ruohan)
Three times supervising the construction of Songyuan’s stupa, Huangya Qiao reached the heavens. Where on Vulture Peak was there a direct transmission?
Knowing for oneself that from beginning to end there is no point of contact, he offered a single *doulou* incense stick before the stupa (as Tianmu did).
For over twenty years I have dwelt in the "gate of death" at the ancestral stupa on High Peak; how could my soul and dreams ever fall upon the green mountains?
At the moment of departure, there is no place to hide these white bones; I cast them onto the tongue of the Golden-Haired One (Śākyamuni). (Zibai Ke)

The image of the late Emperor Jianwen was enshrined with secret plots to end the resentment against Yao Guangxiao; the old Buddha once transmitted [the teachings] to Yang Yingneng. Gathering up the remaining pieces of the chessboard, who would claim victory or defeat?
Within Jambudvīpa, there are two monks. (Orthodox Dharma, Part Two)
Action leaves no trace; dwelling has no gate. Only the images installed in the empty mountains remain. Disciples, do not be startled by these precious royal robes;
from the beginning, where has there ever been one who is not honored?
The Eastern Old Man’s pagoda:
when the tiger was three days old, its breath swallowed an ox. Who can raise a son like Sun Zhongmou?
With four eaves of an old house and heaven above, this heart feels ashamed upon reaching Hangzhou. (Yutang Yi)
Līduàn’s Patriarch’s Stūpa:
"On the front of Qianzhàng Rock, he once suffered humiliation; father and son did not transmit the true wondrous secret.
The tiny gnat raises its voice, and the great earth, mountains, and rivers are a single expanse of snow. (Liújíqiān)
Ritual at the Stupa of Ancestor Xixian:
Nine Cauldrons once teetered on a single thread of peril; The Golden Mountain fills the land, its stupa towering high. The Imperial Court’s Shengzong visited it three times in person;
Throughout the realm, his descendants have all received his grace. (Daoweng Yue)
Showing his disciples:
"We have lived together from the beginning, yet you do not know my name. We proceed together spontaneously, just as we are. Even the sages of antiquity could not recognize me;
how could ordinary people in their haste possibly name me? (Shitou Xiqian)
Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real; it is only because they have recognized the spirit from of old.
The root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas—fools call this the "original person" (Changsha Cen).
The dragon’s roar from a withered tree is the true seeing of the Way; the skull, though lacking consciousness, has its eyes first opened.
When joy and consciousness are exhausted, all news and traces are gone; how can one distinguish the clear within the turbid? (Cao Shan Ji)
Human sentiment is thick, while the Way-sentiment is faint. The Way employs human sentiment, yet the world does not know it.
There may be human sentiment alone, but no employment of the Way; how much longer can human sentiment endure? (Longya Dun)
Yangqi has just settled in; the walls of his hut are sparse. The entire bed is strewn with snow-white pearls. He shrinks his neck and sighs in secret.
Suddenly he recalls the ancients dwelling beneath the trees. (Yangqi Hui)
This is not a matter brought from the mountain pass; how could it have been transmitted from Chicken Foot Mountain? Since antiquity, all sages and worthies have been like this;
it is not I who am fashioning it for you today. (Ruilu An)
At dawn the sky is clear of clouds and the heavy frost is white; a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks are locked in cold hues. Does the black dragon know or not that it has lost its pearl?
Countless ordinary people suffer the branding of their foreheads. (By Mingjue and Xian)
The gate is closed, yet the years still hasten on. Upon the stone window, rain has gathered moss and ferns. On a single bed, with pillow and mat, I grow old as Vimalakīrti;
From time to time, I see drifting clouds and the solitary moon arrive.
A clay-formed Vajra runs beneath the water; a brush-painted Bodhisattva walks through fire. Though there are eyes upon the crown of the head, they cannot see;
eyebrows two feet long grow beneath the forehead (Baoning Yong).
All who travel the Way know the Gate of Emptiness; only those who arrive realize its flavor is long.
When the mind-ground produces no weeds of idleness, the white-hair light naturally radiates from the body. (Dongshan Yan)
This segment originally has no front or back; one must resolutely and vigorously practice and maintain it. The five vajra-eyes are throughout the entire body;
when the myriad objects of perception come to invade, do not concern yourself with them. (Yuanwu Keqin)
In days of yore, the Great Patriarch of Yangqi displayed his spiritual powers while pulling the plow and dragging the harrow. His descendants go about trailing water and mud;
the tea-kettle and the frying pan are not the same. (Dahui Zonggao)
Swallowing the Buddhas of the three periods in a single gulp—this is truly a hired laborer from my own house. How does this compare to Chan Master Pu, who has no use for anything?
Upon the tip of a single hair, he immediately forgets all artifice.
The green mountains above the river are truly not yet old; The spring colors at the eaves of the house are allowed to unfold slowly. People say the peach blossoms within the caverns are tender;
Yet it is not certain that such branches exist in the human world. (Lung of Huqiu)
Dancing the *Santai* with rapid beats on a precipice; the dead tiger’s startled eyes suddenly open wide.
In a sacred ground, no ordinary weeds grow; indeed, he has personally seen Xiatang (Yuan) arrive.
The courtyard of Shaoshi is as cold as ash; for many years not a single person has come.
If you now understand how to feel shame and remorse, why not take the effort to return here once? (Ying’an Hua)
Five hundred and thirty monasteries with seven hundred monks—donkey jaws and horse chins, detested by all.
Had the various quarters possessed hands capable of ensnaring them, today they would have had no way to reach Jingming.
When casting the line at the head of a rapid torrent, the scarlet-tailed fish still hesitates.
Suddenly leaping forth from within the vast waves, it seizes mist and grasps clouds, making the universe seem low.
Yuantong does not open a pharmacy for the living; he sells nothing but the heads of dead cats. Who knows which one lacks calculation?
Upon eating it, cold sweat flows over their entire bodies (Jiandang Ji).
Sitting in meditation at Nantai, a single burner of incense; all day long, he remains composed, forgetting ten thousand anxieties.
This is not for the sake of stilling the mind or eliminating delusive thoughts; it is simply because there is nothing to deliberate upon. (Nantai An)
When emotional understanding vanishes, the golden screen blinds the eyes; when the mass of doubt is shattered, the ghosts divide the spoils.
When one’s innermost thoughts are spoken of by another, even an iron heart and liver would break with grief. (Oran’s Verse 9)

The conduct of the patched-robed monk is by no means ordinary; the "hair-cutting blade" drawn from its scabbard leaves nothing hidden. Seizing the food and driving the plow, he maintains the true command;
east and west, there is no longer any room for ghosts to divide the spoils.
Darkly scattering mani pearls, they become mere rubble; idly pouring lethal poison, it becomes the finest nectar.
Taking vengeance for kindness by exterminating the Huns—raising one's eyes, no one is a relative; such is the true man.
Standing on tiptoe in isolation and peril, where no grass grows; do not travel heedlessly to places where you might lodge.
With the wind blowing, you open wide your empty mouth to swallow air, sending your entire family down into a pit of fire.

A fierce birth is of a different sort from the village; he evaluates the sages of old and treats later descendants with disdain. Casting off [all constraints] atop a solitary peak, how could he ever be bound?
Within the eye of the staff, it covers heaven and earth.
The blind donkey tending grass needs no reliance; the ancient gate was won with a mere flick of the hand. When the lakes and seas were peaceful and clear, he walked alone;
the merit returned to his inch-long blade as it took the blood of the great whale.
Risking body and life to seek out the enemy; with hot blood spraying against one another, how could they ever stop?
When they finally reach the point where not an inch of land remains, they depart empty-handed, taking possession of the clouds above.
With the strength of his bare bones exhausted, he carries a single plank; wild and crazed, with leprosy-like sores, he raises his eyebrows. His sudden manifestation is difficult to describe or name;
Buddhas and Patriarchs must listen to his commands face-to-face.
A single punch was also struck at the Master. Before victory or defeat is decided, do not let go. He has sacrificed his blind and wretched life;
with a crooked mouth and a flattened nose, he reveals his complete talent.
Swinging on a swing over the water in midwinter; rowing a fishing boat atop a hundred-foot pole. I send word to the assembly of dragons and elephants in both halls:
do not trouble yourselves to dig through the earth to seek the blue sky. (Miam Jie)
In the third month, the partridges cry out south of the Yangtze; people walk upon a brocade map of a hundred flowers.
Without violating the subtle distinction between separation and union, they transmit the news—laughing the blue-eyed barbarian of the Western Heaven to his wits' end.
Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city: by day one wards off the six thieves; by night one remains alert.
When the commander-in-chief of the central army can carry out his orders, peace is achieved without the movement of weapons. (Master Xingkong Anzhu, No. 2)
Eating without plowing and wearing clothes without sericulture; pure and leisurely beyond the mundane world, one finds fulfillment in this sagely age.
Yet, until one has penetrated the pivot of the Patriarch’s barrier, one must still maintain mindfulness and act with expedient skill.
Do not vainly seek complications outside the essential; the source is cut off right here and now.
Every stitch of the embroidered mandarin ducks is perfect—who would be willing to casually cast away a single inch of needle? (Yuet Tang Chang)
Without relying on one's own lot, one must practice Chan; sell off the ancestral fields before the mountain.
Departing empty-handed to establish one’s livelihood—such a fine son never uses his father’s money. (Songyuan Yue)
The Mind-King has passed the imperial examination, yet has not transcended emotion; under the blow of the staff, he takes it up and blinds his own eyes.
Do not say that people at Shaolin do not see: the oriole calls out two or three times from time to time.
The worn-out broom-handle of many years—casually picked up, it establishes the fundamental纲 (guiding principle) of the school. This particular style is naturally unique;
it does not compare to the "Old Eighth" of other quarters.

To see while still being detached from seeing is not true seeing. Returning to the exhaustion of the eight returns, there is nothing further to return to. Leaves fall from the autumn sky, and the mountain’s bones are laid bare.
Who knows who can recognize Old Gautama? (Pō-ān Xiān)
The great earth is gathered up like a grain of millet; ninety days of foot-binding deceives the infant. The seeds of Yangqi leave no inscription on a stele;
at times one plants the hair of a tortoise within the eye (the lineage of Wujie).
We dwell together upon the Panṭa rocks; the waters are distant and the mountains high—there is nothing else.
Only the moon on the mountain peak possesses much sentiment, its shadow shifting onto the steps as night deepens. (Wan’an Rou)
In times of great peace, the clash of arms ceases; along the roads, one hears only the chanting of songs of victory. Reaching this point, one should not lightly remain stationary;
one must further close one's eyes and leap across the Yellow River (Wuyongquan).
The Great Way has neither north nor south; east and west are as level as the palm of a hand. Walking alone without a companion, I bow high to those capable of Lingnan (Dachuanji).
The four elements gather to form the horns of a rabbit; the six sense organs bind the hair of a white tortoise. Within the shadows of foam and flowers, I turn my sinews.
The Dipper appears and disappears over Jambudvīpa; how many times has this occurred? (Zhongfeng edition, vol.
4) When turbid waters are completely cleared, the pearl possesses its power; when the distracted mind is unmoving, the Buddha remains unimpaired. Before one’s eyes, everything is the road home;
there is no need to seek from others the direction back home.
An ancient bronze inscription on a single brazier, a lotus branch—gazing at the cold void, ten thousand cares are cast aside. One can return to one's native land of purity and peace at once;
who would distinguish between the Eastern Land and the Western Heaven?
A single hook-laden moon illuminates the pine hut; outside the gate, no one dwells in the thatched cottage.
The Lord of Transformation, with his billions of purple-gold bodies, does not depart from the present thought—this is to be a fellow practitioner.
I intend to continue the lute-string of Xueyin from years past; I urge myself on further in the practice of the Bodhisattva path. Suddenly, I defecated upon myself and did not realize it was foul;
with wings attached to my straw sandals, I flew up into the heavens. (Yuejiang Yin)
The entire body bears a weight of ten thousand *qun*; a single scroll has been transmitted from a thousand *li* away. How joyful that both the heavy gates have been thoroughly penetrated;
singing aloud, he returns home riding his donkey backward. (Dongshan Yuan)
Without marks and without form, fundamentally silent and vast; where one attempts to lift the eyes, it becomes ever more remote.
Resting quietly upon the meditation cushion with nothing else to do, a single cry of "pó-bǐng-jiao" sounds outside the window. (Lóngxī Wén)
The springtime radiance of the third month has nowhere to be gathered; it is all at once scattered upon the tips of the willow branches.
Alas, one cannot see the face of the spring breeze, yet one watches the withered red petals drift away with the current. (Zhiweng)
Having passed through the Gate of Repaying Kindness, it is difficult to return; facing death at the crossroads, how can one turn back?
If you touch even a trace of his poison, it will force even an iron heart and liver to burst asunder. (Hé'ān)
The earthen bowl was smashed just as the cat pounced; the *kāṣāya* robe rotted away in the rain, leaving no trace.
There is no need to come at the third watch to hand it over; tomorrow, with dignified bearing, descend Mount Tuo (Moweng).
The donkey’s business is not yet finished when the horse’s arrives; hook and chain, ring upon ring, with no end in sight.
Merely managing from today to tomorrow, one casually lets a lifetime slip away in vain. (Tianru Ze 5)
The dung beetle carries its load, ever fearing it is too light; the rat moves its gold, never dreading it is too much.
They think only that they can take it with them at the end of life, yet at the moment of death, nothing can be done about it.
When illness comes, accept it as death; this is the single-transmission secret prescription.
If you have no mastery before your eyes, you will be like a crab in boiling water, unable to find a way out.
Cultivating practice is like purchasing goods in the marketplace; if one is willing to break open the bag of stinginess, the task will be perfected.
To merely engage in idle verbal discussions is exactly like having paid the price but not yet returned the money.
This illusory body is approaching the age of following the heart’s desires. I walk beneath the pines and sleep upon the rocks. Cherish you, O assembly of dragons and elephants of Beishan;
when will our conversation from the Putong era be completed? (Xingzhong Ren)
Having reached sixty-one years of age, I ought to have retired from activity and waited for death to rest.
Unforeseen, the winds of karma have blown me here once more, to again bind up grudges with fellow monks (Xing Yuanming).
The day of welcoming guests within Kaixian Temple; the moment of requesting a verse before the Chan-moon Hall. The traveler’s path is like the sky, the spring is like the sea;
the nightingale cries until the branches of falling blossoms are severed. (Yuan’an Ji)
A patch of wasteland and a single hoe; turn it over and over again with diligent effort. With one stroke of the hoe, the spring breeze is turned;
there are melons and eggplants, and there are also gourds (Shiwu Yong).
The vegetable garden relies entirely upon the efforts of many; yet one’s own effort must not be lacking.
Once the manure is abundant and the eggplants grow large, one will finally know that the soil is fertile and the roots of the vegetables are thick. (Xiaoyan Bao)
Before one’s efforts have reached the ground of perfection, how many times has one leaned upon the railing in solitary sorrow? Today is the third day, tomorrow the fourth;
snow and frost easily take their toll upon the human head. (Juezhao Hui)
Yesterday a Confucian, today a monk; transforming the mundane into the sacred requires no great skill.
Reflecting back on the Old Man of Vulture Peak in days of yore, he too attained [enlightenment] at this very age (Tianyin Xiu).
Before even stepping onto the gunwale, thirty blows! How could there be any shore left to climb? A dragon from the clouds stirs up waves a thousand fathoms deep;
a bottomless boat beckons the old resident monk (Sōng-nyu-mil).
In the long, dark night, none can awaken; the Buddha-dharma and True Suchness are a lamp that illuminates the world.
It pierces the eye at the crown of one’s head; as before, it strikes three o'clock at noon. (Heling Monastery, Gate Two)
The ancient regulations of the monastic groves nurture outstanding talent; today, this field for selecting Buddhas is opened with empty hands.
The seven daily necessities, ever-luminous, must arise from the faithful heart of the donor.
Who can endure a single stroke of the white staff? Leaning against the wall for years, it is never lifted. It is not that this mountain monk’s nature is indolent;
among ten thousand, there is not one who can follow up with the grass-sickle. (Yin Minglun)
Holding a short whisk aloft while serving as the Guest Master—this practice found in various quarters is entirely improper.
At the gate of Bōen, the green moss is slippery; there, they let only the hairless hawk fly. (Nan’an Yi)
Those who are not karmic enemies do not meet; following the stream, one attains the wondrous—what more is there to seek? Come and help me steady this bannerpole of the Buddha-land;
with its iron walls and high winds, it shall shake the Nine Provinces. (By Ruyong Gao)
Molten silver surges high, sounding like thunder; the Great Being’s entire body appears several times.
If you wish to see him upon Mount Putuo, when will you ever emerge from your donkey years? (Bachi Yuan)
A patch-robed monk shouldering the affairs of a patch-robed monk is nothing more than the most ordinary; there is nothing extraordinary about it.
One should consider those of the present age who drift aimlessly, failing to contemplate that their life of wisdom is like a thread hanging by a single strand. (Daiweng Yue)
When you have been pressed until the mind is like a wall, you must know that a single blow shatters it into a hundred fragments.
Two-zhang eyebrows grow beneath the brow; who would dare look upon the Māheśvara Eye?
One must know that when the source is pure, the stream is also clear; yet on narrow paths, even enemies are devoid of sentiment. The secure barrier lies on level ground, as perilous as a mountain;
though the official seal is manifest, it does not permit passage.

This old man’s single phrase throughout his life has always been kept within his bowl and bag. If one says there is yet another weighty instruction to be given, how is that different from placing a head upon a head?
Fifteen years at Nanjian and Xihu; the "tiger's head" and "tiger's tail" discourse on squareness and roundness.
At midnight at Huangmei, with a heart full of bitter concerns, he once again lit the lamp to transmit [the Dharma] to his disciple.

In all things, there is a fixed condition; cease your forced striving. The straight hook has fished for the golden tortoise since antiquity. Yet one may also follow the twists and bends to place fragrant bait;
though one might catch fish and shrimp, what is their worth? Not even a hair’s breadth.
Parting with my straw sandals, I first board a southbound merchant vessel; The bronze pitcher still holds spring water from the Northern Mountains.
