After returning to the old temple in Hengyang this autumn, The gate is locked by the cold pond, where several trees ring with cicadas’ song. (Qingsai)
I have chosen this secluded dwelling to satisfy my rustic sentiments; throughout the year, there is neither parting nor welcoming.
Sometimes I ascend directly to the peak of a solitary mountain, where under the moonlight, I strip away the clouds and let out a laugh (Li Ao).
The unfolding and rolling up of the gate of transformation—how could they ever be simultaneous? To emerge from the frontier, one must first sever the myriad affairs of state;
once the Way prevails, one may instead spend days beneath the forest trees, leisurely watching the mountain clouds return as the curtain is drawn. (Yunfeng Yue)

The clusters of peaks shrouded in mist cannot detain him; on his distant journey, he relies only upon his rattan sandals. To whom shall the old hermitage, its cave-dwelling draped in ivy, be entrusted?
In the deep night, the cold monkeys cry out from the high trees. (By Mingjue Xian)
The spring light stretches to the horizon as the waters reflect the sky; the sands and marsh grasses along the banks are lush and verdant.
From three thousand *li* away, living beings look on, as he alone leans against a cold vine, shaking forth the ancestral wind.
The clear river flows with emerald light beneath my oars; A cold wind blows through the reeds as the rain has just ceased. To whom can I entrust these new verses from this night of parting?
Upon the white duckweed flats, the moon rises over the autumn hills.
The snow remains on the spring island path, stretching far and wide; the waters end and the clouds part, revealing the azure sky. Since our parting, who has shared this profound sentiment?
Only the solitary moon should be as vast and silent as we are.
Riding the inspiration, I unfurled my sails and reached Green Peak. The water’s glow, at the end of spring, coldly reflects the void.
If the man of the Way asks for the meaning of Caoxi, simply reply: "Lu Neng is downwind."
Zen rocks and flying torrents splash against the emerald moss; returning to benefit living beings, one joyfully descends the cloud-slopes.
If three thousand guests should stand along the way, there is no need for much more than raising one’s eyebrows.
Within the sandalwood grove he brandishes his golden mane; as he surveys the four quarters, how many times has the pure breeze brushed him?
Having once pledged to manifest clouds and rain with full majesty, who knows where worldly toil still remains?
Cloud-garments lightly sweep over the lower ridges; pines and cypresses stir the wind, chilling the sleeves. Who will ask about the intent behind this personal journey to the Milk Peak?
After a thousand or ten thousand years, with whom shall it be viewed?
Ancient strategies soar on high winds; the waves in the bottle stretch wide. Spring clouds, fragmented, reveal a sense of pure isolation. After midnight, the golden basin’s solitary peak is cold;
who goes along with it as the waning moon falls?
The late autumn of the Yin River has suddenly turned to spring; how much more so now that the Star of Tai serves as its master. Depart, departing, carrying high the ancient ruler and square;
the destiny of two thousand years continues this fragrant dust.
For more than thirty years throughout the four seas, I have never ceased seeking teachers and choosing friends.
This morning, having reached the ground of no-mind, I was instead pursued by that very no-mind out of the mountains. (Xian the Ascetic, II)

It is not that I lack the intent to continue the ancestral lamp; I am ashamed that my Way has not yet reached the level of Neng of Lingnan. At the third watch, beneath the moon, I depart from the mountain cave;
with lingering affection, I remain speechless as I gaze upon the azure peaks.

Shifting the myriad differences toward the ultimate pivot, he seizes the banner and snatches the drum, showing no quarter. Turning his body and crouching upon the ground, he manifests the full power of life and death;
only then is one a true cub of the golden-maned lion (Wenyu Qin).
When the bottom of the bucket falls away, the great earth is vast; where the life-root is severed, the emerald pool is clear.
Take this single point of snow from the red furnace and scatter it as a lamp to illuminate the night among men. (Dahui Zonggao)
Meeting and parting, both without a word; at the Ten-Thousand Willow Pavilion, they board the ferry boat. Do not say that one comes empty-handed and goes empty-handed again;
when you raise your head, you see clearly the mountains and rivers of old. (Songyuan Yue)
Coming from the south, he scratches the head of a venomous snake; caught in a single bite, his resentment knows no rest.
Even were there the waters of the two rivers and three gorges, they could never wash away this grievous enmity.
Old Master Xue welcomed him back with a smile filling his cheeks; the fame of his brilliance was shared with that of Taiyuan.
For three years he remained solely at Tianfeng Temple, unlike those who come to Yangzhou to listen for the bugle call. (Treasured by the Abbot San)
In the south, they discourse grandly on Chan; how can this compare to your family’s vast field of rice?
Once my winter clothes are all mended, I shall come with tea in my sleeve to visit the side of the mattock.
The silver threads in my temples cannot be woven into cold-weather clothes; the characters for "cooking" cannot cure hunger.
I wish to bestow upon you the Dharma of peace and happiness, yet I am so busy that I have no leisure moment.
Before the green bamboo hat, heaven and earth are vast; beneath the blue straw robe, water and clouds are wide. Without speaking or saying a word, what do they know?
They simply take their own hearts and do not deceive themselves. (Jiedi)
The family home dwells upon the highest peak of Mount Kuanglu; where the solitary monkey cries, the moonlight is bright. What is it now that makes you long to return?
Do not recall the sound of that heart-rending cry from years ago. (Zhe-weng Yan)

For many years he waged fierce battles across the desert fields; who can measure the magnitude of his achievements through blood-sweating toil? Now the fires of war have been extinguished throughout the four seas;
he returns home treading upon flowers, the scent of his horse’s hooves fragrant in the air.
The rice baskets at Cold Spring have been empty lately; there is no help for it, as the harvest has not been bountiful this year.
There is a wondrous prescription for ceasing to eat grain; monks vie with one another to ask Tiantong about it (Shitian Xun).
A solitary figure vanishes beyond the eastern sea gate; the streams and mountains of Wu and Yue stretch for tens of thousands of layers.
Rising from one prostration, he bows once more—knowing not where he shall encounter Yuancong (Xutang and Yuyu).
Just as I was busily warming you against the cold, you suddenly came to bid me farewell to go wandering in search of teachers. I have pared down three catties of iron from the tip of a needle;
I give it to you to cast a backbone for your journey ahead.

As soon as a thought of illness arises within the mind, the eyes immediately depart; the entire body must be clear and free from sickness. Before the foot has even crossed the threshold, one has already taken a step forward.
On the six bridges, the official willows are swaying in the spring breeze (Gong of Shilin).
Going to the Twin Trees to see old acquaintances—eyebrows arch like the new moon, eyes span the autumn sky. Before exchanging greetings, one should first ask:
Why is it that while the bridge flows, the water does not? (Stone Creek Moon)
When Xinghua struck Kebin that year, the story remains a talk within the monastic groves for a thousand years. Let the yellow clouds and the staff be set aside for now;
simply brew some tea and send him out the gate. (Daxie Qian)
In his day, Xinghua [Zhaojue] acted for the sake of Kebin; with the tip of his staff, he struck out the Jade Qilin.
Dun’an let pass the Zen guest Ding, desiring only that the man’s own eyes be clear (Dun’an Yan).
Three calls and three responses, then a somersault; in the sixth month, the Luojiang River is frozen through to its depths. Having returned home, the man is not recognized;
a single bright moon shines upon Luling (Kuchenjing).
Once I heard the wailing gibbons by the Gorges of the Ba River; My myriad thoughts and thousand sorrows cannot be fully recounted. A wind from a hundred thousand li awakens my dream;
Under the bright moon, I am on a boat upon the Jinjiang River. (Yanxi Wen)
Gazing to the horizon, all is vast and still; the waters reflect the empty sky. White artemisia and red smartweed battle the western wind.
This profound meaning from three thousand *li* away—who could have offered such an iron bond to burden my ancestors? (By West Rock’s [Xiyán] Huìwǔ)
On white paper, a black brush has written without cause; a single phrase, though distinct, is yet blurred.
Amidst the green lamp and night rain upon the Xiang River, it adds to the painting of wild geese alighting on the level sands.
After the accumulated snow on a thousand peaks has first melted, spring returns to the ten thousand nations and all things are new.
What a fine moment for a turn of the body—this jade qilin cannot be locked behind an iron gate.
The dragon follows the flowing water with a cool, clear resonance; a single melody of Shao-yin cannot be harmonized.
It disperses as a tune upon Poyang Lake—how many people beneath their mats listen to the sound of autumn?
I dwell at Shuangjing; you are on Ling Shan. A single word spoken in the wind is difficult to express. Fortunately, my paper robe has no ink stains;
it shall suffice to ward off the cold on the roads during the three months of winter.
Clouds shroud the Jianke Pass for three thousand li; waters separate the twelve peaks of Gutang. I have shaken out my bowels and entrails and spoken it all;
do not mistake a jar for a bell. (Dachuan Ji)
A single-leaf boat upon ten-thousand-li waves; the autumn wind is like an arrow, the moon like a hook. There is no need to inquire further about matters on the road:
once you have passed through the Three Bās, simply rest. (He’an)
Shuoyan has a verse to send Dongyan: Before it is raised, it is clearly two or three. Do not say that no one understands this meaning;
at Shiqiao, flowing water winds around the pines and cypresses. (Shaoshi Lu)
The phoenix chick beneath Mount Fenghuang—its patterns just revealed, its wings now complete. Though an iron net covers the heavens, it cannot hold him back;
his heart of returning already rests upon the green *wú* tree branches. (By Guyun Quan)
We have met at the head of Mount Wushan; we meet again by the side of Linglong Rock. As you depart, there is nothing to part with as a gift for your journey:
ten thousand li of western wind sweeps away the severed clouds. (Dongshan Yuan)
The cuckoo cries until its blood dyes the mountain flowers; by the tip of my staff, my兴致 (zìxìng) grows ever more distant. Before my eyes, all that stretches afar is but the road of a traveler;
tonight, at whose house shall I take off my straw sandals? (Zhongfeng Ben)
An empty fist strikes into the long-serpent formation; the battle grows more intense as the murderous miasma reaches the clouds.
Rolling on until reaching a place where there is no interference, the ox-head points north and the horse-head points south (Wuwen Can, II).
Countless flying blossoms dance in the morning breeze; Heaven has opened twenty-five gateways of perfect penetration.
If you wish to know from which door to enter, ask the Stone-Ear Peak by the stream.
In movement and stillness, how could one ever be entangled? Why need one further penetrate that which existed before birth?
Returning now to my ancestral garden a thousand miles away—on land there is the path, on water there is the boat. (Dongzhou Yong)
Buddha’s incense drifts like mist, lingering through the curtains by day; the spring stream chimes with its source, augmented after the snow has fallen.
Having returned from begging for alms beneath the twin trees, he reads the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as flowers fall like rain (Jianxin Fu).
I once heard of your return to Yujue on Danyi; I still remember your majestic presence as a hidden dragon.
Nine thousand li from the crimson cliffs to the blue seas, you fly freely with your single staff amidst the idle clouds (Xiaoyin Yun).
Coming from a hundred thousand *li* to deliver a single message—seventeen hundred envelopes. Upon arriving home, there is not a single word.
I ask you: do you know how to unfold them? (Qianyan Chang)
With the old eyes of the former days at Mount Lu, what was not peaceful about you, Master? Let the flies go;
do not break the paper window. Wind and rain, falling flowers—spring is truly cold. (Tianru Ze)
When the mind is not yet at peace, I shall bring you solace. Falling petals and light rain brew a spring chill;
across the broken bridge, the flowing water marks the solitary mountain path. Willow threads brush against the painted railing. (Yujihui)
White clouds fly down beside the Sword Pond; Newly pasted paper, a square of jade. The shadow of the pagoda suddenly stands inverted;
For his sake, I suspend my brush to write this outline. (Chu Shi Qi)
A carp on the mountain grows a single horn; suddenly it leaps up into the blue sky.
The practitioner Juiti has no place to seek it, yet he pierces the nostrils of Tianlong.
High atop the peak, towering amidst the clouds; even an eighty-year-old stream-side elder has eyes as empty as space. When meeting one another, do not speak of traveling on pilgrimage;
it would only burden his two ears and make them even more deaf (the Wild Elder agrees).
The black-lacquered bamboo whisk gleams and flashes; take it up and do not deliberate further.
For his sake, I shall break it into a hundred fragments; let us see what you will do, you, Meng Bala (Ruhui).
The old man of Mount Jingshan meets you with ill intent; he demands that you swallow the thorny *liji* fruit whole.
Once you have pushed your toes into its narrow opening, we shall all roll together into the thicket.
Fifty-three people suffer from deep-seated ailments; the ocean waves assist their moaning day and night.
I beg you, Great Master, to fully extend your life-giving hands and administer a single needle to the vital point of the *gao-huang*. (Jue Zhao Hui 2)
Born with an iron heart and a cold countenance, he treats Buddhas and Patriarchs with indifference, his vision vast and wide. Try pouring a single drop of Caoxi’s water;
it will swell up the eighteen rapids of the West River.
Holding up a bald broom upside down, he silently bestows his merit; before even the first excretion, all is swept empty. The entire Tripitaka is but paper for wiping excrement;
the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas are but insects within a latrine. (Biaozhitang)
The River waters flow on without sentiment, never returning; they leave behind only the fine green mountains on both banks. Light clouds conceal their traces and can return to the peaks;
they do not follow the east wind, but turn toward the pure countenance [of the Emperor Jianwen].
Where has the Superior Man gone to pay his respects? It is difficult even for Yuji to point out the way.
There is a certain Han Budai of Changting; he is now traveling abroad for alms in Raozhou (Dongsheng).
Carrying a long, long staff upon his shoulders, he travels through misty mountains and waters to seek a teacher. Stonehead kicks open the mother-born feet;
this brings misfortune to his straw sandals, which suffer broken leather (Pōshān Míng, 2).
Sickly, he eats black rattan; "Duo duo" as he returns home. Meeting people, he vainly blows a foul wind. A sand cauldron and earthen stove buried deep in a mountain stream;
boiling fresh spring water alive to meet the dull faculty.
He is titled the Gate of Emptiness, Thoroughly Empty. This year’s poverty surpasses last year’s poverty. Do not say the pit of poverty is difficult to fill;
it can withstand how many winds from the Dragon King. (Originally by Chen Min)
How many times have you wielded your staff, thinking of returning for a visit? You have trodden the sound of the stream until it is severed; everywhere is home.
Do not trouble your white-haired mother leaning on the gate with anxious words; look well at the willow threads slanting across the opposite bank. (Yulim Xu)
Nowadays, there is no place to seek deep mountains; simply when the mind is at ease, one closes the gate. The waters and paths of Wu and Yue are indistinguishable;
the autumn colors intoxicate the person as the moon becomes full. (Ruo’an’s Question)

Clouds weary of the spring mountains as the sun reflects their crimson glow; in my old hut, I have newly tended to and planted pines. Incidentally, I share this pure appreciation with you, though it remains somewhat clumsy;
I fear seeing the great and small hollows upon the neighboring crags (San-yi-yu).

The husband’s enterprise is accomplished by the husband; the leaves flourish and the branches prosper as the roots are firmly deep. Reaching the nine stages and ascending the three levels, he has thoroughly penetrated the source.
Looking at it, one only fears those with a calculating mind (Shi Qi Yun).
Breaking through waves and riding the wind, he came in the sixth month; In the clear autumn, he again mounted the celestial breeze and departed.
Returning to the eighteen rapids of the West River, For the sake of others, he gladly points out the road to Caoxi. (Daiweng Yue)
*Zadu hai*, Scroll Two;
*Zadu hai*, Scroll Three.
Re-edited by the Berlin-based successor to the Patriarch, the Śramaṇa Xingyin, in the Capital.
A seeker of the sword who has searched for thirty years; How many times have the leaves fallen and the branches sprouted?
Since first beholding the peach blossoms, To this very day, he has had no further doubts. (Lingyun Qian)
Staying overnight at the Flower City and the Wine Tower, a single sound of song and flute stirs the sorrow of parting. A sharp blade severs the red silk thread;
if you have no heart for me, then I shall simply leave. (Lanzi)
Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Only when one personally consents will one truly encounter it.
In the past, I mistakenly sought it along the road; today, looking back, it is ice within fire. (Changqing Ling)
Recalling those years before I attained awakening, Each blast of the painted horn brought a wave of sorrow. Now, upon my pillow, there are no idle dreams;
Let the large and small plum blossoms blow as they will. (Master Fu)
The eminent one of the forest was Zhaozhou; there is a reason why this old woman could see him through. Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror;
let not the traveler make the road his enemy. (Huanglong Nan)
I have a bright pearl; for a long time it has been locked away by the dust of worldly toil.
Now, as the dust settles and the light arises, it shines through and pierces the myriad peaks of mountains and rivers (Master Yushan).
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Standing alone on a ten-thousand-fathom peak with but one foot, he snatches the bright pearl from the jaws of the black dragon.
With a single word, he exposes the deception of Vimalakīrti. (Tianyi Huai)
Before the mountain lies a stretch of vacant land; with palms joined, he earnestly questions his grandfather: "How many times have you sold it only to buy it back again?
It is for love of the pines and bamboos that draw in the pure breeze. (Dongshan Yan)
The golden ducks and incense have faded within the brocade curtains; amidst the sounds of pipes and songs, one is supported home in intoxication.
Of all the youthful affairs of elegance and charm, only the beloved may know them alone. (Yuánwù Qín)
At the limit of deliberation, one sees the title; at the end of the journey, one enters the examination hall. Grasping the tip of the brush, wind and rain rush forth;
this time, I shall not be a "Plum-Blossom Scholar" (or, in the style of Heshan Ocan).
Sitting upright in the study hall, ten thousand cares cease; The sun is warm and the breeze gentle, the plants and trees are serene. Who recognizes the distant events of two thousand years?
They reside right now within the range of one’s own eyes. (Chen Liaoweng)
Casting aside the floating bag and smashing the lute to pieces, I no longer refine mercury for the gold within.
Since first beholding Huanglong, I have finally realized that all my previous efforts were misplaced. (Lü Dongbin)
It cannot be pinched into a ball, nor can it be split apart. What need is there for Nanyue or Tiantai? At the gateways of the six sense organs, no one employs it;
thus, it provokes the barbarian monk to come here on purpose. (Puan Su)
The drum has fallen silent and the bell has subsided as he returns with his alms bowl. A single thrust from Yantou was like a clap of thunder; indeed, it seems he will only live for three more years.
Is it not because he has received a prediction of his future from him? (Zhang Wujin)
A unique peak crowns the summit as clouds drift slowly upward; the source has no separate tributaries as the waters flow cool and clear.
Having traveled the mountain yet not reached its ultimate end, one is often obstructed by the green peaks that block the eyes (by Baiyang Shun).
Withered trees bear no flowers through many autumns; severed clouds still hang from the treetops.
Since the horns of the clay ox were fought and broken, even now the waters flow upstream. (From *Bǎohuá Jiàn*)
A dark-lacquered Kunlun man grips his fishing rod; The ancient sail is hoisted high as he descends the turbulent rapids.
Amidst the shadows of reeds, he plays with the bright moon, Drawing the blind turtle up onto the fishing boat. (I’an Quan)
For several years this matter has hung in my breast; I have questioned all quarters of the land, yet my eyes remain unopened. Now, at this moment, liver and gall are utterly shattered:
"A cry sounds upon the river—the Minister arrives! (Master Fentan).
Under the moon at the third watch, a single frog croaks. It breaks through the void; we are one family.
At such a moment as this, who can understand? Lingtou’s feet ache—there is Yuansha (Zhang Jiucheng).

From of old, his bearing has loved elegance and refinement; he often laughs at those of this age who seek outwardly. Amidst ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, there is no place to find it;
yet once attained, it was originally right upon the tip of one’s own nose. (Preface by Minister Jiang)
Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand forms all beg for their lives. A bottomless basket holds dead snakes;
adding much or subtracting little leaves nothing behind. (Yuan Ning)
Ascending the Qingfeng Tower for the official vegetarian feast, on this day my lifelong eyes are opened wide.
Only now do I believe that the events of the distant Putong era were not brought from the Pamir Mountains. (Yue Shan Nai)
The great earth, mountains, and rivers are a single expanse of snow; once the sun shines upon them, they leave no trace.
From this point on, I have no doubt regarding the Buddhas and patriarchs; there is no longer north, south, east, or west. (Duan Yan’s commentary)
Sweeping away all entanglements and intellectual views, whatever is grasped by the hand is the total manifestation of reality. The radiant circle behind the head penetrates the great void;
a thousand mechanisms and ten thousand functions are turned all at once. (Japanese attendant Jaku’a)

Left as a gift for the former attendant-in-attendance, Cold Box—its autumn waves shoot toward the Dipper and Stars. Iron armor follows him; ancient frost is clear. Do not inquire about those days at Xuanchi.
Matter. A single gust of majestic spirit stirs the earth (awakening clarity and manifestation).

Presented to Kuí Tiānjì, as he takes up his brush, poems are completed—each verse fresh and new. In joy, he lets out a bold shout, wishing to scale the clouds; yet most difficult to cure is this wild rhapsody.
Sickness. I have just now recovered and come to you (Yuanzhi).
I present this to Commissioner Zhang of the Judicial Office:
Your gaze pierces through the livers and gallbladders of men; you hang up your formidable, layered mask of iron. All matters are settled with singular impartiality.
Accomplished. A man of great stature who stirs heaven and earth (Qian Yan Chang).
Seeing off Li Zongyuan as he returns to San Shan in Guangdong:
the trees are bare, the geese cry out amidst the frost. At the Tiger-Crouch Pass, he purchases a small boat. Tomorrow, longing for him, I shall gaze toward the south.
The Dipper; the river flows on without end, the heavens of Chu stretch long (as seen in *Xinfu* IV).
In this Great Peace, I withdraw from office—what more need I worry? Returning to grow old in the Southern Mountains, I inquire after my old homestead. Thirty thousand trees of uniform plum blossoms;
at night, with the bright moon, I am intoxicated upon Mount Luofu.
Hearing tell of High Lord Gao, my spirit and gallantry grow wild; I have spent much time comparing poems by his white-cloud window. Since autumn arrived, the coconuts are as sweet as honey;
you must send me five hundred pairs, sealed tight.

In the parrot-cup, deep purple mists overflow; one marvels at such elegance, as if in the home of the Immortal from the Other World. His brocade robe lingers for guests while spring swallows hasten their flight;
throughout the eastern garden, the *dòukuò* flowers have fully blossomed.
The Head Cook remains by the hearth of Cold Mountain to provide firewood; Shide gathers vegetable scraps before the hall.
Thus they win the right to sit and deliberate within the Fragrant Accumulation Kingdom, where eggplants bloom once again in the back garden. (Xingkē)
As Yan, the Magistrate of Duanchi, returns to the region of Yue, the trees shed their leaves and the geese soar high in the sky; along the way, green mountains escort his passenger boat.
He shall surely visit the old traces of Hanshan by the Teao River, listening to the autumn tides at the pine-gate as the setting sun slants down. (Tuiweng Chu)
I present this linen cap and white ramie robe for the Layman Ma at Mount Sha; you who cast yourself far from the solitary peak are now close to us.
You bring with you a seven-foot bamboo from before the frost, cleaving through the celestial clouds so they do not rise too high. (By Mingjue Xian)
The physician’s teeth are clearly but a set of bones; of ten, now only two or three remain.
If you, Master, do not replant them, how will you chew on radish roots when you grow old? (Yuansou Duan)
The maladies of the masses have already reached the vital organs; who in the world transmits the life-saving formula?
This herb, when plucked, is entirely medicine—what need is there for the fragrance of the nine-transmutation elixir to permeate the bottle? (Wuxue, 2)
A single phrase is the medicinal herb of Jīvaka; the various sutras of the Great Canon are the compendium of prescriptions.
Having brushed away the three miserable realms with a smile, there is no need for acupuncture or moxibustion to rouse the vital organs.
The physiognomist said, "The Master’s physiognomy is most auspicious. Allow me to ask you one thing:
before the mountain monk had even emerged from my mother's womb, how many hairs were there on the gallbladder? (Dongyan said.)
The wind shakes the emerald bamboos, their sounds striking jade; the rain washes the myriad peaks, their colors drenched in azure.
This very one is the majestic and solemn wondrous form—Master, you have a mouth, so how could you possibly speak of it? (Guyeon)
The two eyes are so piercing they strike one with a chilling cold; in a single instant, the wise and the foolish are fully discerned.
As for the face prior to the birth of one’s parents, one must turn the light back upon oneself and look within (Zhu’an Guang).
His face is like cast iron, his brow like Mount Kunlun. What grounds are there for you to discuss prosperity and decline? In vain do you speak of the green bamboo by the pavilion;
of the many who have flourished in the spring breeze, how many now have descendants? (Wuwen Can)
Long and short are both equally produced; the wise and the foolish distinguish between superior and inferior within their own eyes. I ask you:
what are the characteristics of the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya as seen by the all-seeing eye of Maheśvara? (This is the wisdom of contemplation.)
Presented to the Immortal Liaokong:

the radiance of his sword coils like lightning as it cleaves the azure cliffs; Lady Mother presents him with red snow from her golden platter. Hand in hand, they share a smile for three thousand years;
once more they vow to ride upon the giant tortoise to gather the moon from the sea. (Xiaoyin Yin)
The diviner turns the stalks and the tortoise shell, yet he fails to grasp the subtle mechanism. Misfortune has its womb; fortune has its foundation.
Last night the planet Pei shifted one position, but the Master slept through it and did not know (by Shitien Xun).
The True Person of No Rank is stark and bare; who knows as he enters and exits through the gateway of the face?
The Great Void shares its very life-span with him; you must carefully investigate his celestial coordinates. (Chijue Chong)
"You drill the tortoise shell; I drill the heart. When the spiritual source is penetrated, it is worth ten thousand pieces of gold.
With a sudden burst, the hexagram lines are revealed; the six lines are tranquil and still, beyond all seeking. (Wanfeng Wei)
Yan Shi asked about his travels, and he carried a single black cane; sitting alone for many years, he faced the green peaks. He did not listen to his disciples discuss matters of rise and fall;
who would have known that he was a monk of the Great Peace? (Master Yi-weng Ru).
The wars between Wu and Yue were truly formidable; how many times has the spring breeze brought forth the green grass? I listen intently as he recounts his history;
before my eyes, a thousand ridges are crossed by ranks of gathering clouds. (Guyun Quan)
The singer plucks the pipa three times and sings the "Wei-cheng" song; his resonant voice pierces the clouds as it travels. How can one play the melody of non-arising?
Let the Buddhas and Patriarchs glare with their eyes wide open. (By Bai Chi Yuan)
Tailoring a single length of living white silk from the Poshui River; A half-span of old green mist from Mount Lu.
Master Li takes hold of the corner of my *kāṣāya*; He mends it whole, lacking nothing at all. (Zhongfeng Ben)
Carrying a knife and a ruler in hand, he travels through all directions; the thread departs and the needle arrives, busy day after day.
He measures the long and the short of others to their end, yet how many times has he measured his own length and brevity? (Shiwu Yong)
Attaining it in the mind, it responds in the hand; it fills empty space without any leakage.
If there is even a hair’s breadth that remains uncomprehended, perform a somersault upon the point of a needle (Jue the Head Seat).
Inside the lacquerer’s workshop, everything must first be thoroughly covered with ash; only then can one begin to polish the exterior.
Although the numinous light is inherently present, it requires diligent effort to bring it forth (Shiwu Yong).

The carpenter drags it away and pushes it back; the wondrous meaning is the same. When masters meet, they apply their skill in secret. With the eyes and hands of the whole body, they are able to shift and interweave;
all is contained within a single thread in the midst of the present. (Wuqu Kong)
The cobbler’s extraordinary skill is praised by all; they laugh at his contemporaries’ chaotic stitching of needles and awls. From head to toe lies the path that reaches the heavens;
bright moon and clear wind follow at every step. (Qian Shuji)
Outside a small bridge by a rustic shop of a bell-founder, at twilight when snow was about to fall, who was it that leaned over to listen to a single sound?
For a thousand ages it calls out to the ignorant and deluded— (Ying’an Hua).
What need is there to cast bells when the world already has names? You have come from afar to visit this old man of the crags. In my house, the fire is cold and ice has formed;
yet, take advantage of the glowing furnaces found everywhere else (Qianyan Chang).
The officials and men have captured and bound alive a hundred kinds of prisoners; they beat their shackles and cuffs to question them as to their origins.
If one can penetrate and transform even a single word among them, one brings to life the path that was previously dead. (Wuquán Fàn)
Raising the razor, the frosty blade is chillingly sharp. Two, three, four, seven—lower your heads. Observe where he stands as a man:
only when not a single hair remains does one finally rest. (Zhe-weng Yan)
Shaved, it grows long; grown long, it is shaved again. How many times in a year does one undergo this distant vexation? The Great Officer merely continues to come seeking blessings.
But how could my blessings be so numerous? (Shiwu Yong)
Seeing the monk depart to pay homage at Mount Potalaka, I point my finger and say:
"This is true diligence; how truly marvelous! A single lotus flower blooms upon the fingertip.
If you wish to know the true countenance of Avalokiteśvara, come now and visit Mount Potalaka yourself. (The Precipitous Cliffs)
Sending off Iron Mountain Daoist to pay homage at Potalaka:
beneath his heels, Iron Mountain rises ten thousand fathoms; before his eyes, white waves stretch for a thousand fathoms.
If you do not take responsibility here, you must go back and observe Avalokiteśvara once more. (Zhongfeng Ben)
Sending off the Wayman of Limitless: Paying Homage at Potalaka.
The Wayman has no affairs, yet his heart goes wild; he wades through waters and climbs mountains, seeking it beyond the seas.
With each prostration he rises to prostrate again, unaware that Guanyin is within his own house (Xu Bai Tan).

Seeing Master Guan off as he travels to worship at Potalaka—what does he seek beyond the cliffs of Potalaka? He will not rest until he beholds Avalokiteśvara; once he has seen Avalokiteśvara, he will laugh to himself:
"It turns out that a flatbread was actually a steamed bun! (Tianru Ze).
Sent off attendant Zhiguanhui to pay homage at Wutai Shan Qingliang;
wishing to prostrate, he did not shrink from the toil. Traveling back and forth across ten thousand *li* of a scorching sky, he has thoroughly discerned the path beneath the old woman’s tongue.
Upon his return, it is fitting that his voice be raised high. (Daoweng Yue)
Mañjuśrī, old as he is, does not avoid shame; he bluntly speaks of the three before and the three after.
Go and inquire further how many people there are, and see how he continues to contend and act with such foolishness.
Seeing off a Monk Who Visits His Parents:
The face of one’s own birth has already been made clear; Far, it is not distant; near, it is not intimate. Try asking the traveler on the road as he returns:
Who is the person leaning against the gate? (Chijue Chong)
The patched robe has been exchanged for a variegated court gown; from the Buddha-land he returns, having passed the imperial examination. When his mother asks what office her son holds, he replies:
"An official of the Hanlin Academy in the palace of the Empty King. (Zang-sou Zhen)
My gray-haired parents, both eighty years old, remain; gazing daily toward the south, my heart must break. To see them once more, they lift their brows and show their familiar faces;
do not say there is nothing to offer the Honored Hall (Xutang Yu).
In this life, one’s parents should be closely attended; look carefully at one’s original father and mother. In every movement and action, they provide full strength;
once they are raised up, one’s hair stands on end with awe. (Biepu Zhou)
One seeks the stem of a flower in the sky at its moment of birth; one must seek the waves where a mirage first arises. It is not that the weight of worldly affection prevents one from leaving home;
it is simply that the soul in dreams dwells most often in one’s native land. (Chu Shi Qi)
Presented to Zhenneng Zhuge:
In years past you were called a recluse; At three visits to your thatched cottage, you emerged from the mountains.
If the pine blossoms receive the power of spring, Even roots deep in the crags will surely break into bloom. (Xiangcheng Shun)
I offer coarse sand from Mount Fuyin to the Buddha, and the Buddha joyfully accepts it; I present a strange rock to the Sangha, and the monks do not disdain it.
I come with empty hands—do you still require anything? There is nothing else that could be added. (Su Ziyou)
Answering Subhūti:
Holding it in empty hands, it is difficult to put down. The Three Sages and Ten Saints gather their heads to gaze upon it.
Such an offering can be enjoyed; even the wooden horse and the clay ox rejoice (Foyin Yuan).

Reclining in Wolun Hermitage, within the Golden Garden, horses gallop to and fro; A mere inch often becomes a cause for suspicion as one draws his sword. The moon shines upon a thousand trees of plum blossoms amidst the clouds;
When one awakens from a dream upon that single pillow of reclining in the clouds—(Xuan-an Shi).
Presenting Miaoxi:
It is neither mind nor Buddha; his entire body is a single string of golden bones.
Zhaozhou met the old Nanquan and was able to say, "Zhengzhou produces radishes" (Wu Xueshi).
The Great Being Lingyuan resided in the Eastern Hall of King Yuezhang, while Master Hengchuan lived in the Mountain Lodgings;
though their noble spirits were separated by three hundred years, they were as close as the Southern and Northern Courts of human history. (By Yudang Yi)
Congratulations on the restoration of the Thousand Buddhas Hall at Jingci Temple, where the paintings of the Fifty-three Pilgrimages have been rearranged and two new gate plaques erected;

the Thousand Buddhas are now relegated to the high gallery above. "The misty waters of a hundred cities are swallowed by a single hair"—even if one were to possess a separate path that pierces the heavens, it still falls within the second gate of Nanshan (Kōkai).
The practitioner who thoroughly understands the body is no different from one who has realized the mind and rests at ease. When the mind is realized, the body has no cause for sorrow.
If both body and mind are thoroughly understood, what need is there for immortals to be further enfeoffed as marquises? (Ying’an Hua)

Having long since understood the field, I stayed overnight at the home of the Layman of the Western Mountain. Sitting around the hearth, we conversed face-to-face about our lives. From the beginning, there has not been so much as a single thread;
it is simply the flowers in the eyes of a weary life.

When bidding farewell at the head of the Jiang River by the Xiangchan Turbid Port, the azure clouds and autumn waters lingered in their gentle stillness. Do not disdain my extreme old age, clumsiness, and indolence;
I shall come again in another day to knock upon your bamboo gate.
Entrusted to Ten Thousand Peaks, lush and verdant;
yellow chrysanthemums fill the eyes in autumn. Baiyun sits upright atop the emerald peak. Lightly he brings forth the phrase "no guest and no host";
with one shout, the waters of the thousand rivers flow backward (Qianyan Chang).
To Xue Shouzuo of Yangshan Wunian:
The Linji school has been transmitted through five lineages; upon entering the gate, a single shout reveals the sharp edge of the spiritual mechanism.
With a compassionate heart as urgent as that of a grandmother, it is easy to understand—just look at the mud snake transforming into a dragon (Wanfeng Wei).
To the Elder at the Summit of the Verdant Peak:
In your practice, you must cause the path of the spiritual mechanism to be severed; when speaking, do not allow the faculty of thought to arise.
The Great Jewel Flower King Throne of the Tathāgata is not comparable to an ordinary black-lacquered shed. (Shuzhong Yun)
Entrusting this to Chief Seat Miaoyuan:
"Yellow yams roasted in the ashes can satisfy hunger; the mind is like a wall, the eyes like eyebrows. Since Zhaozhou departed, few have sought the Way;
there is a fist—whom will he raise it toward?"
Entrusting this Dharma to my nephew Yan Sidao:
having eliminated the two wonders of Jianyuan, the five-colored phoenixes shall finally disperse their wings in the azure heavens.
The achievements of Tengzhou are not difficult to inherit, all the more so since the universe within your breast is vast.
It has been more than eight years since I parted from Master Dongyu. You have been guiding the assembly of disciples while I have lived in seclusion.
Amidst white clouds and flowing waters beyond the realm of heaven and earth, we shall never meet again; hence this letter sent to you. (Yuansou Duan)
Iron Whip Monk contemplated the four lines and sent them to Chengtian: "The whole is assembled, yet half is missing; it is neither a verse nor a poem.
How can one bring this forth before others? (Nutang Bian).

The Chan Master, my nephew Huaji, who has taken his seat atop the First Peak of the Golden Wheel, has caused all manner of demons and monsters to hide their tracks. In recent years, he has received true news:
it is reported that the authentic lineage of Yangqi has been restored (Dahui Zonggao).
Entrusting this to Elder Wolong:
Snow and mist shroud the cold, never parting; longing for you, I can no longer ascend the high terrace.
Since the rivers and mountains stretch for thousands of li, I can only hear your illustrious reputation spreading across the earth. (By Mingjue Xian)
Entrusted to the Inner Chamber Attendant, Grand Guardian:
A thousand fathoms of cold cliffs spray forth chilling sounds; in the thatched hall, clouds are thin and the bamboo wind is clear. Resting occasionally upon the rush mat, there are no other affairs;
throughout the long days, all is vast stillness, thanking for the Great Peace.
A letter sent to Master Zhuan’an:
The spring colors first emerge upon Qianfo Ridge; The sound of the bell travels afar through the pines of the Six Dynasties.
As the Dharma Hall is just opened, celestial flowers fall; Where does one stand amidst the cold clouds? At which layer? (In the manner of Nan’an Yi)
After Master Jiqiu An shouted, it is said that people heard nothing for three days; from this point, the school’s style arose in the West River.
Without a moment's hesitation, he cast forth a full moon, hanging high upon the foremost peak of the noble mountains.
As the autumn of the Dharma-path approaches, I have recently received the flourishing growth of empty echoes. My house does not prize the excellence of its own gate and courtyard;
it simply loves that the person’s own eye is wide open.
Entrusting this to Huan with these celestial verses and other famous works:
Incense curls from the stone bed; fragrance rises from the earthen incense burner. Among the thousand sages, one measures their strengths and weaknesses.
Two mouths, as it turns out, truly possess not a single tongue. Do not let this news reach the various quarters. (Nanshi Xiu, 2)
Majestic descendants of Linji: pressing heavy and lifting light, they open wide the crown of the head.
Regarding the flavorless talk that pierces through the seven apertures and eight openings—what prevents one from chewing it into pieces and swallowing it whole?
Upon first arriving at Huizhao Hermitage in Shanxi, I stayed with Zhang Wujin Shiben:
"It does not hinder one’s boneless tongue; Fine mountains cannot bind this free body. Let others laugh at my broken-legged cauldron;
For now, I wish to come south to recognize the phoenix and the qilin. (Hong Juefan)
Entrusting this to Master Zhian at Shitou:
The paths of the world are treacherous, my nose already aches; I seek a stable place for my broken-legged cauldron. Who sees me, after sleep, idly shaking my staff?
The pine wind blows against my ears, a cold tide at night.
Entrusted to Master Pingshan of Jingci, he broke through the fetters and pierced the hooves of five hundred oxen; within Nanping Temple, they were gathered into a single pen.
Having traded away their hides and fur until their radiance shone forth, they once again raise their heads as they pull the plow and drag the harrow. (Shiwu Yonggu)
Master Tianmu, eighty years old, has sprouted new teeth once more. He chews the void until it is a pulp, then spits out the dregs.
Scattering them toward the trees by Linglong Rock—branch after branch, leaf after leaf—is nothing but *tánhuā* (the rare, wondrous flower). (By Xisou Tan)
I have long not seen the tracks of the oxen among my many friends at Bai Zhang; dreams of clouds and mountains have been severed for tens of thousands of layers.
Could it be that, greedy for water and grass, they followed the herd, only to be tethered by others atop Mount Daxiong? (Standing alone and transcendent.)
At the red furnace flames atop Iron Hermitage, sparks fly upward. Who can deliver a single blow right to the head? One might think Iron Hermitage is made entirely of iron;
yet with one stroke upon the crown of the head, it is as soft as mud. (He’an)
The Ox of the Mountains and Waters has never been pierced by a halter; once the nose-string is pulled, he goes mad with wind.
I ask you, sir, to take back the broken rope and let him sleep at ease among the forests and springs. (By Chief Seat Qing)
Wu Bi-dong requested a verse:
At the tips of the hundred grasses, the eyes of a thousand sages; Upon the tip of a single hair, ten thousand layers of barriers.
There is no further Buddha-dharma nor any mystic subtlety— Fit to be shared and exchanged with those who truly understand. (Ying’an Hua)
Delighted that the Magistrate Han of Puyuan has come to visit me, I suddenly hear that Mei Fu has arrived to pay his respects. Laughing, I emerge from my thatched hall wearing a lotus-leaf robe.
My children, unaccustomed to seeing carriages and horses, scramble to hide deep within the reeds. (Hu Dingjiao)
In response to Wu Yuanshao, he said:
"This entire body of mine is a set of golden chain-bones, fit to serve as a model for devas and humans.
To truly know Linji’s little page, one must recognize him as the 'white-handed thief' of those days (Dahui Zonggao)."

Hearing that Famen Yun was moving from Daxiu to Qixian, seven hundred eminent monks of the high sangha went there to engage him in the field of dharma-battle. Master Lu’s single verse caused them all to surrender;
no one could block the road to Huangmei, for they were inevitably led far away across the Nine Rivers (by Guishan Xiu).
When Master Qing’an resided at Nanhua, a single opportune shout was like a thunderclap rushing forth; it stirred the Yellow River until its winding currents became turbid.
Today, he has freshly overturned the old tracks: at Caoxi, the bottomless water leaves no trace. (Tiéguan Shu)
In response to Prime Minister Li Zhongsī:

Ten thousand layers of clear clouds enshroud the myriad mountains; A thousand-fathom cascade falls amidst the trees. Within my meditative absorption, I am startled by the news that Your Jade Chariot has arrived;
Surely you have come to wrest the stillness from this old monk. (Zhongfeng Benru)
The whip has not yet been raised to turn back; for now, linger and enjoy the scene. You must know that even on level ground, dangers abound.
Cease using worldly sentiments and the marks of names and forms to burden this old dhūta in his mountain cave.
In response to the Imperial Censor Feng Haisu’s “The Incense Altar is Swept by the Silent Child”:
Announcing that the Scholar of Changsha has arrived; The sand-pot boils the orange peel to a froth, now cold;
After many years, the signs of life have joyfully returned in secret.
In response to the Layman of the Eight Mountains:
The Precious Mirror Stand of the Mysterious Pass of the Great Ultimate. The livelihoods of the three families are all but dust;
The Daoist has a separate method for settling oneself, And does not come by way of the paths of the three families. (Yuzhi Ju)
I visited Scholar Yu;

amidst ten thousand layers of clouds and mountains, I have not yet returned home. In my silent solitude, I entrust my heart to the Elder Lu to know it. Amidst rain and snow in the river city, I wrote my name upon paper;
having failed to visit the Great Scholar, whom else shall I visit? (By Mingjue Xian)
Zhao Ti-gong requested a verse:

"Having already attained realization before the words, one is at the edge of the world; after the phrase, one takes up the burden as the road grows ever more remote. A single blow shatters the iron barrier like dust;
the waters and sky are vast and wide, the geese fly in a slanting row. (Dahui Zonggao II)
Sent to the Layman Wugou:
In the imperial gardens, the jade pools have just begun to thaw; Among men, the willows again droop in spring.
I sit in my mountain hall burning incense all day long, Constantly remembering the man of Vaisālī who remained silent.
A Verse for the Imperial Envoy, Vice Minister He, Sent to Guanshan Hermitage:
This mountain is already superior to Tiantai; atop its peaks, the vast void reveals the True Eye.
Limitless waters and clouds find no place to settle, yet they allow the Prime Minister to come and sweep the ground. (Ying’an Hua)
Li Xiangyan begs for a verse:
"The hundred schools and various masters are but dregs; the waves of the ocean's depths are turned with bare hands. Sitting steadily in the hall of one’s own home, who is the master?
Ask Xiangyan about what was before birth. (Ruo’an asked twice.)

The misty waters of the Southern Lake seem to wish to detain me; how could I bear to neglect the verse we chanted hand-in-hand by the stream? This single word that cannot be transmitted is the true secret instruction;
one must put it into practice through the "investigation of things."
On the day of the harvest moon, I replied to Tang Qiyuan regarding his journey:
"The heart has already become still; one cannot help but find delight in fine forests and springs. What, after all, are the pines, the wind, the water, and the moon?
They form the karmic conditions for our meeting throughout many lifetimes. (Muyun Mon)
In response to Wang Fengchang Yanke’s “Silver Hooks and Iron Clamps” hanging in the Dharma Hall, He personally opened up the mechanism of life before a single stroke was made.
A million spirits all gaze upward with bated breath, Willing to let their eyes be pierced through just to behold it. (Tu’engwēng Chǔ)
On an Autumn Day, Sent from Afar to Huang Jiezi:

His lofty reputation, formed since youth, is as heavy as a mountain. He would rather disdain the selection of Buddhas than the selection of officials. Wearing a flower-patterned turban, he departed from Shaoshi;
Carrying a straw hat in his hand, he left Chang’an. (Hongjue Ming)
The writings of Yuju Duwei on Chan and the words of the Master of Deceptive Emptiness are likewise transmitted in stone inscriptions. No one has offered more than three hundred coins for them;
yet they have won me eyes that pierce through the Five Heavens.
Among the myriad masters who have left the Stone Creek [monastery] to go forth into the world, only Kāśyapa remains guarding his withered meditation.
If this old monk were to follow the current, he would betray thirty years of mountain dwelling. (Qianyan Chang)
Master Cāntián Tōng, the origins of Jùbǎo lie within the mountains of the imperial capital. Verdant peaks, locked by clouds, are beyond scaling. Behold where the wooden horse neighs in the wind:
clear ice within the fire, cold as the sixth month. (Yùzhī Jù’èr)
Following the rhyme of Dong Lianghu:
You are like the Five Willows, always steeped in wine; I am like Mount Mui, not practicing Chan. The coming and going of kalpas is but a single laugh;
in vain do we debate which year this is in the human world.
Though there are hundreds of thousands of idle days and months in this world, no person possesses even a single point of goodness in body or mind.
Knowing that others are occupied with matters of no consequence, one only serves to deepen the vast and boundless ocean of karma (Zhongfeng’s second version).
In response to Li Sizai:
Stratagem within stratagem, yet another stratagem is seen; Autumn frost, drop by drop, penetrates the soldier’s robe. The conversation ends beneath the three-watch moon over the mountain ravine;
Once more we agree to return, wrapped in felt, amidst the celestial clouds.
Answering Master Song (Master Song had composed a poem in jest to mourn [the master] and sent it to him; after the master finished this verse, he threw down his brush and passed away).
Who else has been so in accord with me throughout our lives? Xianqing knows my heart better than anyone.
Had we not intended to part from one another at the outset, I feared I might have missed this single poem for my fellow practitioner (such as Bunan).
In response, I say:
Reverend Wanshi, let the Buddha-dharma rot as it may and leave it at that. For many years, I have covered my head with a paper quilt; for my livelihood, I have only a few yam tubers.
Even when they ripen in the mountains, I am too lazy to gather them. (Qianyan Chang)
Answer: Chan Master Xuedou Xian said:
"A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; as soon as the blue falcon sees it, he seizes it. Later hunters' dogs lack spiritual nature;
they vainly search for it at the old spot where the withered stump once stood. (Han Dabo)
In the snow, I long for Dongru, who is like tattered rags yet has been my companion for thirty years; we have shared the coldness of ice and frost and possess a steadfastness like iron.
Now, with another foot of snow piled outside our door, my aging eyes can only endure the smoke from the firewood. (Yulin Xiu)
Answer: At this time, Master Zhu Yuan had a monastery but did not care to dwell there; it was heard that he was living in seclusion on the marshy banks of the Yangtze.
When the kalpa-fire turned the great chiliocosm to ashes, the seal of the universal light-mind remained only as suchness (Yuan-sou Duan).
Entrusting this to Master Yuanwu:
Leaving the forest, one returns once more to the weeds. The heavenly net is vast; there is no escaping it. Who would believe that karmic conditions offer no place of refuge?
Returning home, one need not fear a loud voice. (Huayan Jue)
Carrying my bamboo staff and straw sandals, I sought you out, Master Baopo; Layer upon layer of mountain valleys, smoke rising from the villages.
When we finally met, there was nothing left to say— Ten li of plum blossoms, a single stream of clouds (Xueqiao Xin).
I send this letter to the Honored One:
one bottle and one bowl, simply following conditions as they arise. This matter I must repeatedly and forcefully proclaim. Knowing ones do not come; spring gradually grows old.
A solitary peak, bright moon, facing cold spring water. (Dongshan Yan)
Sending a letter to an old friend, I gaze toward him before it even reaches him; though he sends no word, I already know his heart.
Passing my days among the forests and springs, free from worldly cares, I knit my brows as I steal glances at the white monkeys.

Entrusted to the thatched cottage of Master Xuedou, within the ancient terrace and courtyard: milk flows from the green peaks, snow rolls at the gate. Raising this fist, one is already weary of seeking understanding;
would you be willing to entrust this iron contract to your descendants? (Lingzhang Yun)
Entrusted to the Kunlun karmic winds, the *jinxian* crown is blown asunder; at the threshold of birth and death, it is difficult to find one's footing.
In six hundred years, such an encounter occurs but once. Do not regard this great matter with indifference. (Venerable Wan)
Entrusting this to Master Wuzhun:
the turtle and the monkey cannot be separated; the elder brother calls and the younger brother responds as if they have forgotten their own minds.
Yet when it comes to speaking of the point where things become paradoxical, once again, one’s heart and liver cannot be brought along. (Nantang Bian)
To Reverend Xia’an:
Whenever I encounter a traveler from Changsha in the far south, they all say that the ancient Buddha Huangtan is at peace. Like Baizhang, he plows his fields and sows his rice;
his lofty spirit is so brisk it chills the bones. (By Da’weng Yue)
To Fan Jiujing of Rugao:
In these times, a true lay practitioner (upāsaka) is hard to find. I constantly recall the old Chan master Fan of Donggao;
he was much like a dry-as-bones monk who, whenever he opened his mouth to speak to someone, his breath would strike the heavens.
The Master of Dongxing borrows the entire Tripitaka to wipe away his sores and scabs;
yet right and wrong, past and present, are as numerous as hemp seeds. Will he truly succeed in wiping away those sores and scabs?
One must examine him from beginning to end, point by point.
Sent from the Grass-Hall on Mount Shen in Wujiang:
I have heard you are supporting your parents at the Grass-Hall; this news brings me distant comfort and makes my own sorrows fade. Does a willow branch still hang by the stream?
I hope your reed sandals are woven together for your mother’s tasting. (Tianli Zhen)

In the *Dàohuì Jì*, Dàohuì records that he did not die at first, yet speaks of death; Kōng was originally without emotion, yet seems to possess it. Grasping the posthumous letter in his hand, he sheds a single stream of tears;
at Qinxi, for three nights, the rain falls continuously through the day. (Kōng, Dongshan)
In mourning for Master Yunchao, people say the teacher has been dead for a long time; I alone linger in hesitation, undecided in my doubts.
Now that the nest is empty and the clouds have dispersed, even in the depths of spring, the cuckoo still cries out. (Nutang Bian)
Lamenting Master Dongshan:
With a lotus fiber he drew forth and bound empty space; with a damp scrap of paper he picked up and wrapped a tiger. These arts have now been displayed for the last time;
it is unbearable to shed old tears in the eastern wind.
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year of Daoding, the dream was severed; among hundreds of thousands of samādhis, he entered while still alive.
Piteous indeed, though he had been ill for but a few days, after my visit I have come once more to enter the shrine (the sun has passed through).
Born, then dead, and again cremated—just as if it had never happened before.
On the day it was said they were escorted by cremation, willow branches were distributed among a thousand monks (Xibai).
The Attendant of Tiantong, while serving at Lingyin, died amidst three calls;
bearing a sense of grievance within his voice, he raised an army of a million to besiege the city.
Who would have known that on the road ahead of Handan Peak, one must carve names upon wood to lie in ambush? (Yunwai Xiu)
Consoling Chan Master Shan for leaving saṃsāra only to enter it again: Ultimately, when has there ever been any coming or going?
Last night, flames burst forth from within the river of ice, burning empty space until it is reduced to a single heap of ash. (Baoning Yong)
Lamenting Master Zhigong:
Last year you once traversed the peak of White Clouds; our meeting in our final years was likewise by chance. You have now cast off your skin like a cicada and become a withered leaf;
I, like a spring silkworm, have already completed my third slumber. (Hong Juefan II)

The harsh mourning has not yet ended, yet the spring stove is warm; in this chamber of a master, the cold of the Daoist bones is especially suited. He waves his hand and departs, calling out but receiving no answer;
let us try to remove this idle reputation while it still exists in the world and see.
On Shuangji Peak, I long for Master Gaofeng;
the peak is deep and the ancient path perilous. I have not come to knock upon the wooden gate at midnight. After six years of fruitless endeavor, a lingering regret remains;
In the desolate empty mountains, the cuckoo cries out. (Zhongfeng Benru)

Hearing the news of a death while a guest, the report of the passing rests upon my traveler’s bedside. When the conversation turns to the cycle of rebirth, even ghosts feel sorrow. Flesh and sleep remain unemptied;
dreams of past and present persist. Under the frosty moon filling the heavens, a skull lies exposed.
Lamenting Master Huigan (who, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, bequeathed a inkstone):
Lightly he followed the west wind with his single sandal; Not a single thing remained within his robe-pouch. Leaving behind only this earthen inkwell—what will it be used for?
This old man has no brush to inscribe upon the void. (By Minister Zeng)
Inscription on the Meditation Hall:
No Doors, No Entrances, and No Passages on the Four Sides. Students labor in vain, frantic to grasp a shadow.
Be careful of the moon of the old garden through the ages; Through the night it remains as it was, never hidden. (Wu Xun, 2)
A former disciple of Layman Lufeng has captured the Master’s true likeness with perfect fidelity.
Gathering the entire earth into a single eye, it turns out to be something entirely new and extraordinary.
Knocking on the horn, the events before and after my person are vast and indistinct; wishing to speak of these causal conditions would surely break one's heart.
Having searched the mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue in vain, I turn back with my mist-shrouded boat toward Qutang Gorge (Tuzai).
Beyond the mountain man Sun’s old residence, wild bamboos by the stream reflect the cold sands; A thatched cottage amidst green mountains is the dwelling of a recluse.
The swallow returns amidst the rain of Cold Food Festival; Spring winds open wide the fields of apricot blossoms. (By Jianxin Fu)
Lamenting Master Gulín:
From antiquity to the present, a single yawn; across the vast ocean of kalpas, clouds of dust arise.
Last night, space performed a somersault, startling those gathered on the Vulture Peak. (Yuejiang Yin)
Tu Shun wept for his teacher;
Feng Yuan was brilliant and clear-sighted, seeing the Way beyond the mundane stream. He forged ahead to the ultimate peak without ceasing.
Hearing it said that his hundred limbs were as emaciated as a crane’s, one cannot help but pity him—already a withered skull even before death.
The Dharma-gate is no source of merit; I lament that you have abandoned the succession of the heavens. You do not rectify your followers and cast them aside.
Though you may pursue excellence in this land or other regions, with a bowl that has no bottom, who can be entrusted to transmit it?

The school notice from Xian County, stuck like a snail on a wall; my own hand-copying of the *Jiannan* poems in tiny characters—these shatter the iron-stone heart of anyone who encounters them, far surpassing the sound of three cries of a monkey.
The seventy-six years of the late Layman Zhengshen’s life were entirely a dream; being dragged and pulled along, none of it was real.
He has now released his entire body as a treasury of radiant light, leaving the people of this Jambudvīpa world in a state of doubt (Zhiguanhui).
*Zadu hai*, Scroll Three;
*Zadu hai*, Scroll Four.
Re-edited by the Śramaṇa Xingyin, Successor at Bailing Monastery in the Capital.
The Yellow-Faced Old Man in the Great Hall has eyes full of rheum; he employs a thousand schemes and ten thousand stratagems to seek advantage.
Now, with no place for himself to stand, he must have his descendants cover him over (Songyuan Yue).
Old Gautama’s face is yellow; his entire body has nowhere to hide.
Let us all join in covering him up, lest he remain bare-bodied and exposed in full view. (Xiu Yan Rui)
The hanging bell is as light as a goose feather, yet as heavy as a mountain. Hung out in the open for all to see:
one sound penetrates directly beyond the realm of Wei-yin, shaking the heavens and chilling the stars (Zhe-weng Yan).
As soon as it is cast from the mold, it turns elegant and refined. On level ground he tells him to stop, yet he refuses to stop.
If you wish to let your great voice resound through the universe, you must simply ascend one more floor (from the *Kuchan Jing*).
Fifty-third Case:
Xiǎngbì said, "Fortunately, the ten directions have no walls. Who would take five colors to paint empty space?
Within the eyes of Śraddhāgupta, cataracts have grown; remove one layer, yet another remains. (Xīyán Huì)

The entire body of the cast bell is but a single mouth. Rolled forth from the furnace of a hundred refinements, it sends the setting sun back to its rest and further urges the bright moon up the watchtowers. (Xueyan Qin)
Turning the body to emerge from the great furnace and bellows, one does not suffer the pressure of the tongs and hammers weighing ten thousand *qun*.
With a single blow, a pure wind pervades the universe, calling back how many who are still dreaming within the world. (Jiān’ān Qīng)
Turning over within the great furnace and bellows—open your mouth and you shall know there is one who appreciates the sound.
How many monks stand side by side, tilting their ears to listen as his commands shake the monastic groves! (Dai’an Zhuang)
The Eight-Faced Transformation Treasury is entirely free from the marks of axe or chisel; piling gold and smearing green, they strive for novelty.
Meeting a hand of statecraft upon leaving the gate, he turns the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
Gautama, you old thief, your mouth is a personal latrine; donkey dung mixed with plenty of horse dung. You beat them all into one lump and toss it away;
as for that sky-piercing stench, what can you do about it? (Changweng Jing)
A single point of the transformed lamp has not yet radiated its brilliance; the lanterns and the pillar knit their brows in the dark.
Suddenly, one stumbles upon the "Star Son," who shatters the iron mask of Gautama. (Jiandang Ji)
When the light of the mind is ignited, the flower immediately blooms; let it illuminate the sands of the Ganges for a thousand ages.
Even if the great earth were to be struck by the Vairambha wind, how could it ever be extinguished? (Guyuan said.)
A single point of radiant light at the beginning of the kalpa, forged forth by fierce and intense effort;
poured into the azure lapis lazuli, the smiles of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas unfold (Wuyan Ran).
Water-lanterns stretch across ten thousand *li* of misty waves into the pure autumn; silver lamps shine brightly as they float upon the central current.
Since that single point of radiance was first seen, they have followed the surges and trailed the ripples, refusing to cease (Chijue Chong).
The Lotus Sutra written in blood:
a man of great character has blood in his skin; when he pricks himself, he knows it himself.
On the tip of a single hair, he can manifest transformations—three or four branches of red lotus flowers. (Yungu)
Transcribing scriptures with characters that do not form the eightfold path is an error; when held up before the light for all to see, Śākyamuni’s tongue has no bone.
Picking up yellow leaves to frighten small children—Cloud Nest Rock.

From the beginning at the Deer Park to the end at the Antelope River, for over forty years his mouth has spoken too much. Upon the glowing embers of the furnace, he shall suffer the punishment of having his tongue pulled out.
Do not say that his offense is not subject to a heavy sentence. (Huanglong Nan)

To write out the *Lotus Sūtra* for the sake of monks—where has even a single character of this scripture ever been? Do not write stupas and slander the Old Barbarian (the Buddha). If you slander the Old Barbarian, there will surely be retribution;
it shall certainly cause you to have not a single hair remaining on your head or body. (Guyeando)
Transforming salt in a red furnace, the surging waves establish the teaching of dryness. A silver mountain emerges, its brilliance chilling to the heart.
Even after Master Ma’s reckless behavior, one must not be deceived by his tongue (Songyuan Yue).
Mixing water and mud together in one place, they are boiled until the water dries and the mud is spent, and the "snow-flower" (a fine white powder) emerges.
Seizing the moment to collect it, its price reaches the heavens; with clear certification, who would dare to dispute it? (Qian’an Guang)
A single stroke of the axe splits the firewood in two, cutting off all confusion and error; yet one cannot avoid still entering the thicket of weeds.
Only when the entire body has been thoroughly scorched until it is red and raw does the transformation of the raw into the cooked depend entirely upon him (Zhe’ung Yan).
Transformed into black soot and lacquer, his entire body is a skin of iron. When he strikes the head, sparks fly. O *dānapati*, do not offer a light price;
for smelting both sages and commoners, it is always he (Fuaran).
The circumstances of Heze’s repairing the Nirvana Hall, the Needle-Piercing Pavilion, and the Pit for Drowning—these matters have all been overturned along the path to Nirvana.
When the work is applied at every point, seeing it is not difficult. While washing one's face, one suddenly feels the nose;
the mountain is well-hidden within the eye of a needle (Master Heze).
Seeking the celestial scripture to cross over, it enters the hand and the crown of the head opens; understanding that the mind is empty, he comes as a successful graduate.
He laughs in turn at the old man of yesteryear who carried the mortar, who spent half his life lingering at Huangmei (Zhe’ung Yan).
I myself detest being a Buddha and refuse to be one. You want your *kāṣāya* draped over one shoulder.
As we walk together along the mountain path, let each of us look at the wind and smoke before our own eyes. (Tianmu Li)
The transformation bath:
bathe the whole body until naked and bare. Fill the ladle to the brim and pour it upon the itchy spots.
Once cold sweat breaks out over the entire body, all ailments will naturally vanish at once. (Zhuan’an Gui)
The more one washes, the more dust and grime there appears. Cast down the ladle and see what happens. This is not to air one’s family’s private faults before others;
it is simply to add firewood to assist the boiling cauldron. (Pointing at the hall.)
I have transformed the tiles of Mazu’s Hall to deliver this message to the old adept of Jiangxi: let them be scorched by the sun and blown by the wind;
it is not that his descendants lack the means to manage them, but one must see the moment they melt like ice and crumble like tiles. (Tuzhu Wuer)
Debin composed this verse for the Double Yang Pagoda:
The nine-story pagoda soars beyond the azure heavens; The sacred traces of the Seven Buddhas reside above. The mountains are cold and the clouds are chill at midnight;
One hears only the celestial music and the fragrance of heaven.
This old monk begs for a verse to solicit funds for his burial niche;
with no place to hide his body, what else is there to hide? His icy bones are the immortal’s robe made of jade.
Even the Buddha-eye vainly claims it cannot be seen; clearly the Big Dipper basks in the slanting sun. (By Mei Fengren)
Repairing a broken boat upon the river of birth and death— Perforated here and there, half-sinking and half-floating. In this Sahā world, the ocean of karma has fierce winds and waves;
I earnestly exhort you all: exert yourselves in cultivation! (Guyun Jian)

The heavy-sounding Dharma drum hides its courage within its entire body; let its harsh sound spread freely in all directions. Heaven and earth have yet to believe that those who truly know it are few;
though its bones are exposed and its skin pierced, there is no harm at all. (Daiweng Yue)
At Mount Mao, the Jade Terrace Peak is so high that it is difficult to set foot upon; many travelers rest halfway along the path.
Opening the gates where there is no place to lodge, he leads each one to the very ground. (Fozhao Guang)
The Great Pavilion welcomes guests;
at the mouth of the Three Rivers, the tide rises and falls. People come and go at the crossroads of the four paths. Let it all go and you will know the place of peace and joy.
Master Sizhou was originally not in Yangzhou (Wuzhun Shanfan).
The Great Furong receives guests;
where can one find the traces of those who come from the waters and clouds? Having traversed every peak of Tiantai and Yandang, when physical strength is exhausted, all news is exhausted.
Little Furong receives Great Furong (Wuzhun Shanfan).
Receiving guests with wind and moon, he does not store even a stalk of leek or a grain of rice; those who wish to partake of the wind and moon may do as they please.
Do not disdain this cold and flavorless state—once satisfied, it can dispel the hunger of ten thousand kalpas. (Shangyuan)
At the crowing of the cock, I welcome guests;
a single grain of rice is begged from the perfection of giving. A stalk of vegetable was planted by another. My private affairs are not to be compared with those of other quarters;
yet I must open my door to receive those who come and go. (Shangyin)
Huang Hanling opens a reception path that winds around the head of ten-thousand-fathom cliffs; when travelers reach this place, they are filled with sorrow.
Suddenly finding a place of rest, they wander at ease through the layered passes and mountains (High Plateau Spring).
Fishing Village Receiving Guests:
Beyond the Wu Mountains and before the Yue Mountains, there is food to satisfy hunger and mats to sleep upon. Upon arriving here, one can find rest;
yet the imperial capital remains separated by but a single tide’s journey by boat. (Jue'an Xiang)

Advancing toward the Moon Pavilion, the cassia orb shines solitary and bright against the vast azure sky. The curtains are drawn; the clear breeze brings a chill to the seat. Why is it that people do not realize this luminous reality?
Once more, following the shadows of the flowers, it climbs the balustrade. (Dachuan Ji)

Leaving the solitary islet in the center of the river, where the waves splash against the sky, the old fisherman comes to look at his fishing boat. His smoke-smocked robe and rain-hat are utterly useless;
he rolls up his line and sleeps with his legs outstretched. (Zhuan’an Gui)

The three teachings each establish their own schools and each honors its own path; they speak of Chan, they speak of the Way, and they speak of literature. The peach is red, the plum is white, and the rose is purple;
yet in the end, their roots and sprouts share the same spring (Yunshan).
In the *Three Smiles*, three figures are difficult to distinguish as inferior or superior. Your heart is like my heart; it is not fit to be explained, only fit for laughter.
One laughs until the Year of the Donkey, yet refuses to stop. (Wunian Fan)
Zutang and the others were people of a peaceful world; yet because of trivial matters, they allowed ignorance to grow long.
If they had caused everyone else to be able to abide in their proper lot, why would they have names inscribed upon the ancestral portraits?
Lineage charts are empty fame;
they are but marks carved upon a boat to find where a sword fell into the water. Our ancestors originally possessed not a single dharma. What flows forth from their chests covers heaven and earth;
even now, there are sons and yet more grandsons (Dongshan Yuan).
The various schools and sects are established according to this chart; they are linked in succession like a string of pearls.
One does not know whether, before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had yet arisen, there were already many such messages or not (Chijue Chong).
The withered pines depict gnarled, skeletal bones, enduring the cold of the years. Deep within the azure clouds, an old dragon coils. One laughs at those who pluck leaves and seek branches;
when they reach this point, how can they find a handhold to climb? (Guyeon-do)
In the Hall for Selecting Buddhas, there are hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and sentient beings; do not strive to compare them within that hall. The Mind-Seal is cast forth directly before you;
majestically and uprightly seated, one dwells in the field of tranquil light (the single source of spiritual efficacy).
Inscription on the Tiantu Mountain:
Lamenting for the Elder Westhill (Xiqiu), the Master He’an, Who Was Over Eighty Years of Age. His hair is entirely white and his yellow teeth are sparse;
he has purchased a small boat as large as a leaf. I weep for Master He’an as I pass over East Lake. (Zhu Yuandao)
Crossing the great river, I gaze at the white-haired peaks until the myriad layers of mountains vanish from sight; the waves of grace accumulated over vast eons have dried up to their very bottom.
It is not that there is treachery hidden within my breast, but truly, for one who has left the household life, it is difficult to repay one's parents. (By Tianmu Li)
Returning to the lake, the birds do not startle in flight and the waters do not flow. The azure depths are vast and empty, coldly reflecting autumn.
Upon the tip of the single line there is no fragrant bait; the wind rolls the reed blossoms onto the fishing boat. (Shi’an Fàn)
Seclusion on the Sea Mountain:

A Musing at Noon Having arisen from meditation at the midday window, the day is deep and still. Wherever my eyes touch, the mind is a single expanse of empty composure. The warbling of a fine bird knows my intent;
It sings its heart out, shattering the shade of the green willows. (Da-xie Qian)
A wild monk of Ch’wigak Temple welcomes guests descending through mist and mists. If you ask what “Ch’wigak” is, the gate is near Hong’a’s thousand-fathom well;
The stone bridge divides the waters as they wind around the pines and cypresses. (By Chang Mujin)
The three pagodas before Mount Sandalwood must be renovated; both ordinary and holy beings alike are instructed to take up their positions there.
Would you rather be like the destitute ghost-child of Shushan, who could not spend a single coin yet boasted of his elegance? (Oran’s Verse)
Beneath the cliff of Sunchon Cave, the cold spring murmurs; within the cavern, the alchemical hearth gives rise to purple mists. The gateway stands manifest yet cannot be entered;
in the vast whiteness of day, one walks with a torch in hand (Snow Mountain).
Of the seventy-two peaks of the Southern Marchmount (Nanyue), Mount Zhurong is the highest. It rises nine thousand seven hundred and thirty *zhang*;
looking down from it at the surrounding seas, they appear like fine autumn hairs. (Xutang and Yuyi)
The Min and E mountains and Mount Huading bow from afar; the Jiuhua and Wulao peaks come to pay their respects. The old monk above has no affairs all day long;
when inspiration strikes, he reaches for the clouds and the sky with his hand.
At Donglin, white campaka flowers drip with dew; the green bhikṣu-grass is shrouded in fragrance.
Upon this ground, not a speck of dust remains—what kind of person is worthy to dwell therein? (Chan Yue)

Within the mists and clouds between the north and south of the single mountain, Between the east and west of the two temples at the foot of the forested slopes. Opening my eyes now, it all seems like a dream;
Do not say that this is truly Mount Lu (Guizhu’an Gui).
From Xilin:
viewed crosswise, they form ridges; seen straight on, they become peaks. Their orientations and elevations differ in every way.
One does not recognize the true face of Mount Lu simply because one stands within its midst. (Su Dongpo)
The master’s forge smelts Buddhas and patriarchs; when guests arrive, he beats the drum of bitter tea.
Last night, the turtle-nosed snake of the South Mountain bit to death the white-fanged tiger of Mahāvīra. (Zhuan-an Gui; one version attributes this to "Titled: Xuefeng")
