The poisonous vapor of the Turtle-Nose Hermitage blazes fiercely and refuses to cease. He rolls about amidst the weeds, leaving no trace of his whereabouts. Now he lies across the level slope;
who dares to go first and touch the tip of his nose?
Praising the Giant Pepper:
When ten thousand trees have withered and fallen, it alone puts forth its brilliance. Hanging low, its fruit clusters first upon the branches. Its natural pungency has always been innate;
Once bitten, white sweat flows from every limb. (Master Meng’an’s Verse)
Presented to Master Yuanlu:
Who can comb their hair twice in a single day? Once the topknot is securely gathered, one should simply leave it as it is.
For the most part, his natural physique is so excellent that even without applying rouge, he remains elegant and refined. (Yuantong Xiu)
The green mountains of Jangjeong clearly reflect in the flowing river; half is Mingzhou, half is Yuezhou. Below the pavilion, the cold tide rises;
above the pavilion, the traveler—unaware of how many times the coming and going shall cease. (Pak Ong-hyeom)
Upon the Terrace of Nirvāṇa stands the Ghost Gate Barrier facing the sun. Those who attempt to pass with their unextinguished, thieving minds find it difficult.
If you can swiftly turn over and open your eyes, you will see that the house-top is but the old green mountains.

When a unique sprout of numinous growth emerges from the Incense Pavilion, you must know that the flower blooms upon a branch that never sprouted. Within this state, where the vital breath is impossible to conceal,
there is no need for the spring breeze to blow with particular intent.

Master Sheng’s voice as he preached the sutras still lingers within the pulley; yet, to truly behold Master Sheng is difficult indeed. A single curve of the railing holds the intent of a thousand ages;
the old monk remains silent, for the stone is stubborn.
In this lotus-leaf pond, who could be more destitute than I? My tattered robes hang down like lotus fibers.
As the spring wind adds fresh green to the surface of the pool, I see once more the ice-silk silkworm spinning its cocoon.
Encountering this object, people are made to look up to the patriarch’s style. A worn-out robe was left behind in a pool; the autumn wind blew it apart, and the spring wind mended it.
Not a single thread of effort has violated the pure ripples.
The Tasan Dam blocks the cold current with its tiered stone foundations; from here, the ocean tides follow their cyclical return. Travelers grow old, yet the green mountains remain;
as the ravine widens, the sound of the water flows without ceasing. (Yinshan)

Wearing out straw sandals, he has traversed every mountain side and water’s edge. Returning, he takes them off before the Dharma Hall. When monks come for an audience, they need not wrap themselves in their monastic robes;
tell me, when did the soles of your feet begin to wear through? (Meng’an Ge)
The shadow of the former residence of Master He falls deep into the clouds, its name unknown. At noon, incense burns while gǔ-millet and *huángjīng* are mixed together.
One does not know where it lacks intimacy; there are always those who come to ask about Er-ling (Xiangtan Yong).
The Stone of Three Lives deceives one another across past, present, and future. Cease playing with the spirit and the mass of karmic consciousness; a single slab of stone has been brought to ruin.
How many people come to brush away the moss and examine its traces?
A single sound—a crash of tiles and debris—lost the skull amidst the din; from this moment on, the lineage’s style turned desolate. Most pitiable are the ten thousand bamboos standing by the railing;
washed by rain and polished by wind, their sorrow does not fade.

The chessboard stones are clearly black and white, yet they have not yet been distinguished; a single square slab is as steep and perilous as a cliff. Try casting one before the pivot of the mechanism and see:
with spring winds and spring rains, how many patches of moss will grow?

On Su Gong’s Embankment, the spring breeze is gentle as willows sprout new shoots; ten *li* of lake light fall upon my painted skiff. Facing the site where the Immortal of the Slope once stood, I realize I have passed it by;
yet his ancient shrine still remains at the Third Bridge.

The Dragon Pool waterfall hangs ten thousand fathoms from the precipice like a perilous eaves; as it lets down its pearl curtain, even the sixth month is cold. Though the wind blows several times, it remains half-concealed;
it allows no one to roll it up, permitting only to be gazed upon.
In the midst of the Dragon’s Nose Water Cave, it suddenly bursts open; the jagged green stones are as smooth as moss.
The peach-blossom waves surge across the five lakes and four seas, all flowing forth from the tip of the nose.
The stone dragon drips water drop by drop into his nostrils; twenty famous springs cannot match this skull.
An old monk with white hair greedily rinses his teeth, leaning on his staff as he passes daily to the west of the cliff. (Hyŏnggwam Hŏng)

The stone platform was originally perfected by the very birth of heaven and earth; where it is most precipitous, it is level and smooth. Within it, there is naturally that which nods its head in agreement;
it is simply that no one understands how to preach the sutra.

An old horse from the military camp is led to bathe by the willow-lined pond. Spitting foam and drooling saliva, its steps grow slow. Washing it, one sees the scars of arrows and knows it harbors resentment;
The General has forgotten the time before he was enfeoffed as a Marquis. (Cangyun II)
In the painted scene of Peach Blossom Spring, colorful clouds unfold as they drift askew. Cocks and dogs are silent; there are but a few households.
Amidst the rise and fall of five hundred years, crimson rains fall in profusion upon the peach blossoms.
The Ox Diagram:
Three hundred fifty-five oxen frolic across the level marshes; they trample the spring wind until the hundred grasses wither.
Do not paint the monk of Mount Mui—someone might mistake it for a portrait of the Patriarch (by Xishou Tan).

In the central peak, foxes and monkeys howl as the moon descends into the middle crags; the wild traveler’s lamp burns on through the night as his verse is finished. Who can truly comprehend this scene at this moment?
A monk sitting in meditation deep within the thick white clouds—Amitābha.

On the Terrace of Mount Sumeru, drakes and egrets haunt the ponds; rain falls upon the lush green grass. Silk and brocade hang behind the curtains as the plum-blossom wind blows. How does this compare to the night when the moon rests upon the balustrade?
A single long cry resounds amidst a thousand peaks (the moon through the vines is crystalline).
Pines wither, rocks grow old, and frozen clouds collapse; reaching this point, the void seems to gradually lower. When one’s physical strength is exhausted, the spirit’s aspiration reaches far;
with whom can one take hands and ascend the celestial ladder? (Xutang Yu)
The Lapis Lazuli Bubble Guanyin is produced in a single breath of effort; perfectly round and polished, it is utterly free from even a speck of dust.
It is, in its entirety, a single realm of universal penetration; its gate is not opened lightly. (Gume Youyi)
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written in blood entered the Buddha’s belly;
drop by drop, it was the mother’s own lifeblood. Amidst the chaotic disorder of the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, no one in all the world could contain it;
yet it has returned to its origin and reverted to its source.
Lamp-flowers should not be compared to springtime cultivation; they transcend the clever artifice of human labor.
Though travelers fill the garden, they cannot find them, for they bloom within the fire. (Qingshan Xiu)
Look at the hands and eyes of the one on the spot when the firecrackers burst: the poisonous gas within the breast has been cultivated deeply for so long.
Borrowing a single spark of ignorance, it shatters thousands and tens of thousands of layers. (Zhuan’An’s Question)
Wrapped in paper and bound with hemp, it cannot be untied; when the conditions and time arrive, it emerges from its head. A single clap of thunder startles heaven and earth;
the ignorance of kalpas is reduced to ashes in an instant. (Compassion for living beings.)
The numinous clarity of the lantern—how could it rely on the light of the three suns? It habitually performs great deeds within the dark thoroughfare.
Because its single mind is ever unclouded, it shines upon heaven and mirrors the earth with natural brilliance. (Langya Zhen)
Tattered and ragged, this patched robe has seen many years; Picked up at random, it is draped over one shoulder. At midnight, returning from meditation, I fold it and set it down;
Who can be entrusted with the message within? (By Bairyam Ning)
Dwelling in the mountains as my years draw to a close, this pauper’s private property is not worth a single coin. With this one robe of patchwork cotton, I pass through both winter and summer;
when heat comes I strip it off, and when cold comes I put it on. (Ruo’an asked twice.)
Tearing off his robes and covering his head with them, he lies down; though earth grows old and heaven wastes away, he knows nothing of it. This is the true enjoyment of Sīti (Dead Heart);
even when losing advantage, one gains advantage.
The robes are so worn and tattered that not even an inch of thread remains to ward off the cold; why need one go to such lengths as to drape a long pole?
Now, everything is falling apart, scattered and sparse—where can the names of the Seven Buddhas be placed? (To Head Seat Yin).
The horse-lanterns gallop in circles, racing on without pause. There is no enlightened person to point out the way.
Extinguish the slightest spark within the mind, and the swords, spears, men, and horses will all cease at once. (Wuji Wu)
Spears fall like rain, horses gallop like the wind; they charge into the heavy encirclement without slackening. It is not that there is no room for a needle to prick the void;
how many heroes would stop their feet before them? (Yang’an Xin)
The winds of karma blow them along as swiftly as a shuttle; they vie for victory and contend for superiority, never letting up.
Before the sparks in their midst have been extinguished, one knows not when the weapons of war will cease (Qian’an Chū).
A broken coin, its half-moon shape obscured by dust; faintly visible are the characters of the Kaiyuan era.
In dim reflection, I imagine the time before its luster was shattered, when it could have settled all the injustices of the world. (The Woman of Biling)

Fragrant Pond—Fragrant Pond, the rain has cleared and the greens are newly lush. I have plucked green branches dripping with dew to bring home. On a single tree, remaining blossoms provoke the clamor of sparrows;
red fragrance fills the path, flying toward and overwhelming me. (Tianyin arrives.)
The fisherman’s basket holds no fish; he lacks the money for wine. The tavern keeper leaves behind his fishing boat.
Several times he wishes to trade his raincoat for cash, yet again fears that tomorrow will be a rainy day. (By a monk of West Lake)
At Huomushan, the "Buried Alive Hermitage" has long been renowned;
its burdens have never been light. To drink from the ox’s trough is ultimately the purity of the highest stream. My Master was buried before he had even died;
once again, he walks upon the very summits of Chao and You. (Zibo Ke)
Staying at Yongqing Temple (Emperor Jianwen):
Carying my staff, I traveled south; years have passed since then. Amidst mountain clouds and river moonlight, I chant idly. The dust of worldly mind has vanished entirely, leaving nothing behind;
I am no longer subject to the encroachments of human scrutiny. (Emperor Jianwen)
Staying Overnight in a Deep Village:
Traveling along, I stayed for one night in a deep village. Cocks and dogs bustle like a marketplace in this year of plenty. Seeing a guest at dusk, the whole family rejoices;
Under the moon, they catch fish by bailing out the pond water. (Chan Yue, No. 3)
In the deep mountains, I met an old monk;
his patched robe was coarse with thread, and his mind was like the moon. Holding his own hoe, he worked alongside the firewood blocks;
by the green stone stream, he walked treading upon fallen leaves, while a few wisps of cloud followed the snow of his two eyebrows.

Along the road through Linchuan, exiting one valley and entering another, the path winds and turns. The autumn wind has already arrived, yet the time for my return is late. Raising my head, where can I look for the tracks from which I came?
Ten thousand fathoms and a thousand mountains—the birds have flown far away.
At the Xuefeng Hermitage, the lingering snow is deep;
deer leave no tracks. Beyond the clouds, where does the woodcutter return? His flute plays on. The old Chan master rides a tiger without startling anyone;
the monkey gathers moss from the ruins and hangs upon the high rocks. (Xiaoyin Yun)
At Tiger Hill, I pay respects at the stupa of Patriarch Liang;
once his claws and fangs were displayed upon this peak. A slumbering tiger, majestic and fierce, none dare compare to him. Throughout the ages, who is there that recognizes his kindness?
On the empty steps, fallen leaves rustle in the deep autumn. (Muyun Men)
Seeing off Chan Practitioner Kesheng on His Visit Home:
Six feet tall and dignified, endowed with the most supreme intelligence, He must clearly understand the origin of this body. The spring breeze escorts him upon the road to Xin’an;
With a single heart of lingering affection, he gazes toward his mother.
The Verse for the Practice of Receiving Precepts:
The ancient Buddha who traveled on foot left behind radiance that could not be retained; Even an iron ox without feet must still go forward.
Although you have not yet trodden the path of Caoxi, I am glad that today you have escaped the fire pit. (Dahui Zonggao)
Staying overnight at Beishan, I present this to Master Weishan:

Clouds and pines carry the old resonance, clear waves echoing in the distance. Turning several times through the bends of the stream, I see a thatched hut. The bamboo fence is tightly closed, unconcerned with spring;
Mountain birds cry out in disarray as they tread upon the tips of blossoms. (Sanyiyu)
Along the road to Linping, the wind-whipped rushes playfully dally in their lightness and grace. They wish to stand still like dragonflies, yet they have no freedom to do so.
On the road beneath Mount Linping in the fifth month, countless lotus flowers fill the marshes and islets. (Daoqian)
Carrying his mother across the Qiantang River—the mother in the sedan chair, the son on the road. As the son could not keep pace, the mother called out from ahead.
Beyond the broken bridge and flowing waters, amidst the slanting sun, he felt ashamed to encounter the "filial" crows returning to feed their parents in the withered woods. (By Ji Gongxing)
Amidst the path through Shimen, the cry of the Sichuan cuckoo from a branch resounds once, once; across a hundred li of spring mountains, it bids farewell and welcomes.
Picking up the moon over Tan-tan at Letan, it shall directly cause ten thousand ages to shine with clarity upon people. (Guxue Zhe)
Ascending the Vimalakīrti Golden Grain Hall, I recall Master Dongwen;
green mountains fill my eyes, exactly as they were before. Seeking my teacher from the first stage, I remember years past;
the Dharma-gate of non-duality has no marks of difference—only the empty courtyard gains the lush growth of grass. (Muyun Mon)

To let one's feelings flow, flowers do not remain forever on the tree; humans do not remain forever in this world. When there are flowers, one must surely enjoy them; when there is wine, one must surely become drunk.
Autumn frost climbs upon the hair at the temples; the spring breeze cannot blow it away. (Deng Qingyang)
The communal labor has ended; I write this verse:
Tea buds, rustling, have just left the kiln; Bamboo shoots, in a frantic rush, again emerge from the mud. In this mountain hermitage, the spring tasks for the year are complete;
If one finds leisure, who cares that the head of the meditation seat is low? (Master Zhizhi Anzhu)

To pass the time, I used a small pot to boil vegetables and steamed rice over them. The vegetables were cooked and the rice fragrant just as the people were at their hungriest. Once the hunger-wound was healed, there was nothing more to do;
tomorrow morning, I shall follow this model to paint a cat (by the master Zu).
Spontaneously at ease amidst the snow, the plum blossoms bear the news of spring; within the pond, the moonlight possesses the spirit of night. Have there been no fine pleasures this year?
Do not take up our family tradition and show it to others. (Lan’an Shu)
Spontaneously composed:
"A dense web of spiders hangs from the eaves; beneath the steps, earthworms and mud are piled high.
Daruma’s eyes are utterly disregarded; usually read as a single verse. (Zhongfeng edition, two lines)
Autumn clouds drift in fragments across the vast autumn sky; Autumn leaves fall deep as the autumn rain chills. The wild man beneath the trees finds it hard to dry his clothes;
His eyebrows remain forever damp throughout the day.

To let one’s spontaneous inspiration flow, one should surely emulate Jiaoran: "In this life, I shall grow old in the serenity of poetry and Chan. What harm is there in producing even more startling lines?
Let me compose ten thousand poems throughout the rivers and mountains" (Mingjiao Song).
The Jade Pavilion stands upon the mountain, erected alone upon a precipitous cliff. Bamboo and trees encircle it in ten thousand layers of green.
Looking down at the setting sun from the depths of the ravine, one does not know there is a monk returning from beyond the clouds. (Yuzhi Ju)

Each wall-painting in the Cold Spring Gallery is a solid and dense body amidst the dust; changing heads and faces, they transform their spirits. Who would have known that striking the east wall is striking the west wall?
They are all people from the assembly on Vulture Peak. (Shuangshan)
This house is a composite of bricks, tiles, mud, and lime; its joints and crevices have been worked upon with great depth.
Within it lies a place to rest the body, yet how many deluded people fail to recognize the door! (Do not waste your efforts in vain.)
The pit of the Hell of Molten Iron in the Hall of the Buddha-Mother—this calamitous womb is reborn today once more.
Countless people beneath Mount Huangmei; who can pass before the gate with arms akimbo? (Zhongfeng Edition)
A thatched cottage by the lake, a mountain dwelling where I do not purchase the peaks of Shan; The thousand peaks upon the lake are idle at every turn. Verdant grass and white clouds detain me here;
What concern of the world could have anything to do with me? (Jiaoran)

The Stone Bridge of Tiantai spans the rushing mountain torrent, towering and majestic. The cascade plunges a thousand fathoms, roaring like a wrathful thunderclap. Five hundred *śrāvakas* could not see through it;
to this day, they remain "buried alive" at the edge of the cliff (Tianmu Ritual).

Passing by the Memorial Hall of Dongpo, he strove mightily to set right the orthodox teachings and refute the heterodox. He dreamed of Huangzhou and Huizhou, where a few bamboo-roofed rooms accommodated his aged form;
the great river flows eastward alone through the ages. (Dahui Zonggao)

Passing by the shrine of Qin Hui, I see a pair of new stone pillars by the roadside. I am told that in years past his official rank was no small one; who would have known that today cold smoke and sparse rain would bury him in the wild grass?
Where shall one ask Xiezi about the Zen staff? Turning my head, the village of Xu is locked in evening mist. Beyond the banks of Qiupu, a single song of the fisherman resounds;
a stinking wind blows across the ferryboat. (Mengguan Ren)

In a single thought of the spirit at Lei Qian’s stupa, his compassionate countenance was never distant. Why must you suddenly act so willfully and perversely? Lowering the high and conforming to the low—his compassionate heart is urgent;
he has vexed the Thunder God into a night of frantic toil. (Shitian Xun)

At the head of the mausoleum of a court lady, a dead tree sprouts faintly; at the crossroads, the ruined pavilion leans half-tilted. Her jade bones, through the passing years, have received no offerings;
she has become a butterfly that flutters among the pine blossoms.
The golden arm within the pure body at Foshouyan on Mount Lu; as the layered clouds of Kuanglu open at dawn, his single hand has no place to extend for the sake of others.
Listen, you weary beings, as he gazes vacantly over the precipice. (Zhongfeng Ben)

The distant peaks shine brightly as the mountain shadows slant across the overgrown grass paths. A cold clarity pierces to the bone through the half-drawn window gauze. A few cries of birds break the profound stillness;
the evening hues do not intrude upon this thatched-roof cottage. (Xueqiao Xin)
The Spring of the Blue Dragon does not rely on the power of clouds and thunder to boast its pride; with a single spray, it turns the level ground into surging waves.
Merging and flowing into the waters of the Zhejiang River, how could those who drink from it fail to have their temperaments refined?
Where does the birth-platform lie? The crows cry out as they go and return; morning after morning they ascend my birth-platform.
When the conditions for porridge and rice have finally exhausted themselves, the skin and fur fall away and the eyes open wide.

Setting out at dawn, I roll up my clothes by the *ge* tree; autumn rolls up the banana leaves. Traveling at dawn, the cold dew drifts over the tips of the grass. In the village, the fires of cooking smoke have not yet risen;
for now, I follow the crowing of the roosters across the plank bridge.
The Heart-Testing Stone:
Lofty and precipitous, it can test the heart. How many times have I stood alone, fearing the depth of the cliff? Suddenly, my feet tread upon the shattering void;
Wind arises upon the stone, and spring comes to the great earth. (By Xiu of Qing Shan)

The Shrine of the Floating Mother: A single promise is worth a thousand pieces of gold; how could one dare betray such an oath? Only then do I realize that righteousness is weighty and the body is light. The vast waters of the Huai River flow on forever;
I am filled with shame for the Prince (Wangsun) and grieve that his resentment remains unappeased. (By Zhuo’an Wensan)

The tombstone at the grave of Huaiyin still preserves his name from the Han; the surging waves lash the shore as if still vying for his glory. When success was achieved, it was said only that heroes are noble;
yet what difference was there between his crouching beneath the crossbar and the dog slaughtered after the hunt?
At West Pavilion, reminiscing about antiquity:
For thousands of years, Zhu Jing has earned its name for fishing. Where did the capsized boat go? I ask for the way back.
Under a sky of frost and moon on a night without a soul, it scatters into the whistling sound of broken reeds.

The Precious Saber of Long has long been renowned as a blade sharp enough to shave a hair; ten thousand pine fibers are bound securely by it alone. Do not say that those of dull faculties lack the power to sever;
herein lies the very sword that brings life to men. (Lianchi Hong)
*Zadu hai*, Volume Four;
*Zadu hai*, Volume Five.
Re-edited by the monk Xingyin, successor to the Patriarchs at Berlin, Kyoto.
Bimoyan blocks the heavy ford;
those who pass through find it difficult. One must believe that the skull is dry when holding up the pitchfork. Only after reaching Huo Mountain will you know the essential point:
that "dying together and living together" is not yet worth observing. (Mingjue Xian)
At the foot of the Piyun Terrace, beneath the forest, he constantly cherished Old Yaoshan. When skin and flesh have fallen away, the myriad functions are at rest.
Sometimes, under the moon, he roars while parting the clouds; his timeless elegance fills the world. (Cishou Shen)
I have built a thatched cottage outside the bamboo grove and a pavilion beneath the bridge; half the pond is covered with lotus leaves, and the other half with water chestnuts.
Sitting all day upon a square bed and a curved desk, there is but one old monk amidst ten thousand folds of green mountains. (Quanshi Le)

From the time I came from Nanyue to Xuedou at Qiyun Hermitage, more than twenty years have passed without my descending the mountain. Having dwelt in hermitages in both places, my body is already old;
I seek out secluded valleys to nourish my failing strength (in response to the Hermit Master).
The worlds of the ten directions are wide before one’s eyes; casting aside Yun’an, I pass on to other mountains. When the three robes are worn through, they are mended;
with a single staff of *qili* wood, I am companion to my leisure.
A monk of constant practice, yellow skin wrapping bones; with tattered robes covering his head, a hundred anxieties stilled. Old in years, too weary to frequently receive guests;
he climbs once more the steep, azure peaks, grasping at the vines.
Sickness arises, sickness comes, and again sickness clings to skin and bone. Shaking it all off, there is not a single thing. Unable to take a step in walking, the voice for speech is low;
the nostrils remain as they were, stark and bare. (Dongshan Yan)
I beg to return to grow old in the mountains;

for six years I have chanted the Patriarch’s mechanism in the imperial capital. Twice I attended the celestial majesty within the golden halls. Now that I hide away among the green mountains, what joy could I find?
In my satchel, I carry nothing but the Imperial Verses to take home. (By Da’jue Lian)

A thousand clusters of cloud-capped mountains, ten thousand valleys of flowing streams; With an idle body, I return to grow old upon this mountain peak. For the remainder of my life, I pray for boundless longevity;
A single incense stick of pure fragrance fills the stone pavilion.
Inscription on the Wall upon Occasional Mooring at Zhai:
A hundred years are not yet finished; finish them as they come. At fifty, I have no home; I do not make a home.
Knowing what my face will be tomorrow and in days to come— Who would seek out this *pāṭa*? (By Dāiwēng Yuè)
Jinshan Remembers the Past:
Returning today, I recall times gone by; before the portrait hall, my eyes well with tears for the former Master. The Way of the Patriarchs lies desolate as dust settles once more;
how many clearly distinguish the skin from the marrow?

Having finished reading the *Zhuan Deng Lu* (The Transmission of the Lamp), my hair has already turned white; how many more *lakṣas* of worldly achievements can one still strive for? Having woken from my midday nap, dust covers the desk;
the sun sets idly through half the eaves as flowers fall upon the courtyard. (Sū Shòuzuō)
Dawn passes over West Lake;
the water and mountain colors are devoid of people. At this clear morning, who beholds the first spring? As the red sun gradually rises, strings and pipes begin to play;
the mist and fog across half the lake are but the dust of travelers. (Tianyin arrives.)

Visiting Donglin Temple again, its terraces and halls rise in tiers amidst auspicious mists; cassia flowers drift like snow as the waters flow with a murmur. Do not doubt that you will have no news of me as I depart for afar;
seventy thousand years shall pass as but half a year. (Guanxiu, No. 4)
The old carriage of Xuánxuān proclaims its presence as the lingering clouds remain damp; at the solitary tomb of Yeshé, the setting sun lingers long.
There is a mountain monk leaning against a pine tree to sleep, fearing that someone might come to take his white ape.
The jade image and pearl niche are crossed by drifting clouds of incense; many brocade-like mists arise beside the stone walls. Where is the snake-wardening practitioner now?
Amidst the flowers, one hears only the cry of the poison-bird.
On the stone wall of this mountain retreat, a red sandalwood stupa rises six or seven stories; white lotus blossoms bloom in two or three branches.
When Zen travelers meet, they merely snap their fingers—how many can truly understand this mind? (The preceding author)
At the abandoned temple of Lengyan, amidst ten thousand flowers, a painted pavilion rises anew. A jade maiden leans upon the railing as spring unfolds in the heavens.
A single bright moon, cold beyond the sky, once at night’s depth shone upon those who sat in meditation (Zibai Ke).

At Niutou Monastery, I have wandered through many paths and asked for directions again and again; deep within the forested clouds, my arrival was late. When the monks of the temple saw me, they did not speak;
I stood alone facing the setting sun, reading a broken stele (by Lu Shan Tai).

At Changle Temple, a single mound of mountain greenness contains the monastery; streams wind around it on all four sides, and the sound of bells is heard from afar. Having found the monks' quarters, they are sealed by clouds;
tiger tracks cover the courtyard, where two or three pines stand. (Zhi Zhuhai)

Sitting cross-legged by the earthen brazier at night, I sit motionless as the withered leaves burn out. The young attendant sleeps soundly and does not answer when called. The great trichiliocosm is empty and void;
there is neither Buddha nor Patriarch. An old insect turns over the lamp in the night shrine. (Chushi Qi)
The lamp in the mountain window has burned down to its last drop of oil; the hearth is cold and desolate without a fire.
Leaving the meditation topic to be raised again tomorrow, the monk strikes the bell and ascends the tower once more. (Gong Duseo)
With a dull axe for planting pines, I shoulder my burden through snow that has not yet melted; I do not refuse the weary steps up the steep slopes.
Having planted these numinous roots with ease, one shall soon see green branches grow in the spring breeze. (Yuansou Duan)

Planting seedlings with sparse and humble skill, he was unable to dwell in the marketplace. Questioning farmers and learning the ways of cultivation, he strove to be the first. Lately, he has attained the true samādhi;
throwing them up or tossing them across, they fly straight as a bowstring. (Ji Shuǎng)

The woodcutter suddenly takes up his sharp axe and chops at the root; he cares not for the flourishing or withering, nor the long or short branches. Bound away, they will not burn out even through a whole winter;
whether existent or non-existent, the phrases follow one another entirely. (Shichao Ning)
Spontaneous Verse:
Ditching a trench to draw water for irrigating the vegetable garden, Placing bamboo to form a fence protecting the medicinal sprouts. Willow catkins like silk are easily disheveled by the wind;
Plum blossoms like snow find it hard to melt in the sun. (Haizhou Ci)
Observing a young boy fishing by the riverbank:
a child with disheveled hair learns to cast his line. Sitting sideways upon the moss, his body is hidden by the grass. When passersby ask for directions, he beckons from afar;
fearing that the fish might be startled, he does not answer them. (Hu Dingjiao)
The Golden Mountain emerges from the waves, its peak first rising high; it cleaves the Long River into two flowing streams. Red dust from the opposite bank cannot fly across;
here, groups of three and two ferry people in their boats. (Tiantong Wu)

"Empty Space Gives Birth to a Rock (the space within the rock is habitable by humans, while its surface above is as level as a whetstone; a pavilion was built therein, hence it is called 'Space-Born').
Everyone says it is solitary and precarious, never standing firm; who knows that the Great Earth itself is supported by emptiness?
If you wish to see a pavilion built in mid-air, please walk upon the back of empty space. (Mumen Chuanxin Mu, Case 2)
The sleeping ox is stubborn;
its hide is like iron, its bones like steel. Its nostrils are perfectly integrated, governing all with forgetfulness.
It is simply because the ancestral fields are so excellent that it is permitted to lie through the moonlight and sleep amidst the frost.
A single leaf from Wuzhi Mountain floats beyond the heavens; a thousand peaks fall into the mirror. Who can raise a single hand and cleave through the vast void? (Hanshan Qing)
Xue Mili emerges from amidst a mound of white jade, his entire body revealed; dragging his cloth bag across, his cold countenance breaks into a smile.
It is solely because sentient beings suffer so much from feverish afflictions that he descends to be born here, rather than waiting for the future. (Langya Huijue)

The twin sword-crests hang down from the edge of heaven, towering above the surrounding peaks. When the sun shines upon their cold blades, the blood-red luster deepens. In the past, the void was once carved and divided by them;
even now, wind and rain continue to polish them. (Monk’s marginal note)
Crossing Caoxi, I tread upon thousands of layers of empty green; winding through Caoxi, it encloses the Buddhist palace.
If one wishes to ask what was transmitted in Lingnan, it lies amidst the green mountains, white birds, and the sound of water. (Zibai Ke)
Mount Yandang unfurls its banner, inviting me to pass through the Celestial Window; the Stone Maiden and the Twin Swallows display their smiling countenances.
The brush is poised, dipping into the dragon-nose spring until it runs dry, as I casually inscribe across the stone screen (Kuchan’s Mirror).

I have beheld famous mountains across the four seas, yet among them, this landscape is difficult to capture in a record. On the mountain’s edge, I once saw an old man with white hair who said of himself:
"In a lifetime, one can never look upon it enough. (Attributed to Wei Yi-run)
Having sold his hair-broom, his entire body has fallen away in the cauldron of boiling water;
now, with not a speck of dust upon his billion hairs, he wanders with his staff in hand, waiting for someone at the crossroads. (Meng’an Ge)
When I call upon you, O Flower-Dragon (Huajing), you immediately come; yet you must labor in vain carrying water and hauling firewood.
Out of pity for those who merely follow the herd and the crowd, I stretch out my hand to ask others for straw sandals. (Zhongfeng Benji, Vol. 2)
Sweeping the ground, one clears away the heaps of refuse from before; yet the dust still covers the earth. In a moment, both the handle and the bristles are cast aside;
the five-petaled wondrous flower blooms upon the broom.
A fire broke out in the hall of beggars, killing several people;
the male and female mendicants suffered under the intense heat. As their innate ignorance (*avidyā*) flared up, the entire family perished in a single night;
from their dead skulls, not even smoke arose.
Basking in the sun at a thatched cottage facing south—when the weather is cold, basking in the sun is best; the great sun surpasses a soft fire, for first of all, it produces no smoke. (Śiṣyendra)
Abandoning my lectures, I returned to Yunqi to cultivate the Pure Land path;
across a hundred cities and through misty waters, I had lost my sense of direction. Forty years have passed since I became deaf to the Dharma, yet I still recall the guests by the Lotus Pond;
amidst the sound of pines and the moonlight, we shared the joy of joint practice (Yuetam De).
When Qingshan first opened [the monastery], clouds shrouded the high fortress leaning against Jingnan; I idly trimmed the vines and creepers to construct a small hermitage.
Sitting alone as the moonlight shines upon the door, nothing else reaches the mountain peak. (Composed by Qingshan Xiu)
The Lotus Sutra written in blood, layer upon layer of precious treasuries, all upon the tip of a single hair. Reveal it from that single hair-tip and look!
Sixty thousand words, drop by drop of blood—gold could not cast such a heart and liver. (Xiao Yin, 2)
Inscription for the Calligraphic Manuscript of Master Zhongfeng:
The Dharma-mechanism of all Buddhas pours forth like clouds from a vase; Unable to bear gazing upon it, tears fall in profusion.
Yet I still fear that the dragon-slaying sword within its jade casket Will pierce the roof and fly off with a clap of thunder.
Reading the "Spontaneously Accomplished Sentences" from Miamu’s discourse, they lack full integration; seize a monk with them and his entire lineage is extinguished.
The True Dharma Eye transmitted by the Seven Buddhas—people call it a broken sand pot (Yutang Yi).
Reading these words from Chan-an:
A Persian from the South Sea holds secret mantras; of a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, few know them. A spring breeze comes from nowhere;
it blows down three or four branches of peach blossoms. (Zhongji Cai)
The Master of the Peak, Fǒngzàng, wrote out the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in blood;
it proclaims everywhere, proclaims in every land, and proclaims with blazing intensity. Boundless fragrant waters flow with dripping blood;
within the groves of various flowers, it is as red as brocade. The fifty-three patriarchs are drunk like mud. (Yuejiang Yin)
Shattering a single mote of dust, the Great Sūtra emerges; bloodstains and stinking sweat fill over a hundred cities. Sudhana has gone south with no news;
his weeping breaks the cries of the cuckoo on the spring mountains.

Writing the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in blood surpasses the gift of the seven treasures; it was amidst the spring blossoms at the Jeta Grove assembly that one must know the Bodhisattva’s blood for copying the scripture flowed forth from the Tathāgata’s body of forbearance.
The *Avataṃsaka* in its nine assemblies was written in blood; as compassion descended, hot blood was sprayed forth. The precious ten bodies were soiled with dust.
Had they not been gathered up upon the tip of a hair, all people on the great earth would have been stained by it. (Tièguān Shū)
When did Vajraśīrṣa, the Head Seat, transcribe the Lotus Sūtra with his own blood?
Who was his father? Who was his mother? That he harbored such defiance in his breast makes him a true son.
Behold the place where righteousness severs sentiment and attachment: three or four branches of lotus flowers bloom. (Wuyun Gu)
Inscription for the Painting of the Fishing Terrace:
The river is empty as the sun sets and the evening clouds return; The gorges constrain the flying sails as they emerge from the treetops. Of the Han empire’s legacy, only the wind and moon remain;
Ten miles of green mountains lead to the fishing terrace. (Yuzhi Ju)
Inscription on a Scroll Concerning Dwelling in the Mountains Seclusion in the mountains is excellent for cultivating practice. Firewood and water are already provided when one opens the door.
If there is always rice in the pot, what suffering is there in leaving the household life? Why must one tread the worldly path? (Muyun Men)
Hanging the straw sandals before the abbot’s door; drifting with the flow or stopping at the pit, let fate take its course. The old monk’s soles have always been broad;
it is not certain that his skull will be buried here.
Monk’s Shoe Chrysanthemums:
Who scattered these monk’s sandals by the eastern fence? Whenever autumn deepens, their fragrance wafts abroad.
Could it be that when Yuanming visited Huiyuan, he once returned from Tiger Creek carrying a pair with him? (Langya Zhen)
I contemplate returning to my former state, yet I can only turn my title; but to turn one's title is to turn toward what is increasingly unfitting.
How could it compare to leaning against the railing atop the lofty pavilion of the Benevolent King, idly singing "Wang Jiangnan"?
Entrusted to Yanguan An:
A withered tree leans against a cold forest; though it encounters spring many times, its heart does not change. Woodsmen see it yet do not gather it;
why does the man of Ying labor so hard to search for it? (Damei Chang)
The śāla tree, the precious śāla tree, was planted by my Master; it has come directly from a single stream of the Dragon Pond.
Its branches cover heaven and earth, its roots are already firm, and for generations of descendants, they shall witness its blossoming. (Stone Chariot)
Chan Master Yunju You’s Incense-Burning Verse:
“One body enters samādhi, a thousand bodies emerge; Yunju does not strike that drum or play that flute. Tuhota Hua entered Goryeo;
The Persian’s nostrils prop open the white sun. (Huang Tingjian)

Secluded behind closed doors, my withered body and skeletal frame have had all hundred thoughts reduced to ash. The mountain monkeys and wild cranes suspect me with bitter distrust. With the door shut tight, I alone face the rain upon the green pines;
even when meeting people, my smiling mouth is too weary to open (as seen in Jianxin Fu).
I went to Tiantong;

all day long I remained in quietude within my mountain hut. I did not speak of the Buddha-dharma, for dust gathered upon my lips. Merely to pass through a single thread of connection, I opened the rush-mat door;
a royal decree had arrived at the head of Liangzhu Mountain (from Tianmu).
In response to the letter from Xi Hua Tanhu requesting the date for his entry into the mountains:
To till the fields and seek out a meal is the lifelong vow of this old man. How could I dare trouble you further by beckoning you?
I shall hang my gourd once the *mugua* flowers are in bloom. (Daiweng Yue)
Accepting the invitation to visit Cui Feng, he bid farewell to Master Lingyin;
as he departed, his emotions were such that he could not bring himself to speak. To proclaim the essence of the School is also a matter of leisure.
"I deeply revere the Teacher and the assembly of the sea; my longing for the Vulture Peak is beyond measure. (By Mingjue Xian II)
Concealing his traces, he finds delight in painting;
he cherished Dongting Lake in years past. Seventy-two peaks rise green from the heart of the waves. Now, reclining in high repose, he reflects on those former times;
Lu Gong has been added to lean against the stone screen.
In the mountains south of Jingnan, I long for my kin;

evening clouds and autumn grasses spread across the west of the lake. The mountain colors are dim and vast, and as I gaze, my way grows lost. Wild geese have reached Eastern Wu, yet no letter has been sent.
Under a sky of frosty moonlight, I listen to the crows’ cries. (Wonmin)
Enduring heavy sitting, severing the solitary peril, he refuses to rest; he bears the burden of magnificent pavilions and tiered towers.
The patriarch’s livelihood is as heavy as a mountain, yet the full power of it returns entirely to his crown and forehead. (Shu’ān Zōng)

To the north of West Lake, bamboo shoots from Chunyuan pass over the wall; beneath the wall, the lush grass is even more fragrant. With warbling birds and wild flowers, there is no place for questioning;
the azure mountains firmly hold back the setting sun. (Hong Juefan)
How many times have I boarded a boat alone upon West Lake? The boatman recognizes me and does not ask for payment. A single cry of a bird breaks the profound stillness;
It is precisely at this moment, as the mountain stands before the setting sun. (Daoji 2)
Beyond the shore, peach blossoms bloom like crimson brocade; On both banks, willows sway with light green silk threads.
Gazing afar at where white egrets spy for fish, They pierce through the placid lake—a single speck of azure.
The golden-grain pine stands at the gate, its courtyard desolate and sealed with green moss. It alone reveals the countenance of Master Kang from those bygone days.
Out of pity that the clouds have no place to return, he takes up his hoe and plants green pines amidst the rain. (Guyun Jian)
The circle of dharma-disciples gather around the hearth, deliberating upon the Water-Buffalo of Mount Gui. If a single word strikes home, people clap their hands;
beneath a sky full of frosty moonlight, they descend the western tower. (Zhongfeng Ben)
The matter of the hoe and the mattock leaves no trace; who throughout antiquity has understood how to repay this debt of gratitude?
As soon as the gourd is planted on the eastern wall, the radish of Zhenzhou takes root (Gu Xuezhe).
Dispelling Doubts:
How could a pawnshop ever understand the pawning of an ox? It is simply because the price is so high that it is truly difficult to repay. I suspect your resources are not very great;
in the end, you will find it hard to sustain this one head of cattle. (The Pawning of an Ox)

Wandering among the immortals, the ends of the earth are but a few inches from Penglai. Shell-palaces and pearl-halls open one after another. Gazing afar, the multitude of immortals pay court to the Emperor;
five-colored clouds and mists guard the Jade Terrace. (Hanshan Deqing)

In my heart, I long for the peak of Mount Zhurong on the Southern Marchmount to hear the celestial cocks crowing; there, soaring directly into the clouds and mists, it is most fit for dwelling. Worn out by toil, I wish to lie down beneath the pines;
having fully sated myself with smoke and mist, I am as intoxicated as mud.
In the midst of the army, I made a black robe, intending to exchange it for military attire; only then did I believe that following conditions is the true site of practice.
Even if the southern lands are like a blazing fire, they cannot melt a heart as cool as ice and snow.

Moved by the circumstances of my military post, I have quickly constructed a thatched hut in ten mu of wasteland. My mustard and Chinese cabbage are exhausted and now resemble common weeds. The Imperial Grace has not yet permitted me to return my monk’s robes;
for now, I shall simply circumambulate the steps several times. (Dahui Zonggao)
Moving to Mei Yang to show Yunnan:
Only when the wild geese return does one realize how far Xiao and Xiang are. At the head of Shigun Beach, do not resent Heaven; having lived here for ten years, Qin and Chu have been separated.
Now the wooden bow resumes its old karmic ties.
I planted plum trees by my cottage raft;
from beginning to end, my coming and going have merely followed conditions. Having returned to this place for the fifteenth year, I am ashamed that I have contributed nothing to the mountain gate.
The plum blossoms still grow before my old room. (By Dàwēng Yuè)

Passing once more by Yantán, the solitary tower stands firm and the old man’s cap is new. For what reason does it retain the springtime of Qīlǐ? In the end, there is nothing to be caught amidst the misty waves;
one can only gaze coldly at those who come and go.

Reaching Haihun, his former incarnation was surely Chitu Can; his wind-hat slanted of its own accord, and he wore robes of hemp and ramie. Having long been a guest at the Jade Rock, he contemplated the laws of poetry;
with the seashore mountains hidden within his sleeves, he returned home. (Hong Juefan, No. 2)
Heaven has no stratagem to cope with this old man; from time to time he is cast back into the bonds of restraint. Send word to my old friends that they need not worry for me;
fortunately, by virtue of royal service, I am able to roam the mountains.
The Song of the Fisherman’s Wife:
I, this old woman, dwell by the shores of Lake Tai. For twenty years I have come and gone amidst the misty waves.
I do not wish for my husband to go off to serve as an official; I wish only that he cast his nets and ply the oars with vigor. (Lushan Tai)
Self-delighting amidst a mass of white clouds is the ancient family tradition; ten thousand *li* of frosty skies share the same moonlight.
With few people reaching the forests or by the waterside, one only then knows that the joy of our Way is inexhaustible. (Dongshan Yan)
Picking tea, one plucks a *qi* and releases a *qiang*. For the most part, they measure things by their branches and leaves.
With the whole body entering the grass and the whole body emerging—what monk there is who lacks even an inch of growth? (Wumen Can).

Mist fills the garden as she carries her basket; amidst the song of yellow birds, she says it is midsummer’s height. Having finished her gathering, she does not realize the mountain is about to darken;
before the wind, she sings intermittently the *Bolanang* (Lingzhangyun).
Splitting wood does not require exhausting one's natural strength; what need is there for the wheel and mallet to come face-to-face?
If you recognize the place where the root and the fibers meet, a single axe-blade is enough to cleave it open. (From *Mengan Ge*)
The pack-donkey travels all day on a long road; for what reason does this lame donkey become exhausted in the mud? Most pitiable are those who labor as hired hands upon the journey;
one simply wishes to see them delivered home.
Retiring from affairs at Longxiang, I travel to Yandang and inscribe these words upon Longbi Water to express my intent:
The rain has fallen and the clouds have cleared, granting a moment of leisure; I shall now cast my horned head into this empty mountain.
At the tip of the nose, there is not so much as a single drop, Yet it draws everyone to this very place. (Longxiang Heng)
On this Cold Food Festival, vast clouds drift, shifting between sun and shade. Wildflowers hang heavy with moisture as evening deepens. Let not the traveler resent the heavens for their many rains;
all the more so, for spring is already deep upon the eastern ridges. (Mingjiao Song)

Declining the invitation of the King, he requested only a few thatched huts and ten thousand pine trees. Reclining on a rush mat, he sleeps soundly as the morning sun turns crimson over the sea. It was not that the worthy king could not have summoned him;
rather, the mountain man ought only to dwell within the mountains. (Inscription for Zisheng)
A smile arises from an incident; its cause has always been distinct. Who would have known that the Great Mass of Earth cannot tolerate a speck of dust?
From this moment on, gather in your natural feet; the iron stake shall bloom without waiting for spring. (Zibo Ke)
A single mat seven feet square before one; from of old, the sages of antiquity have departed by this path.
Never has it been heard that one could seek out the meaning of the Ancestor who came from the West by rummaging through old paper (by Daoweng Yue).
At Gaonan Beach, Linji met with misfortune in his prime; at the water’s edge, he lost his footing and fell into the surging tide.
To this day, when the moon sets in the third watch of the night, his vengeful spirit still harbors resentment that has not yet been extinguished. (Lingxi Yu)
In the moonlight, I harbor thoughts of Mount Heng;
by chance, my shadow lingers at a temple at the tail-end of the Xiang River. My dreams and soul have already ascended to Mount Zhurong. I rejoice that the affectionate moon remains by my side;
though my life in old age has not yet reached its end, it is nearing its close.
With a single bowl for alms, he holds it aloft with his hand in carefree ease; his elegant livelihood is revealed right before one’s face.
The village old woman does not understand the mountain monk’s intent, yet she still asks those nearby: "What is this?"

The cockscomb flower is pure white, setting it apart from other plants; the sedges before the steps are uniform. Viewing them at dawn while they are still covered in dew, there is only one thing missing:
a single cry (Zhenjing Wen).
The flower blooms like a cockscomb, beautifying the early autumn. Who could dye its purple silk-like head? At times the wind moves it, causing it to lean against others repeatedly;
it seems as though they are still vying with one another before the steps (Dongshan Yan).
A single sheet of paper from a *bājiǎo* tree, upon which I have yet to finish my writing; I do not know what sentiments lie within. For no reason, the night rain has opened it for me to peer inside;
drop by drop, *dang-dang*, I read through until dawn. (Lingsou Yuan)
Each leaf of the blue paper reflects through the window gauze; Moon-cut and wind-torn, they lean in a peculiar slant. A single piece of sincere heart is revealed in its entirety;
Let not the people of this age mistake them for flowers seen in a dream. (Guhang)
The chestnut burr, with its tangled bristles, has long harbored a fetus. Suddenly, bowing her head, she smiles and opens her mouth.
After all, it was his time that arrived; round and perfect, he has come forth (Fushiku Gen).
On the edge of this half-cake of the Great Ultimate Diagram, tooth marks are visible. Who has gnawed through the Iron Kunlun?
Clearly spitting out the crescent moon of the first day, it will not allow the clay ox to swallow it in a single mouth. (By Ruyong Gao)
Willow and poplar trees entwine with wind and rain—what of it? They are still more often than they move. Originally there was no intention to disturb the spring breeze;
it is simply that the spring breeze disturbs them (Beijian Jian).
The true nature of the olive rolls forth from the forest thicket. With its pointed head and sharp beak, it is the sovereign among fruits.
Had it not been bitten into pieces, how could its sweetness emerge after the bitterness? (Qingdao)
Among a hundred fruits, its aftertaste lingers longest; chewing it, a lingering fragrance remains in the teeth and cheeks.
It is solely because its entire body is as green as jade that it has earned a famous reputation spread throughout the four quarters. (Langya Zhen)
The alchemy furnace of the Taoist who sought to refine his form with cherries is empty; in vain he expended the nine-fold transformations of his life.
A peck of cinnabar can nowhere be found; at dawn, the branches play in the spring breeze. (By Suan Cong)
The flavor of the bamboo shoots from the clear pool is exceptionally long-lasting; held aloft in a ceramic bowl, they are all the more fragrant.
One cannot help but laugh at the mountain kitchen’s new banquet for guests—adding salt and sauce makes them unfit for tasting. (Dream Hermitage Style, No. 4)

In the mountains, the rhizomes of square bamboo shoots are entirely overgrown with brambles; only today do I encounter you alone. I know well that your firm and upright nature will withstand the frost;
as soon as you emerge from the earth, you are already beyond compare.
The bamboo shoots pierce the fence and pass through the rocks; the stalks of the shoots grow long. In the eighth month, the autumn wind makes them even more fragrant.
If it were to rain throughout the night at this very moment, next year’s spring colors would fill the verdant fields.
The swallows arrive;
bamboo shoots dot the clear pond, their twin blades light and delicate. Several stalks have just emerged, vying for sharpness and novelty. How much has the eastern wind grown them overnight?
They deserve to be the first spring of the gardens.
How magnificent it is for the brown fish to turn over on land! Its golden scales, like grains of millet, reveal its two gills.
Piteous that it did not enter the vast net of the heavens, it leaps out from atop the head of a yakṣa. (Śu’ān Zōng)

The pomegranate is a single species of numinous root planted beside a rock; its blossoming and fruiting require no artificial arrangement. Its belly is full of pearls and jewels, yet no one recognizes them;
it must wait until it turns deep crimson for its mouth to open of itself. (Guyeon-do)
Mossy jerky grows deep within the azure waves; how many times have I searched as the tides rise and fall? Once it is in hand, it naturally forms a whole piece;
this time, I fear not the height of the surging billows. (Zhe-weng Yan)
Sichuan pepper protrudes from its branches, each grain a vivid red; Within it, a pungent heat is concealed. The autumn wind blows, causing the lids to part;
In every delicacy of a hundred flavors, it reveals its merit.
Enveloped in mist and bearing dew, autumn has already arrived. Each grain is a deep crimson, its fragrance pervasive.
With eyes popping out and a mouth open in laughter, this time he no longer clings to his old branch (no need for broad indulgence).
The water conduit excels within the groves; the mind is already empty. Branches and leaves are swept away, leaving no trace.
Behold the place where he casts off his body and lies across—there he receives the transmission of the true pulse of Cao’an. (Guyuan Dao)
How could the old man Shuigiu ever have known how to roll a ball? There is a reason why he rolled it out into the great void. Observe him as he turns through high and low;
it is well that he follows the current and enters the stream even further. (Zhe’ung Yan)
The "Wicked Mother-in-law" bird wails with grief day and night in this land of misty waters; its cries wound the harmonious qi and knot the bowels in sorrow.
With such resentment ahead, to whom can it speak? The family’s shame has been needlessly broadcast abroad. (Shu’an Cong)
The loom-insect exhausts its efforts until its voice pierces the dawn; not a single thread of its celestial mechanism is revealed.
Deep in the night, beneath the thatched eaves, it hums and buzzes, weaving silently a segment of sorrowful autumnal melancholy.
The spider’s standing place is solitary and precarious, yet its function is intimate; upon a single thread, it settles heaven and earth. This fellow is not merely displaying clever artifice;
he intends to sever the life-root of all sentient beings. (Chuan’an)
Layer upon layer of nets are spread across the ancient dais; see how many come crashing their heads against them.
Unable to turn themselves around when the moment arrives, they are truly forced to die once more (He’an).
Casually letting fall a single strand of hair, one immediately beholds a strategy that spans heaven and earth.
How many sentient beings are lost on the path of life, bumping their heads against it only to forge bonds of mortal enmity (Daguang Gu).
Thank you, cat, for finding this most pitiable marten; its black and white markings are artfully linked, high and low. Within the assembly at Yiyun, it is a seed of compassion;
while the rat turns over the basin, the channel flows on in sleep. (Yiyun)
The cat that lost its way has a remarkably clever instinct for catching mice; yet once it enters another’s cage, it is difficult indeed to bring it back.
How many times have weary people vainly tapped their bowls, repeatedly calling out, "Flower-Slave, come eat your meal! (Nansou Mao)
Seeking a newly born tiger-faced *marmot* upon the hall of the cat—though I offer a thousand pieces of gold, it shall not be moved. My house is poor and truly has no mice to steal;
yet I wish to see the moment it turns over and climbs the tree (*Xutang Yulu*).
The drum’s entire body bears a flat surface with skin stretched across; its belly is empty as it passes through a lifetime.
Before the Hall of Good Dharma, it issues forth the correct command; struck lightly, it roars like a thunderclap. (Master Cai, the Head Seat)
Encircled and sealed, one’s own mind is empty; it envelops the great void within itself. With such a face of urgent urgency, who would dare to touch it?
Heyshan knows how to strike, shaking the primordial wind (Wuqu Kong).
In making a face-bucket, one must apply diligent effort. When used, it is entirely without leakage.
No matter how high one’s nose may reach toward the heavens, one cannot avoid bowing the head to meet it (Chijue Chong).
The cool curtains hold the moon, its light shining clearly like scattered fragments of jade; though there is no wind, ripples arise all around.
In the high hall, one knows not the heat even in the sixth month. This depends on the person letting go and looking (He’an).
The lapwing soars on its livelihood across the ends of the earth; shrouded in mist and clouds, it does not lose its way home.
Having understood this within one’s own house, this time it shall not fall into another’s home. (Duan Yan-yi)
The stream of Shuita Mo flows on directly and unceasingly; the wheel of the mechanism turns, stirring up wind and waves.
Within it, he churns out some little sons, universally granting them to all sentient beings to combat the demon of sleep. (Zhe’ung Yan)
Where the mechanical wheel turns, the water flows with a murmur; when the mechanism stops, the water is naturally still.
If one knows the place of its descent upon the very last stroke, the full splendor of spring fills the world (Dachuan Ji).
A water-mill in the depths of the deep mountains churns clear streams; as it turns its mechanism, it nods its head of its own accord.
It coldly laughs at the fellows from the three-village hamlet: when will this crowding and jostling ever cease? (Jitang)
A single stream of silver flows on and on; the millstone touches it, turning without rest.
Knowing whether the rice is white or not yet white, he nods his head to himself as if no one else were there (Amitāyus).
The sluice gates block the flow at the eighteen rapids; wherever the waterwheel touches, waves surge forth.
When the nodding and turning reach their consummation, the dragon pearl is pounded out, its brilliance chilling to the very marrow of one’s bones. (Gumei You)
The essence of the mind of the rosary is perfectly luminous, empty yet not empty; all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are identical in this.
Though incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas cannot exhaust its count, it resides solely within the grasp of the person themselves. (Ji’ān Zhēn)
With the fragrant staff, one blow and the eyes go blind; how strange that knots and joints have grown out of nowhere!
Had it not been personally grasped once, even a single step before others would have been difficult to take. (He’an)
The rattan staff—bones exposed, sinews sparse—is altogether authentic. Carried along, it suits this body of water and clouds. Rubbing it, the foolish and doting impulse stirs once more;
I simply wish to hold it crosswise and strike someone (Xuehong Xin).
Lapis lazuli, let go, let go; take up, take up. A single spark of spiritual light illuminates heaven and earth (Ding Sheng).
The entire body is translucent, like ice in a jade pitcher. Rekindled by the fire of medicine, the great vessel is perfected. Within this, if there is a mind, it is instantly ignited.
Look at how it radiates light everywhere (Zhe-weng Yan). Externally brilliant and clear, internally empty;
vast and open, a single point of glowing crimson. Where does the darkness of a thousand years go?
In every land and every speck of dust, amidst the blazing flames of light (Xiao-yan Bao).
In the lapis lazuli pavilion, ice pitchers stand solemnly like coiled jade dragons; they spit forth bright pearls that chill the heart. How wonderful it is on a moonless night in the mountain hall:
the stars of the heavens fall across the balustrade. (Suan Cong)
At Lingyun Rock, clouds come and go without intention; clouds come and clouds go without mind. When existence and non-existence are cut off, where is the numinous?
A solitary peak looms abruptly, its greenness reaching down to this day. (Cao Yuansheng)
The wind chimes have copper lips and iron tongues, too sharp and new. Hung from the corner of the tower, they do not reckon the passing of spring.
Beyond words lie hundreds of thousands of *samādhi* dharmas; through the wind, they speak them to those who are ready. (Juchuan Hai)
The entire body is a mouth hanging in empty space; it cares not for the winds from east, west, south, or north.
Equally for them, it speaks of Prajñā: *dīng-dōng, liao-dīng-dōng* (Chángwēng Jìng).
Tattered rags and coarse cloth robes, worn by old smoke-stains; by day they serve as a *kāṣāya*, by night as a quilt. Every seam and fold of the body is torn through;
even at sunrise, one remains too lazy to pick up a needle. (Mengan Ge)
A Letter to Master Xie Ziguan The calligraphy of the hand-scroll of Tao Yuanming’s poetry and prose is a true transmission from his own teacher.
At the pine-window, I have quietly practiced at the ink-well for my sake.
Tomorrow morning, I shall purchase further Chengxin paper, requesting that you write for me the "Return" (Guiquci) of Yuanming. (From the *Jiuxi Xu*)
Releasing a butterfly—how could this be mere idleness? Poring over old scrolls, one knows that beyond lies a radiant brilliance.
The Wayman does not dream the dreams of Zhuangzi; I release you to emerge from the head and fly beyond the heavens. (Ji’an Dà’èr)
Occasionally displaying the West River, he drank it all dry to meet Master Pang; the talkative Mazu was truly a master of empty words.
After his boundless household goods were left in total disarray, he took up a single ladle to scoop up the east wind.
Emperor Huizong ordered the painting of an image of Hui-chi to be circulated; he himself composed three verses:
"For seven hundred years, who could know the news from within samādhi? How can it compare to departing westward with but a single sandal?
What need is there to labor over wood to make a skin for birth and death?"
To hide a mountain in a marsh is also to hide one's person. In the world, there is no Way to be hidden that can be approached. Send word to Zhuang Zhou:
cease your deliberations; it is not within the trees that one finds the person who flees from responsibility.
The bodies of sentient beings are not insentient; each and every person possesses this very body within meditative concentration.
If you can realize that Bodhi originally has no tree, there is no need for arduous toil to question Huineng.
*Zadu hai*, Scroll Five;
*Zadu hai*, Scroll Six.
Re-edited by the Berlin-based successor-to-the-patriarchs śramaṇa Xingyin at the Capital.
The Buddha’s thirty-two marks are like the crystalline structure of snow; his eighty secondary characteristics are a jade-like skin.
O great assembly, gaze upon him without weariness; today he is here, but tomorrow he may not be. (Pointing at the Hall)
A single flower holds forth a Tathāgata; six petals unfold in a round, smiling countenance.
If one recognizes that the skull is originally water, there is no need to enter the womb in Māyā’s palace. (Jiang Sheng)
The proportions of the incense burner have been fully perfected; one knows not how many years it has lain buried in an ancient temple.
Picking up a single spark of the seed of fire, the flames from the cold ashes flare up and pierce the heavens. (Śu’ān Zōng)
The incense seal covers and turns back, striking a single blow; its interlocking patterns and sharp corners send sparks flying.
Who knows that in this place where arising and ceasing never cease, it drives the twelve hours of the human day? (Yunyan Nan)
His origins were from among the paper; originally he lay amidst the wisteria vines. In his practice, he spent much time facing the wall.
Relying on him to convey news across a thousand miles, he made people laugh to death—Bai Touduo (Shu’ān Zōng).
The bamboo poles and wooden shavings of the sedan chair all form the palanquin; through meticulous effort, not a breath of wind can leak through.
Even if it is carried by two people at either end, within it dwells the true master (Zhian II).
The moon serves as the golden bridge-pins for the stringless zither, and the wind serves as its strings. Its pure resonance is not transmitted by the fingertips.
Sometimes, having finished playing the melody of non-arising, the dew drips from the pine tips while the crane does not yet sleep.
The zither reaches the state of having no strings; those who can hear it are rare. From ancient times until now, there has been only Zhongqi.
Several times I intended to play the "Yangchun" melody, but as the moon filled the empty hall, my fingers hesitated (Laike).
The wind-organ ultimately takes the mind as its power of transformation; a single branch of green bamboo, four strings of wind.
After the deepening of night, the two ears are silent and vast, as if on Mount Guo beneath the bright moon. (Guanxiu)
Yangshan pushed up his lute-pillow before Daowei; this single kind of stringless wonder cannot be transmitted. With eyes closed it is dusk;
with eyes open it is day. To whom does the true sound ultimately belong? (Yanxi Wen)
Forged from tempered steel, a cold luster floats; two blades clash, refusing to yield.
In this direct engagement where he acts for others, how has he ever moved so much as a single thread? (Shimen Huai)
With a heart of raw iron, he unties the knots and unravels the tangles; gathering both and releasing both, he does not shrink from toil.
From of old, the sharp and the dull have never been equal; there is no need to doubt his two-faced blade (Pakuan).
The charcoal lump on the dead wood has not yet turned to ash; though broken, it still gathers itself back together.
Rolled into the red furnace and smelted once more—how many people, standing in the cold, perceive the return of spring? (He’an)
The work on the cold ground has already been completed; one should not yet regard it as extinguished ashes.
To casually let go of it here and there—how many monks have been deceived by this "heat"?
Nails for shoes, black-lacquered skin, iron teeth and fangs—do not doubt the length of his heels. Entering the mud and entering the water, he casts away his body;
without traversing the journey, he arrives home. (Xiaowen Kan)
The snow covers heaven and earth, a vast expanse of whiteness. A single sheet of empty stillness makes one’s heart chill with cold.
If you claim this is the true realm of Samantabhadra, know that you have already been deceived by your own eyes. (Hunyuan Mi)
The five-colored thread, when taken up, is used without partiality; within the shadow of the needle’s point, one must strive for precedence.
Gathering and releasing according to the shifting of circumstances—even those with iron eyes and copper pupils are pierced through (Wujingwei).

When the vessel is full, cease speaking; the body is merely lodged upon the eaves. You have mastered the upward-flowing stream of our house. Having been tempered in the forge, you are known to be without leakage;
let your mouth and corners flow like a cascading torrent (Dachuan Ji).
The boat has successfully withstood a thousand blades and ten thousand axes; it sails across lakes and seas, leaving no fixed trace.
Only when the helmsman remains at the stern will there be no headwinds to strike one’s face (Pakam Hyeon).
Using wood, stone, body, and mind with intimacy, the relative weight within this realm becomes naturally clear.
If one can understand the meaning of the hook’s tip, one will see that eight *liang* are originally half a *jin*. (Puo’an)
Three beats of the puppet-drum and two strikes of the gong; there are many masks of ghosts and gods.
Having performed all manner of tricks, let us see how they handle the final act. (Wan’an Rou)
Appearing and disappearing on the stage, he displays his gallantry; this draws laughter from bystanders that never ceases.
Even if one were to let go of one's entire body, a single thread still hangs from the crown of the head (Duanqiao Lun).
I recall my mother;
the snow fell like a withered day-lily, her tears drenched my robes. Her white hair can no longer lean against the rustic gate.
Last year in the fifth month, during the plum rains, I once pawned my *kāṣāya* to buy rice and return home. (By Gongxing)
The fly, driven by craving, drills through the paper seeking light; how many hardships it endures when it cannot penetrate!
Suddenly it strikes the path it came upon, and only then realizes it has been deceived all along by its own eyes (Baizhang Yuanwen).
In the midst of illness, one moment cold, one moment feverish, yet light and revived; searching for the very source where it arises, there is none. At midnight, the sound of mice emerges in a swarm;
they knock over the medicinal gourd at the head of the bed. (Dongyu Hai)
Wrapped in paper within a bamboo steamer basket—how truly elegant! Hiding away in a cool spot, he refuses to rest. Behold him; his entire body is nothing but eyes.
He should naturally push himself out from the head of the furnace (Laughing Old Man Kan).

The Lion Peak crouches upon the earth and soars into the void; its momentum never ceases. How could its claws and fangs ever be content to mingle with the common stream? Heaven ordained it to be born atop a thousand peaks;
even without the support of clouds, it must raise its head. (Xuedou Xian)
The hat is a vast expanse of blackness; at its crown, a single thread barely penetrates.
When it is casually used to cover everything over, how many fail to find their heads? (Dachuan Ji)
The needle case covers heaven and earth; its capacity is all-encompassing. Copper pupils and iron eyes are gathered therein at once.
How many sharp and pointed blades could dare to show their heads here? (No gate opens.)
The dull iron cauldron has personally entered the furnace; its entire body is refined red, stripped of all form.
Behold where it boils the moon and cooks the wind—now, not a single trace of leakage remains (Ziyuan).
Fanning once, it passes straight through the Jianmen Pass; a seamless circle—dare anyone gaze upon it?
With a casual, effortless lift of the hand, a clear breeze blows, its piercing chill overwhelming all who approach. (No gate opens.)
The attendant of Yanguan deliberated incorrectly; he won the reputation for his elegant discourse. Who throughout ancient and modern times has known the handle?
Without ever moving it, the wind brings coolness (pointing to the hall).
Each drop falls with distinct clarity; every arrow strikes its mark. Within the jar lies a separate heaven and earth.
If one were to make it so that not even a drop could leak through, how many would miss the proper time and lose the right occasion? (By Floating Stone Xian)

Last night, the leaping-bead spring and the bamboo dragon played at the foot of the mountain. One bright pearl was spat out and then swallowed again. To look at it is not impossible, yet one cannot contend with it;
listen as it is taught: though struck to pieces, it remains whole.
Clapping Hands at Pearl Spring:
With a clap of the hands and a stamp of the feet, the numinous spring rolls forth and pearls spray out.
Even if tears fill the mountain streams, how could they exhaust the many sorrows of a hero? (Li Youbai)
The mud-warbler does not leave the mud and water to see the heart of fragrance; its skillful warbling, though soundless, is the wondrous voice.
To suddenly hear it intimately with one’s own eyes—why need one go again beneath the shade of the green willows? (By Floating Stone Xian)
White lotus, green jade, long branches, and snow-colored robes—seeing these at night, one cannot help but feel doubt. Several rows of egrets stand amidst the waves beneath the moon;
clapping my hands to startle them, they refuse to fly away. (Beijian Jian)
Who will share this chrysanthemum pillow and green pouch as the autumn blossoms reach their fullness? They are sent instead to the home of an old man deep within the clouds.
Startled from ten years of dreams upon the lakes and seas, I behold the yellow flowers tonight amidst my white hair.
A single bundle of vines, with grapes old and rotten for many years—once arranged upon the rack, they flourish anew.
Where the dragon’s whiskers curl, the black pearls appear; this is no ordinary ghost-eye (the Dwarf).
The waterwheel has carried its planks through life, cherishing its leisure; only when the ten-thousand-li sky is cloudless does it begin to turn.
To achieve a flood that surges to the heavens and covers the earth—what difficulty is there for such a heart-mind to flow forth? (By Chan Master Mei)
When the battle for the Dharma takes place at the tip of a blade of grass, the banners and flags have not yet displayed their full majesty.
Even if Lu Yu had known the essential point, he would still fall into our house’s second device. (Songyuan Yue)
The place where one finds the staff is not on a high peak, nor is it in a shallow stream or deep ravine. Now, fortunately having obtained its support,
old age and illness become one's reliance (Shendingshen).
An ancient wisteria branch from a cold valley after many years; I traveled throughout Lake Xiang and finally found it. Do not ask about probing the water or knocking on the void;
Few people know its equal weight and lightness (Virtuo Hall’s Yū).
His towering presence leans against the void; holding his staff crosswise or using it upside down, he is as swift as the wind.
If you wish to know the point where he fully exerts his power, it lies entirely within the grasp of that very man. (Shu’an Cong)
Giving and taking proceed together to test right and wrong; the life of the plantain tree is like a hanging thread. Countless people are dragged about sideways and pulled down;
who will support the Great Way and bring it home? (Zhiweng)
The whisk—Mazu held it high, yet his mechanism leaked; Zhaozhou galloped forward to offer it, how profound his intent! Seeing another’s flaw, he seized what was his own;
how could there be even a hair’s breadth of error that has persisted to this day? (Xutang Yu)
The firecrackers ignite lightly and fly like stars; the revolving wheel turns without ceasing.
Were it not for the samādhi-hand of an immortal, it would all be due to the efficacy of a small amount of medicinal powder (or the essence of the Hermitage).
Striding back and forth in straw sandals, their function is singular; Nanquan was once deceived by Zhaozhou. Zen monks, step by step, rely on his power;
would they ever consent to hang them upon the corner of the Dragon Throne? (Wu Gong)
Underfoot, he does not shun the vastness of mud and water; his nose-tip is soaked as he busies himself for others. A seal without pattern adorns the faces of a thousand peaks;
the essential gate is fully realized, yet the road remains long. (Bodhirang)
Through diligent and meticulous practice, one achieves mastery; the living path that penetrates all reaches flows freely in every direction.
Behold him everywhere as fierce as a tiger—limitless pure breezes arise from beneath his feet. (Langya Huijue)
An unearthed Han dynasty jade ring—do you see its circular luster?
The lump of clay is shattered, and all contradictions are severed.
Although it has not been tempered in the furnace, it was once carefully polished through diligent effort. (Zhiguanhui)
Pity the incense burner lacks beast-charcoal and the seat lacks felt. Three pieces of firewood are arranged in the shape of the Chinese character for "three" (品).
Do not let domestic disgrace be lightly released; let it scorch the earth and smoke the heavens. (Dachuan Ji)

The resentment of the ox was settled in over seventy cities in a single battle; upon returning home, he was told only that he had been enfeoffed as a marquis. Before the scars from the branding fire had even cooled, the yoke was placed upon him once more.
Under the spring rain and spring wind, sorrow knots itself in secret. (Yixingke II)

Listening to the rain before the eaves, each drop falls with distinct clarity. Sentient beings, deluded regarding their own nature, call it "sound. I too have spent much of these years chasing after external objects;
thus, on this spring night, a single pillow has made sleep difficult to attain.
When the mulberry trees are bare and the leaves exhausted, only then does the heart find rest; the dense and subtle work is gathered within a single cocoon.
One must be willing to enter the furnace coals and the boiling cauldron; for the sake of others, it depends on nothing but that single thread. (Mòzhōngwéi)
Expressing My Feelings:
The earthen stove lacks fire, the traveler’s satchel is empty. The snow falls like willow blossoms as the year draws to a close.
I have gathered scraps of broken hemp to mend my tattered robe; Unaware that I am dwelling in such solitude. (Jiandang Ji)
Casting seals and wearing robes adorned with golden flowers, he rode a small bay horse with its bridle tightened. How many times has he brandished his whip amidst the bright moon?
