Traveling back and forth across the expanse of the Yellow River, even until now he has not established any merit. (Xutang and Yuyu)
The iron sandals, their soles worn away, have endured wind and frost; returning at year’s end, they rest upon the stone bed.
A pair of eyes, dark and piercing, follow half the shadows of the clouds as they hang in the cold hall.
Husk the rice, removing layer after layer; do not harbor resentment toward the grinding, polishing, and pounding. It must pass through the sieve before it can become rice;
offer this to the worthy and holy Sangha of the ten directions. (Pour water evenly.)
Not a single speck of dust or mud beneath the calamus roots; by nature, it loves the seclusion of springs and rocks.
Had it not been for the resentment of the Xiang River at that time, how could there be teardrops upon every leaf? (Master Mingdian)
A sprout takes root upon a single clod of earth; it is fit to keep company with the recluses in their solitude. I regret that in establishing myself I have not even an inch of ground;
to receive even a drop of water from another is difficult to repay. (Wang Yigong)
Orchids painted upon a precipice sway like the spring breeze;
what purpose is served by seeking refuge on such heights? It is from the ground that one creates inverted perceptions;
one must see the moment the hand is withdrawn from the cliff (Huang Wenhuan).

The bitter bamboo shoots have shed their purple robes and become as white as silver; they turn their bodies within the hundred-boiling cauldron. Only those who have personally experienced such suffering can believe this;
when one bites into them casually, the flavor is entirely true. (Master Chang Cangzhu)

The Patriarch’s flower embodies the transformative power of creation and the sentiments of all things. It is precisely at the place of birth that it does not speak of birth; to seek its branches and pluck its leaves is but a weary labor.
When a single blossom opens, a Buddha is realized. (Dongshan Yan)
Moss grows as green as the blood of a *fú* insect, staining the crumbling walls. How many souls are broken at the Han palaces and Tang tombs? Do not mock the desolation of spring in a poor household;
it gradually climbs the Green Gate with the accumulating rains. (Guxinchun)
The chrysanthemum has utterly abandoned all manner of social greetings; it retains only its heart that turns toward the sun. Upon the eastern fence grows the yellow chrysanthemum;
from afar I imagine it to be a kindred spirit. (Hanshan Qing)
In the city of Ten Bamboos, every inch of earth is as precious as an inch of gold. In my secluded studio, I have planted but ten bamboos;
O Spring Wind, be careful not to multiply their offspring, lest they pierce the green moss before my steps. (Qing Shun)

In Xinzhu, bamboos are pruned to clear paths and block offways; their tips like hairpins or horns pierce through the hollows of the streams. Still encased in purple sheaths, they all retain their joints;
only when they rise straight toward the blue clouds do they finally release their branches. (Zhixuan)

The cassia flowers grow from the clouds and their seeds were planted in what year? The western wind blows down golden shavings. Their radiance floats upon the moon’s reflection as the celestial fragrance disperses;
they fill the mounds and block the gullies, creating a profusion of scattered beauty. (Bao Puliàn)
The mountain plum’s angular branches are thin with sparse bones, shrouded in mist; they spend the day at the stream’s edge sending forth the morning breeze.
Tending toward the clouds, it opens but a single eye, coldly watching the thorns vie for heroism (Yinyuan Qi).
The Sleeping Dragon’s pines serve as a small bridge for his pillow as he lies upon the scales of the azure dragon. In the ancient ravine, cloudless, his body alone is revealed.
He still awaits the spring thunder and the rising wind and rain, so that his towering head and horns may emerge from the wild undergrowth. (Top Eye Penetrating)
The honeybees hum in a tide until the light of dawn breaks; day and night they toil and scurry—what such haste? When the lacquer bucket is broken, the family’s shame is exposed;
look at those hundreds of thousands of apertures, all falling apart (Lingzhang Yun).

When the fragrance is pricked upon the stamens of a thousand flowers, one returns with realization at the tips of a hundred blades of grass. A single aperture pierces through to reveal the living path;
wandering without hindrance, one goes, comes, and flies. (Tianfeng Ci)
When the bottom of the bucket was struck off by you, your former livelihood was suddenly cast away.
Transcending and no longer clinging to your old nest, there remains only the layer upon layer of honeycombs.
The bee at the window refuses to leave the empty gate; even throwing itself against the window, it is truly foolish. For a hundred years it has pored over old scrolls;
when will it emerge? (Guling Zhuo)
The firefly is not auspicious light, nor is it a star. Its active way of soaring through the air is a body so light. Behold its single point of radiance;
it serves as the eye within the dark forest. (Gu Meiyou)
The fly that strikes the lamp—what numinous light allows it to alight? One has been cremated, yet another returns. This deluded fly is truly beyond compare in its folly;
though its forehead is scorched and its head singed, it will not be driven away. (Daiweng Yue)
As soon as the fleas smell the stench, they come to burrow; they summon their kin and call their friends to form a dark cluster.
Though they are capable of leaping and bounding when touched, their entire bodies remain pitch black (Huishan Xian).
A paper curtain has never feared the blowing of evil winds; a single sheet of cold clouds hangs down on all four sides.
Fortunately, it remains clearly bright and pure white; do not come within its reach to scatter pearls (Shuzhong Yun).
The bamboo whisk emerges from the mud, each joint rising higher; it cuts away branches and leaves, yet succeeds where tortoise hair is sought.
Casually held aloft upon the Flower King’s throne, the great earth, mountains, and rivers tremble (Shimen Gang).
The meditation cushion is all-encompassing, a seamless, perfect circle. Casting down the entire body, one is naturally at ease.
How laughable that in years past, the monk Ling was needlessly deceived by him seven times (Suyanyuan).
Snow weighs upon the supple branches of the plum; how can they endure such profound cold? It is best to view this wild character while it still bears the snow.
Standing for a moment before the wind, they cannot support themselves; once more they lean askance against the railing. (Rufeng and Gaosan)

Passing through Yunmen’s bamboo groves and treading across the Flower Brook until reaching Old Pan, a single peak looms beyond the heavens where the cold presses in. I have come at the end of summer, yet it is still worthy of appreciation;
the fragrance of the lotus pods lingers as the dew has not yet dried.
When both ends of the fire-tube are severed, the heart is seen to be empty; from a single aperture, the wind for ten thousand hearths can arise. In vain one borrows its breath to extend outward;
even upon dead wood, it glows with a deep red.
The life-faculty is severed and the spreading branches are exhausted; with the single eye perfected, one wanders through the flaming house.
This is the place where, for the sake of others, one extends the vital breath—thunder crashing and lightning flashing upon the head of dead wood (Daoweng Yue).

"Embracing the stillness of coal for a thousand years, one ultimately does not reach the end. One must bring the whole body into the marketplace, exhausting one's skillful means to fully respond to the desires of all sentient beings;
only then can body and mind finally attain ash. (Xiaoyan Bao)
The dumpling emerges with a contented "hou-hou" sound; hands folded across the chest, it cannot be pried open.
Lightly turning and shifting within the boiling water, the three minds are pierced through, cutting off all doubt and speculation (Shimen Gang).
With palms joined before others, one bows with humility; who would have known that within the belly there is vast capacity?
Turning over in the depths of the boiling cauldron, only when the flesh is bitten through does one know the flavor is not the same. (Gumei You)
The skillful work of making soup dumplings reaches its perfect completion; naturally pure and white, it is utterly free from even a speck of dust.
Having turned over in the deep cauldron and emerged, even a fool would open his mouth in praise. (Shimen Gang)
I send this Dragon Ball tea to Master Gaō;
the circular blue wall is not cast in darkness. There is an eye upon the tip of his tongue like that of Li Lou. Do not say that the teacup lacks three inches;
he knows how to ask, "What is it?"—Zhaozhou (Zeng Wenqing).

The Dongpo soup is exceptionally rich and sweet; the yellow bamboo shoots are naturally slightly bitter, as is the heart of the wild rattan. Within the Dongpo cauldron, they harmonize and intermingle.
I beg you, greedy Chan master, to stop wagging your tongue in search [of flavor]. (Hong Juefan)
Hearing the horn, its deep resonance issues from the lone city wall; ten li away on the mountain peak, it gradually fades into obscurity.
Of one and the same sound, there are infinite meanings: some are worthy of listening, others are not (Dongshan Yan).
The autumn night is vast and dim; the misty waters of the empty river are cold. In the empty window, white light arises as scattered stars cluster.
Rising to gaze at the shadow of wild geese arriving from the horizon, Half have alighted on the yellow reeds, half upon the sandbanks. (Yin Ming Lun II)
The autumn winds wither the Han palace;
Qin is subdued and Xiang Yu swept away at the Great Ditch. His merit from a hundred battles stands peerless. Rites and music fall into ruin, the *wēnshù* tree withers;
yet the moonlight still shines upon the autumn of the Han palace.
A million dragons and deities gathered to hear the Dharma inscribed by thunder; once, the chariot of Axiang halted in these empty mountains.
For a thousand years, the painted rafters have preserved the traces of the past, while the thunderous flames and azure mists conceal the Jade Scripture (the *Yuzhi ju*).

I have heard it said that from the land of Yanzhou, emerald robes were presented; in a single day, nets and snares spread across the east and west. Even feathers and plumage can become a burden to one’s person;
how could they find rest in the pure seclusion of an autumn forest? (By Yi Chu-ren)
The bamboo-frog has emerged from its physical root; changing its form is easy. When the mind is empty, all things—including flies—are as such. What injustice could there possibly be?
It is simply that they are constantly staring with their eyes wide open. (Daiweng Yue)
A cast-iron ox rolled out from the furnace after a hundred refinements; its horns are formidable and its body is utterly free of dust.
Though struck it will not move, and though pulled it cannot be moved; this time, it truly shall not enter a womb (Master Chang).
Thanking you for the gift of this rosary:
your initial journey southward in search of the Way never lost its course. You have secured the vajra-bead behind the crown of the head; holding it in both hands, you present it to me personally.
Its radiance is brilliant, piercing the dark thoroughfare (Ying’an Hua).
The incense burner has ears, yet its hearing seems as if deaf; it admits no other object to stir within.
That the extinguished mind is not always like this—by winning this pure smoke, it becomes something different. (From *Huanyou chuan*)
When clearing the wilderness, do not lament the weeds and deep roots; the point lies in the practitioner’s sincere application of intent.
If one can exert effort to lift the plow and hoe, even stones and clods of earth will turn over. (Daiweng Yue Shi)

The pure seeds must be selected and distinguished when facing the light; once they reach your hands, do not let them pass lightly by. If they remain blurred and indistinct, they are but withered seeds;
at another time, you will surely see them as scorched sprouts.
When the rain falls, let not a single grain of rice fall elsewhere; scatter it or gather it, leaving it as it may. To nurture the sprout of spiritual awakening requires diligent care;
with earth on your face and ashes on your head, you must await the proper time.

When planting rice, do not say you must first discern the reality of the soil; the intention to cultivate it is already a high level of functional awareness. When the hand and eye are in accord with the person, one attains a transcendent standard;
though the roots are delicate and the soil lean, they remain firm and resilient.
Tilling the weeds with a hoe without weariness, how diligent! How could one ever have seen or heard of "strange weeds"?
Having clearly and thoroughly uprooted them so they are distinct and manifest, let the wild frogs croak and clamor as they please.

The flowers flutter and the grain stalks flourish, their blossoms appearing most extraordinary; the ancestral fields are filled with fragrance. O practitioners of Zen, do not give way to complacent joy;
you must guard against the sudden onset of wild winds and rains.
Although Che Gai personally saw this fine grain with his own eyes, he still required it to be moistened from time to time. Everyone says that flourishing and withering depend upon rain and dew;
do you know there is another mechanism involved?
The stalks hang with fruit, each one joyful as they gradually bow their heads; I too rejoice, looking forward to the autumn harvest. To obtain this wafting fragrance, one must wait for it to ripen;
old farmer, I wonder if you can endure the hunger?
When harvesting reaches this point, one must beware of ankle-deep mud; only when cutting through root and all can it be called marvelous.
If someone asks about the green or yellow hues, hold up the sickle and show it directly to them.
The rice steams in the *zeng* and is cooked; with a broadening of the eyebrows, one finally knows that effort does not deceive. This white sweat does not merely seep through the raincoat and hat;
how could one now suddenly forget hunger?
Washing the brush, the ancients truly believed in written characters; every character emerges from this. The mind of all under heaven is not deceived; you too possess hidden merit.
Washing it for the orphaned child, reflect on this and you shall not lose it. (Mingjiao Song)
When the bamboo staff cuts off the roots of worldly dust, it is no longer the same; it supports heaven and earth, moving freely in all directions.
Bare and stripped of branches and leaves, one joint is empty, and every joint is empty. (Yangshan’s Bequest to No. 2)

The inkstone bowl remains solitary and round all day long, its ink sharing space with its neighbor; it possesses no characters to debate with others. Let the crooked and the straight remain difficult to distinguish;
once a single thread connects them, the truth is revealed.

Entrusting this bowl from the Western Land of Qián, its measure was brought forth; returning to the Eastern Land of Zhèn, it signifies the Single Transmission. The bag is stored with intent, the lid and base remain joined;
in unfolding this trust, there is no mind—mouth turned toward heaven (Pútí Lǎng).
The scale of these spectacles is made for but a single pair; they stand forth grandly upon the bridge of a person's nose.
Even if one possessed eyes with a thousand feet of sinews, this single mirror is so clearly distinct that it leaves nothing concealed. (Zhi Guan and Hui Er)
Wind-kites and paper kites soar toward the heavens, outshining the sun. With wings fluttering and soaring, now here and now there—
this is the portrait of an ancient eminent monk.
His body is as stout as a crane’s, his hair white as autumn; leaning on his staff, he sleeps across the great earth.
For a thousand ages, the cold pond is clear to its very bottom; without opening his lips, he reveals his throat. (Tianyue Zhou)
Sweeping away all wind and waves, he alone applied extraordinary effort; ten thousand acres of wind and surf were swept dry in a single stroke. I ask you:
before even grasping the handle of the broom, was there any power exerted in the slightest degree?
Seeing off Qiutao as he departs for Mingzhao:
"Your journey afar today is surely not for nothing; do not forget the time you soared straight up on the whirlwind. Ride the venomous dragon to spread the snow and rain;
from the beginning, Buddhas and patriarchs have been like the blind turtle."

Before the Zen practitioner leaves the mountains to seek instruction, before he has even put on his straw sandals, the poisonous thorn pricks his feet. When one sees the moon and forgets the finger that pointed it out, a solitary eagle soars across the azure sky.

The North Wind Blows Upon the Thatch Roof (Qinshan Shuke) The north wind blows upon the thatched roof, Its sound like the snapping of bamboo. Though the bamboo breaks, I do not resent it; The bamboo is shallow, and the clouds find no lodging there.
Next, Chan Master Hong Juefan, following the rhyme of "Catching Fish," observes the fishing nets at Guanzhen.
He laughs and says: "How can one compare this to the schemes of King Min as he approached the riverbank? I have come back to the sea gate, riding on my inspiration."
Ting! Tides ebb and flow; one should take advantage of the right moment (according to Meng’an’s style).
Launching the boat upon the frosty, cold pool where the autumn waters are clear, the west wind blows gust after gust and the leaf-hull is light. Since Zhu Jing departed, who else is capable?
Shao: "Waving oars and displaying paddles, how many are bright?
Setting bait and casting the trap in shallow waters, one laughs at the solitary and cold. If you wish to catch the great whale, look to the sea; only Ren Gong is fit to share this."
The words: "A castrated bull leads fifty hooks; casting lines to catch shrimp and clams is a common worldly practice.
When harbors are severed and ditches are ruined, what can be done about the turbidity? The brocade carp naturally hides in the great depths."
Soaking. It does not hinder the thousand-foot pole casting into the clear waves.

Floating serenely upon the surface, let it sway; do not inquire about the wind. Whether floating or sinking, first act as a mirror regardless of east or west. If you can [remain] three inches away from the hook...
The Way: Who can share in this turning of the body beneath the bending pole?
Should one pull it back, how could one know that the clear waves are not violated? As soon as the fragrant ear is swallowed, one seizes the moment; with a single "pala-la" cry, it follows the line.
Arising, one finally believes that former efforts were not bestowed in vain.
Amidst falling blossoms and flowing waters on a late spring day, having finished fishing, one sleeps by oneself upon a solitary raft. Upon awakening, one gathers in the fish.
Departing, willow branches bend toward the green shade.

Having caught a golden-scaled fish upon reaching the shore, the heart’s purpose is fulfilled. With a long song, he rows his oars and leans against his returning boat. Along the embankment of green willows, it fills the sky.
Snow. Infinite scenery reaches the riverbank;
fresh market goods surround the red dust beyond the golden sands. Hard to find a buyer, I have circled many times. My skeletal remains shall return to the Western Land.
Departing, the horseman vainly recalls the lady of his inner chambers.

Having obtained the price—copper coins and white bullion—he exits through the lofty gate. Calling out "you" and "thou" to brothers and cousins alike, he laughs freely amidst the red smartweeds and white pondweed.
Arrogance. Wandering idly through the marshy lands as morning turns to dusk.
*The Sea of Miscellaneous Poisons*, Scroll Six;
*The Sea of Miscellaneous Poisons*, Scroll Seven.
Re-edited and titled by the monk Shōon, successor in the lineage at Berlin in Kyoto;
Ancient Sail.
In years past, upon reaching the shore, he once gathered it in; today, because of the wind, he unfolds it again.
If you wish to follow him to that other side, there is no harm in washing your feet and boarding the boat (Chuan’an).
The ancient mirror has long been the face of the yakṣa-bodhisattva; a single glance upon its surface leaves no trace behind.
That which remains unextinguished within it is the Yellow Crane Tower and the Parrot Isle (Lingsou Yuan).
The ancient woodcutter [sees] the shadowless tree prior to the empty kalpa; it supports the heavens and props up the earth, bare and stark.
In Xinzhou there was a firewood seller who gathered it all up and carried it away on a single shoulder. (Shiwu Yong)
Once I felled a tree before the cliff; how many times have I seen its withered stump covered in moss? Year after year, my own situation is laughable;
even the axehead has been bored through by woodworms. (From Shimen)
To the south of the western crag and north ridge, and to the east of the southern ridge—nowhere at all can one find his tracks.
Who would have known that where the moon sets and the monkeys cry, a path leads through the precipitous cliffs and hanging rocks? (Donggu Guang)
The Master of Chuntang does not grow old; he dwells merely in a corner of the chaotic mountains. With a single breath of vital warmth, he calls out in a loud voice to bring him back.
(By Hui of Xiyuan)
A scion of Baekam has suddenly appeared; the rock has split open. Unlike pines and cypresses that grow tall brushing the clouds, here not a single branch or leaf is idle.
When its fruit falls among the thickets, it possesses fragrance as well. (Daecheon Jisa)
In the dried-up sea, not even a single bubble has arisen to reveal the source of consciousness; ten thousand waves and myriad ripples are all but false transmissions.
Only the moon upon the coral branches remains as it was, perfectly full for all people as the night deepens.
The Bridge-Breaker and the Blind Donkey—one kick and both ends are empty; thus, the ordinary path is blocked. A single step becomes a thousand miles apart;
the bustling crowds remain mostly halfway there.
The blind old man has never possessed eyes or sinews throughout his life. In the dark, he applies his skill with intimate familiarity. Stepping confidently, he walks the Great Road;
those he meets are mostly people who collide head-on with him (Puo-an).
Singing and chanting through the three hamlets of no-obstruction; returning from a drunken stupor at the crossroads.
Where the fair-skinned beauty dwells as her lodging, he wears his *kāṣāya* robe backward and dances the Three Terraces (Dachuan Ji).
Do not spend your years and seasons merely devouring sleep and devouring rice; let the Buddha-dharma rot away as it may.
If you claim that you have completely set everything down, then each strand of hair remains a strand of hair (Xiyuan Hui).

Without dhyāna, one has had a mouth all one’s life yet never spoke of the profound mystery. Who above could say there was a separate transmission? The old barbarian with the missing teeth originally knew nothing at all;
he has returned to the Western Heaven as before, journeying afar. (Donggu Guang)
The stubborn stone by the side of Master Seng’s platform has persisted for a thousand ages; from the beginning, it has been my peer.
I am a bit superior to it, for even when one speaks until the year of the donkey, it will not nod its head. (Xiyuan Hui’er)
Great wrath is like a swift hailstorm that overturns a thousand worlds; its violent thunderclaps shatter the five Sumerus.
Even if it were to startle the void into falling, it would not equal the moment his own nature erupts.
Beyond the mountains, facing away from the thousand peaks, he smiles and opens his eyes. Chu clouds are sparse as distant mists drift. At the end of the level marsh, do not ask;
for I fear the traveler will ask for directions along the path (Shitai Un).
The lame old man sits and stands with solemn composure, as if nothing were amiss; yet when he steps out the door or enters the house, he becomes perverse and erratic.
Whether his heels touch the ground or not, there are always bystanders to speak of his merits and faults. (By Huantang Ren)
The sick old man sees someone and lacks the strength to descend from his meditation seat; already his innermost feelings cannot be concealed.
If he were unable to discern pain and itch, even crossing the threshold would not avoid a mistaken deliberation (Yanxi Wen).
The indolent old man, with his hair hanging down in white, has long since forgotten his age. Beside his broken-legged cauldron, he rests amidst ten thousand greens;
though the hundred birds do not come and the flowers smile alone, the sun is already three *zhang* high yet he still sleeps soundly. (Fozhao Guang)
The Herdsman:

A thousand clusters of cloud-mountains, ten thousand valleys of flowing streams. Where there is no trace, there is a trace. In his old age, he can let go and take up again, letting his horns hang down;
it is not a matter of a hundred heads in the spring breeze. (Iron Feet)
The old man has died;
under the blue sky and bright sun, his corpse lies exposed. The eyes of all sentient beings upon the great earth remain unopened.
If you are a true, legitimate son of another house, you shall offer a coffin from three thousand miles away (Liangshan).
Once Master Tuìwēng let go, he knew shame; he never again forced his head forward before others.
With cold tears hanging from his chin and sleeves baring his elbows, wherever he went, in every movement, he was elegant and refined. (Xīyán Huì)
In the woodcutter’s hut, that which is withered is so, and that which is flourishing is so. With a single stroke, it is cut in two—there is no room for deliberation.
Having gathered everything up and returned, the thatched door is half-closed; the spring day is long. (The Empty Boat Crosses Over)
No flowers, selling nothing but dead cat heads; ten thousand taels of gold would not suffice as recompense.
This is no ordinary apothecary that competes to deceive the worldly with a hundred goods (seeking the Head Seat).
Master Mo, having fully experienced the affairs of the world, is too weary to open his mouth; having mastered all that exists among men, he merely nods his head.
Do not say that in old age he lacks skill; where could one find him more refined than this? (Wumen)
The snow has cleared;
I repair my straw raincoat to withstand the bitter cold. The water buffalo is one’s own; look for it yourself. Amidst the vast whiteness, there is no fragrant grass.
Playing the flute among the plum blossoms, he passes over the distant mountains (Dachuan Ji).

The moon sails across, flat as a mirror’s surface yet curved like a hook; it falls into the heart of the waves and cannot be stirred to float. With a single stroke of the pole, he shatters it all to pieces;
*dong dong*—the drum beats as he turns the prow of the boat. (Cen Liao)
When it is cast from within the ten-thousand-fold smelting furnace of Mount Ding, it is as heavy as five Sumeru mountains.
If there is someone who can apply the hand of total upholding, they shall serve it to him by boiling the void until it is soft. (Zuoxi)

For how many years has this old man with his severed feet cherished his uncut jade, seeking one who understands it? Twice he has suffered injury, and his resentment grows ever deeper. From now on, he shall roll forward before the eyes of men;
there will be no footprints left for others to trace.
In the ancient field at the beginning of the kalpa, a small patch of land has no high or low; where one sets foot, there is clearly three feet of mud. Between seller and buyer, who is the master?
Under the spring rain, the magpies cry as the plow turns the earth.
Five hundred lifetimes ago, I once crossed this ancient ferry; at that time, I had already waded through the waves and billows. How can one bring forth the matter of the present moment?
When the water rises, the boat naturally floats higher.
Within the forest of iron trees, swords, and halberds, one recognizes him. On the dark, wrinkled ground, there is neither flourishing nor withering. Try to investigate his very root;
solitary and firm, there is nothing like this single branch.
Xueqiao pressed him against the solitary peak where no white remains; his entire body still fell into the thicket of thorns. Having reached home, the burden has dropped from both ends:
the firewood is naturally green, and the fire is naturally red.
Pearl-like sleet falls lightly as firewood rests upon my shoulder; for now, I plan to kindle a fire to pass the final year.
At this moment, no one stands before the courtyard; who can rely upon to continue the broken smoke within the brazier? (Yuansou Duan)
In a single hut, when not making a mark, the whole body is revealed; if you attempt to take it up, you become even more perverse.
To further ask, "Where do the myriad dharmas return?"—the door is closed, and the lake and mountains are long in the spring day. (Zhe-weng Yan)
In Sun’an’s six locations, empty names require no cultivation; there is a reason for the seven holes and eight apertures.
Though frost, wind, sleet, and snow enter from every direction, even one who is not a man of sorrow is moved to grief (Dachuan Ji).
The Patriarch’s barrier of a thousand layers of iron walls grinds against the void; East and West, in China and India, no communication can pass.
When all clever stratagems are exhausted, one must pierce through to the other side; from foot to foot, a pure wind arises. (Shixi Yue)
Once the cold has come to the snowy courtyard, it cannot be restrained; the myriad phenomena of the universe are all submerged in stillness.
Who can enter such a gateway? To set foot therein is clearly three feet deep. (Dachuan Ji)
Layers of rosy shadows in the mists dip into the azure current; several times I mistook them for the headwaters of the Jinjiang River.
Once their radiance has faded away, they are revealed to be merely an island of white artemisia and red smartweed. (Yuepo Ming)
The entire village consists of only three households; they have divided their livelihoods across both sides of the stream.
The barking of dogs and the crowing of roosters are no different on either side, yet the spring breeze is separated by the mist of a single creek. (By Xianji Cen)
How many times has the spring breeze played its melodies in the ancient peach immortal’s garden? After three thousand years, the fruit has finally borne fruit.
Once, with a single drop of blood from a branch, he exchanged it for the two eyes of Lingyun (as recorded by Xishou and Tan'er).
In the past, General Kai once led his armored cavalry to break through heavy encirclement; with bare hands he raised his whip and returned in victory.
The desert sands have now become a land of song and dance, while I myself, with my hair turned white, face the slanting glow of the setting sun.
When there is nothing more to attain, one simply lets it rest; thus, one lets it rest. What purpose is there in this southern inquiry?
Who would have known that among the fifty-three masters, the gate is closed against the west wind, just as it is in autumn? (Xueyan Qin)
Unimpeded, it penetrates one place and penetrates everywhere; like the wind passing through trees or the moon traversing the sky.
With a light snap of the fingers within the hollow of a lotus fiber, one pushes forth the first peak of Mount Sumeru.
The discourse at Ling Shan under the moon-roofed hall and the pointing at Cao Xi—selling off the clear light, they are of one house. Do not disbelieve;
simply look from this very night, as the shadows of plum blossoms shift once more upon the window gauze.
The sea gate, a vast and towering portal, is difficult to conceal; it opens precisely where the waves are most treacherous.
Were it not for those who dare to play amidst the tides, how many would be willing to risk their lives to come?
The winds of karma blow up waves like mountains; how many fishermen find it difficult to set foot upon them? Only by risking one’s life and casting oneself in can one force one’s way through;
then one knows that the jade door was never locked (Master Chang).
Idle fields that neither the Qin nor the Han plowed; at the edge of the mattock, news is utterly unheard of. Yet in recent years, there has been hope for a harvest:
half a measure of pure breeze, half a measure of clouds (as shared by the Wild Old Man).
The Wood-Old Man did not know that heaven and earth originally have no root; until his old age, he remained entirely free from the scars of axe and hatchet.
He invited a fellow traveler, a venerable monk, to support him through the village of falling blossoms last night.
Dreaming in the hut, lingering clouds guard the cold stone bed. Within sleep, one’s livelihood is entirely at ease. The gate opens wide like scattered stars;
with a single punch, one wins the pillow for rest.
The eyes of the Tathāgatas of the three periods have not yet awakened; they establish their gateways upon the delusions of drowsiness and false conceptualization.
When a guest arrives, they do not raise their fists; let them listen to the sleep-talking from next door. (Tianru Ze)

In the Hall of Extinction, a blind donkey’s shout startled heaven and earth; the Linji tradition first began to spread widely. Passed down through generations of descendants, it became a subject of idle talk.
With no gate and no door, there is nothing to be taken up—Zeweng Yan.

In the Ox-Plum Forest there are no oxen; flowers fall and the grass grows lush. Having lost the end of the rope, he claps his hands and returns home. How many times have the spring waters whitened the wild fields?
Through the mist, he listens with sorrow to the horizontal blowing of the flute.
A single peal of thunder from Leifeng Peak—so sudden that one cannot cover one's ears in time; for a hundred li it shakes the earth, and the mountains crumble.
But for those whose hearts are free of guilt, they sit watching the clouds disperse amidst the azure, towering peaks.
Suddenly, as if striking an iron drum, lightning flashes before the eyes like a golden serpent.
Who would have known that atop Mount Emei last night, the Elephant King was so startled that flowers entered his tusks?
The hundred vajras of the Iron Face are difficult to shatter; this form has never descended into a mother’s womb.
This is the Venerable Ming of Lingnan, who has emerged from within the eye of the needle.
At midnight, I gazed upon White Rock; it was no different than by day. Lofty and towering, yet exquisitely refined. A flake of snow that flies away leaves no trace;
it only serves to add another layer of obscuration to the void.
The sun and moon serve as the windows and doors of the celestial hermitage; the livelihood of the patch-robed monk is not yet desolate.
One knows not how many layers of thatch have been scorched by the spring breeze beyond the thirty-three heavens.
The rocky pass is steep and lofty, its walls formed of crags and its gate of *bìluó* vines. Nature’s artistry is utterly free of the marks of axe or chisel. A hundred birds do not come;
the clouds close of their own accord. With whom can one discuss the message of the raised fist?
To plant fields upon stone—this is rare in the world. Even an old farmer hears of it and frowns.
If there were someone who could sow seeds in the hells, one would prepare fragrant offerings in a separate steamer to nourish them.
A "square hut" is but the space of a single sitting mat; who can know its lifelong course? When the rain falls from the four eaves at night, it truly reveals the private secrets of my house.
It is beyond all dependence.
Above, nothing to grasp or look up to; below, nothing to rely upon. From the void, the great earth comes—yet who is it?
This very self-spirit is not even valued; what "handle" (*babi*) is there to show others? (Guyeon)
Liaoweng trampled his straw sandals and snapped his staff; he was thoroughly elegant and could not be lifted by a spoon.
If you attempt to ask "How is it?", he strikes you across the face (Duanqiao Lun).
The Moon’s Bay swallows seven or eight; when it is perfectly full, it bends like a hook. With a single stroke of his oar, the old fisherman shatters them all to pieces;
laughing, he enters the reeds as ten-thousand-li autumn unfolds (Dongyu Sea).
In the bamboo chamber amidst a mass of azure clouds, the six windows are deep and secluded. I recall Xiangyan’s mistaken use of mind;
had he possessed hands, he would not have cast aside idle tiles and rubble. Instead, let us spread a single mat to face the clear shade (by Kongyan).

A clap of thunder resounds through the white day and blue sky; it overturns the seas and mountains and tears asunder the void. There is no need for the spring decree during the three months of winter;
it is hidden within the realm where neither yin nor yang exists.
Like an old man idly sleeping,
idly sitting, and idly walking, one knows not what has become of those affairs. Because I went to the water’s edge to look at my white hair,
the autumn wind blew upon two or three strands.

Master Ming-sou’s discernment exhausts the murky depths; his illumination penetrates the hidden recesses. When the sun is at its zenith and the moon is in autumn, though he comes empty-handed through the universe, no one knows him.
Yet he has won the spring breeze to accompany him unto white hair.

The mirror’s voidness is exhausted of defilement and dust is cleared away; its essence is naturally perfect. The multicolored phoenix leaves no shadow and is not hung again. Where Yangshan held it up, it could not be broken;
its brilliance has illuminated the gate for five hundred years.
Resting outside the hermitage, one ceases all external conditions, like a fish stopping in a marsh; with no gasping in the inner mind, one is like a bird perched in the reeds.
The Old Barbarian opened such a gateway, bringing his descendants into trouble halfway along the path.

Within this secret chamber, which is ten feet square on each side, there are hundreds of thousands of layers of fine mesh nets covering the sky; yet a single thread of passage is left open to allow your breath to pass.
At midnight at Huangmei, they escorted Master Lu away.
The Stone Old Man could not be moved even by five hundred strong men; Xuanzang sat stubbornly through many winters and autumns. Once the song of the Ba region was sung, no one understood it;
spring grasses and spring flowers fill the earth with fragrance.

When Kūkai turns his gaze back and observes until all is exhausted, what further observation remains? Pure and vast, it is swept clean and dry. The moon shines so brightly that the venomous dragon cannot slumber;
yet from this level ground, waves and ripples arise once more.
Master Shi does not depart from arising and ceasing; this is the perfect permanence. As flowers fall and bloom, he sees his own forgetfulness. His pair of aged eyes have no place to cling;
He idly gazes at the yellow chrysanthemums by the autumn fence.
No model—Deishan’s staff falls like rain from the blue sky; Linji’s shout roars like thunder from level ground. All patterns and forms are melted away, leaving Buddhas and patriarchs empty;
what further dharma will you show to those who come after?
Three times or five times he knocks on the wooden gate, thinking the clouds are so deep he cannot find his way back. When they hold hands and speak, it is not at all as he had imagined;
the bridge is broken, the stream flows, and the evening sun is faint.
In the daily life of Zu’an, what has ever been lacking? The thresholds of the four sides have never been moved.
If one says that "knowing where to stop" constitutes true cessation, then the vast ocean remains like a leaking chalice.
The poisonous ocean’s vast waves surge, tossing like the void; not a single drop is anything other than lethal *zhèn* wine. With brows furrowed, gazing at the wind, my heart and gall burst asunder;
I know not what means to save the fish and dragons.
Do not expect that what you hoard in dreams will all turn to gold. A moment of such wealth and honor brings joy hard to contain;
yet when the pillow slips from your grasp and you suddenly wake, you find no trace of it—only the pure breeze blowing through the four walls.
Though possessing a mouth, he is speechless; he is fit only to hang idly on the wall. He does not utter a single word as the vehicle of the school.
Observe him where profound silence is like the roar of thunder—this old Vimalakīrti of Vaiśālī is not yet permitted [to speak]. (Ancient Bell Inscription)
Within the circle, it revolves and rolls like a pearl rolling on a platter. To seek it outwardly is as vast a gulf as heaven and earth.
(Liaotang 1). Noan.
One calls out one’s own name and receives the echo; know that this is not yet the time of arriving home. Now the gateways are naturally distinct;
even before arriving home, he is granted permission (by Qianyan Chang).

Having attained great penetration, though the void is vast and expansive, one still deems it too small; what prevents one from penetrating to the bottom and piercing through to the summit? The mouth of our Patriarch was truly narrow;
once it passed through the window, there was no more ox.
Who has ever built these three bays of thatched huts? And who is it that comes to dwell here as a guest?
Taking only empty space as walls and fences, let the gates and doors stand wide open to the heavens.
The moon-boat and ice-wheel are cold and clear at night; the sky is empty. Ten thousand *li* of pure radiance are contained within a single oar-stroke.
Seven hundred eminent monks could not push it forward; Huangmei won the right to escort Master Lu (Yuanxiao).

In ancient times, during the era of King Wei-yin-wang, he plowed the wild hills; he left this for his descendants to sow and reap again. In this present age, people do not know the method of cultivation;
it teaches them to hold a hoe in their empty hands (Tianru Ze).
In the dark void, a thousand lamps do not illuminate; the six windows are cold. Only when both light and shadow are forgotten can one truly see.
Since the thirty-two thousand people departed, the gates have remained pitch black to this day. (Zhongfeng Ben)
Flowing upstream against the current, one immediately encounters the headwind; it is not like the ordinary rushing waters.
The vast, wild waves surge to the very bottom, refusing to yield even a single drop to flow toward the source.
Mountains are casually gathered and cast into the vast void; the billion Sumeru mountains leave no trace.
Though all the people of the world search for them, they cannot be found—who is it that gathers them within a single speck of dust?
Seven days before the Primordial Age, even Zhuang Zhou had not yet broken through the shell; before the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas had entered the womb,
this single idle name of a patch-robed monk had already come directly from the other side.
The eyes see without concealment; between the ears there is no separation at all. Day is bright, night is dark—beyond all deliberation. Originally and spontaneously manifest, why so much fuss?
One must by all means avoid hiding from oneself at the very moment of encounter.
The seven Buddhas of antiquity dwell among the tenant farmers; over five thousand scrolls of ancient foundations remain. The fragrance of the rice flowers ripens as the yellow clouds age;
how many descendants do not know this for themselves?
A single cry from the hermitage reaches the window; an old monk with white hair is startled from his midday nap.
He leaps down from his bamboo bed and opens both eyes, only then realizing there is a blue sky outside the house.

Dingsou’s nature was scattered and distracted, yet he manifested majestic deportment; for a thousand kalpas, he remained as if seated for but a moment. Throughout the day, he never moved so much as a hair;
the west wind blew white upon his two eyebrows.
The autumn river air is stern and the wind is clear; coolness pervades the world. A few rows of new geese pass over the Xiao and Xiang rivers.
To whom can this fine scenery of the heavens be entrusted? On both banks, reeds face the setting sun. (Jiefeng Yu)
Cloud Hermitage:
sometimes pale, sometimes deep, it drags its rain away; half-unfurled, half-rolled, it comes against the wind.
Out of pity for those on the road with no place to rest, it opens its wooden gate wide through the eternal night. (Gao Feng Miao)
Without a mirror, from the beginning, how could a single dharma ever have been established? This very capacity for manifestation leaves nothing behind;
yet one laughs at the Twin Trees, where there was still a reflection, and even comes to the water to observe one's own head (Nanshi Xu).
No shore;
raising one’s head and looking in the four directions, all is a vast expanse of white. Whether north, south, east, or west, one knows nothing at all.
Without needing an oar to pole to the bottom, turning back the head is the very moment to board the boat. (Shiwu Hong)
The rocky cliffs rise a thousand fathoms from the earth, green as jade; ten thousand feet they soar above the clouds, hard as steel. Beholding such precipices, many retreat;
who is there willing to let go and take up the burden?
With eyes invincible and empty, his spirit towers over lakes and seas; He stands preeminent among the forest of sages, his thoughts beyond compare. From antiquity to the present, who is my equal?
Where you can afford to be generous, be generous.
Fishing for snow on the tip of a hundred-foot pole with a single strand of silk: where there is nothing to grasp, grasp urgently!
When it is suddenly cast away three inches from the hook, that is precisely the moment when empty space shatters to pieces (Wuwen Can).
The mind of friendship is most difficult to know; it is an iron wall and silver mountain a million fathoms high.
When both paths of birth and death are seen through, every stone, great and small, is pure gold. (Chushi Qi)
The Elder Plum-Seeker beholds the southern branches and then the northern ones; let his two temples be made white as silk.
When illusory flowers have utterly perished, the reality remains—this is precisely the time when the green leaves bear fruit.
At the hundred-foot pole, Xis’an has ceased to inquire; atop the solitary peak, he nurtures his idle body.
Though his tattered hut lacks any covering, he cannot easily explain his private affairs to others. (Master Changzang)

Ancient pines from the beginning of the kalpa have no ground to plant their numinous roots. Who knows directly beneath them that there is *fuling* fungus? Their seeds fall into the forest and grow into great trees;
for ten thousand years they do not change, remaining green through the four seasons. (Qianyan Chang)
A small hut with leaves for a thatch—more than enough. Within a single mote of dust, one constructs a dwelling.
Although there is not even the space of a hair’s breadth, the myriad phenomena and all that exists listen as they are rolled up and unfurled. (Xiaoyan Bao)
Living in the mountains, the lotus leaves on my single pond provide inexhaustible clothing; the pine blossoms from a few trees leave me with food in abundance.
Just because the world came to know my dwelling place, I have moved my thatched hut deeper into the seclusion [of Mount Damei Chang].
A single cottage atop a thousand peaks; The old monk occupies half, the clouds the other half. Last night the clouds followed the wind and rain away;
In the end, they are not as idle as this old monk. (Master Zhizhi)
Dwelling in the mountains, alone behind closed wooden doors, there is no other pursuit. Three pieces of firewood are roasted in the shape of a "three" character;
there is no need to wield the brush for literary brilliance to be revealed. (Master Zhigan)
Ten thousand affairs brought to rest, entrusted to the simple and the foolish; his traces allow the wild deer to join him at times. Without removing his hempen robe, he makes his fist a pillow;
for many lifetimes his dreams have lain within the lush green vines. (Master Zhian)
Two or three pints of wild water from the bamboo conduit; five or seven fragments of idle clouds at the pine-window. Such is the livelihood of the practitioner;
it remains for people of the world as an object of sight and hearing. (In response to the Hermit Master)
The road back to my old garden is separated by the ends of the earth; for now, I lodge my family in a quiet room atop the peak.
Having finished transcribing the *Bēṭa* leaves, the mountain moon is beautiful; a canopy of flower shadows ripples across my *kāṣāya*. (Yuansou Duan)
In my clumsy honesty, I know myself to be far removed from the world; in my rustic folly, I am able to dwell deep in the mountains.
For my livelihood in this life, I have nothing else—only a wrinkled staff of one *zhang* (Chun, the Abbot’s age, twelve).
A wooden frame with a few rafters overlooks the water and rocks; a single path through the gate leads to hanging vines and creepers.
It is because this place is fitting for my final years that I have come to dwell here, where I may enjoy the mountain clouds passing by at dawn and dusk.
I laugh at myself for being as reckless as Shi De; who would have known my dullness was like Nanquan’s?
Several times, satiated from eating and weary of wandering the mountains, I simply sleep wherever I am, wrapped in my robes.
Mindless and leisurely, the clouds return to the cave; with form yet clear, the bright moon rests in the pool. This scene is vividly transcendent of the mundane world;
it is primordially manifest, requiring no further investigation.
Carrying nothing but a staff that exceeds my head, I rely solely on a broken-legged cauldron for my belly’s fill.
Wherever it is best to cast off idleness, I wander amidst the sounds of water and the hues of mountains.
Where the earthen incense burner smolders, pure smoke gathers; when the iron chime is struck, its dawn resonance is cold.
A single string of prayer beads, coarse yet heavy—when picked up, its one hundred and eight beads do not deceive.

Yanzi with his single ladle was not merely seeking pleasure; Sima Xiangru with his four bare walls was not yet the pinnacle of excellence. How can they compare to the true livelihood of a mountain dweller?
From the roof of their cottage, the resonance of pines pours forth like an autumnal tide.
Numerous large characters upon palm leaves; a single stick of coarse incense from ancient cypress roots. In the stillness of the stone chamber, spring stretches long through the day;
the cuckoo’s cry pierces the village of falling blossoms.
The Fisherman Father and Son sing the Song of Ambrosia; they compose verses on the Lamp of Dharma in the manner of Hanshan. Do not say that no one hears you in the deep clouds;
the myriad phenomena and all things are clearly known.

Sitting upon the rock, one already feels the chill in one’s very marrow; rinsing in the spring, one always finds the teeth and gums refreshed. Within this experience, there is a flavor that causes all thoughts of returning to be forgotten;
as the body grows old, nothing remains but to harmonize with this sentiment.

Sitting in quietude amidst secluded crags, tigers have grown tame; walking along ancient streams, I have befriended the gulls. This is not because I have forgotten my faculties or severed all thought;
it is simply that, having reached old age, I have attained the rest of the mind.
Afraid of the cold, I am too lazy to shave my hair, which hangs down in disarray; loving the warmth, I frequently add pieces of firewood to the hearth.
My chestnut-colored *kāṣāya* robe is draped in a messy fashion—who could take the trouble to arrange it properly?
Lush and verdant is the thatched cottage on a crisp autumn night; white bean flowers bloom as the lo-lwei cricket cries. The mountain moon, silver-like, stirs the old man’s兴致 (xìng—interest/passion);
walking at leisure, he does not realize he has passed to the west of the peak. (By Shiwu Gǒng)
The mountains are filled with bamboo shoots and bracken, and the hillsides are covered in tea plants; a single tree bears red blossoms interspersed with white.
Generally, spring is best throughout the four seasons, yet it is most excellent here in the mountain home.
Having finished planting the winter melons, he plants the eggplants; he exhausts his body and toils his bones to make his living.
If everyone wishes for the kitchen to be well-ordered, the head gardener must always remain at home.
One day, one strikes sleep three or five times; even this cannot exhaust so much idleness.
Circling several times through the *laṅgān* bamboo, one again emerges among the green pines to gaze at the distant mountains.
In this mountain cave, all day long it is utterly still and silent; how could worldly thoughts ever arise in even the slightest degree?
Though one wears clothes and eats porridge and rice, it is just as if one were dead and had never yet been cremated.
Half the window is pine shadows, half the window is moonlight. A single meditation cushion, a single monk.
Sitting cross-legged after the middle of the night, a moth flies in and extinguishes the lamp before the Buddha.
Five *he* of aged yellow rice are steamed for the meal; several stalks of green shepherd’s purse sprouts are boiled for the soup. Its simple and plain flavor is naturally excellent;
why should one need to add more ginger or pepper?
One day, as the red sun circled the southeast, I pulled up green seedlings myself to plant in my lean fields. My robe was half-saturated with mud and water;
returning home, I took it off to dry before my bamboo cottage.
How can one have the leisure to practice while dwelling in the mountains? Having planted the winter melon, one then plants the gourd.
Were it not for even a hair’s breadth of effort, these vast fields would all lie fallow and overgrown.
In old age, there is nothing left to occupy the mind; on my bamboo couch, I sleep soundly as the sun slants across my pillow. In my dreams, I know not who I am;
upon awakening, the new moon has reached the plum blossoms.
The yam in the earthen stove has no flavor at all; the green pines in the corner of the house have not yet flowered. The crimson leaves depart with the flowing water, leaving no trace;
how many fine households there must be in these spring mountains!
Yellow leaves drift away with the flowing water; white clouds have long since entered the mountains. Solitary are the three rooms by the cliffside;
two wooden gates stand open all day long.

A head-shaven ascetic with matted hair and a soiled face—no Zen master in the world can do anything about him. Even if it were the Buddha himself who came, he would surely receive a blow of the staff;
now that he is old, he has become a demon.
The wind clears over the wheat fields as the plum rains cease; countless people plant melons and sow vegetables. Hearing the sound of the drum, they return to eat their meal;
the hoe hangs upside down from the tree before the gate.
Striking a nap upon the rocks, then returning to sit in meditation; walking away among the pines, then walking back again. Countless mountains within the shadows of white clouds;
flowers are in full bloom amidst the songs of yellow birds.
Gourd vines are planted outside the winter melon trellis; eggplants are further sown by the hundreds and thousands.
With nine-tenths of a fathom tongue and three hundred mouths, let us dwell together for this summer in a thatched hut.
In the fourth and fifth months, bamboo leaves fall; the myriad trees are lush green and the plum fruits turn yellow.
Coldly observing this matter of life and death—how can one let these fine moments pass in vain?
Not a single word of Buddhist dharma or literature; facing guests at his wooden bed, he is utterly silent. What flows from his breast covers heaven and earth;
this decrepit Yantou has lost many of his teeth. (Tianru Ze, No. 2)
I recall passing the Six Bridges along the Su Embankment; A small *fan* cap was blown away by the wind. It bore the snow of the lake and mountains upon its brim;
Though scorched many times by the fierce sun, it would not melt away.
In my leisure moments, I play among the tall pines upon the rocks; My hundred-seamed dharma robe is torn and then mended again.
Today I do not worry about tomorrow’s affairs; My entire life is contained within this alms bowl. (Guankui Chang)
I too have, for no reason, covered it with thatch; a brick rolls in vain against the empty air. The mountain is deep and not a single person is seen approaching;
striking it, I find it was merely the tip of a tree branch (He’an).
The moon in the water cannot be fished out; one merely exhausts oneself, shattering the celestial disk within the waters. At night, deep in the mountain temple, the door opens and one sleeps;
the moon flies of its own accord and arrives before one’s face. (Hyanghwon Go, No. 5)

Contented in heart and satisfied in mind, one may preserve this state forever. Amidst the flowers of spring in the imperial gardens and famous parks, beneath a single peaked thatched cottage, is the home of a Daoist who remains ever free from worldly affairs.
Seventy-two peaks emerge from the surface of the waves; after Master Lu departed, the stone screen remains. Singing several songs, I wandered for three days;
now the painting has been added with one more monk.
The fragrance of yam fires at the base of the thousand-fathom cliff; the sun’s orb is high at noon in heaven. In the lands of the East and West, there is no patriarch;
this white-haired old monk is seventy-five years old.
Buddha after Buddha handed down the torch, yet few were his true heirs; Patriarch after Patriarch transmitted the lineage, as deep as the ocean.
Last night the western wind shook the door panels; at dawn there was no trace left to pursue.

A saffron-colored *kāṣāya* robe, tied with a thousand knots; leaning against a pine tree, I stroke my belly and watch the clouds fly. When someone asks me about the delights of the clouded mountains, I tell them:
"In the depths of spring, the bamboo shoots and ferns are lush. (Yugu Zhì)
Ten days in the mountains, nine of them rain; green fruit falls incessantly from the treetops.
A white dog follows tracks into the grass, startling a bamboo pheasant that flies up into the branches. (Shuzhong Yun)
A single pine tree, a wisp of mist; a full moon, a pool of water.
If one were to depict this in a painting, one would add a *dhūta* sitting by the rock—beyond all seeing or beholding.
A newly sewn paper quilt, warmed by the sun, brings a peaceful sleep until the fifth watch.
Hearing the bells and drums of the upper realm strike, one adds another day to this fleeting life. (Penglai Yuan)
Throughout my life, green mountains fill my view; a single mat, serene, occupies half a room. It is not that this old monk boasts of wealth and honor;
by day there is leisure, and by night there is leisure (Master Wu).
Sitting by the stream for a long time, the sound of the flowing water continues on. Smoke rises from the bamboos beyond the fence;
the practitioner boils tea (Moweng).
Having secured the highest floor of the cottage by the stream, he has cast aside the entire community of monks in the mountains. The small garden lies right at the railing.
Down below, I pluck green pears myself and steam them with rice (Dongshi).
With my back to the setting sun, I emerge from the western weir; spring clouds lie in disarray upon the Spring Slope. Crossing a bridge over a stream, I see a village;
the sound of human voices grows near while the sound of pines fades away (Xueshan Gao).
Taking advantage of a leisure moment, I went out to the green mountains; at sunset I returned, following the wild springs. At the mouth of the valley, I had once passed through wind and rain;
in my thatched hall, the tall bamboos are disarrayed by the spring mist. (Yuzhi Ju)
The plum blossoms broke through the cold marsh last night; the morning sun has just begun to melt them, yet the dew still lingers. The man of no affairs now finds himself with affairs:
a branch is first offered to the vase before the Buddha. (Oṃ [mouth] fragrance).
The wind has no power to send down rain; the water has no sentiment for the drifting flowers. The birds on the branches crying out in spring are even more distinct today.
(Tairu-ka) For half my life I have dwelt alone in a solitary village. Loving the moon, I never close my door. I have made a hut from withered wood to stretch out my legs.
Sleeping. His elegance was no less than that of Xuefeng Cun (Yi Run).
*Zadudhai* Scroll Seven;
*Zadudhai* Scroll Eight.
Re-edited by the Kyoto Berlin Successor to the Patriarchs, Śramaṇa Xingyin:

I have dwelt all along in a three-bay thatched cottage in the mountain retreats. A single path of divine light pervades ten thousand realms of stillness. Do not bring the disputes of right and wrong to judge this place.
I am a floating life, riddled with artificiality and irrelevant (Yinshan).
A cup of clear-snow tea, fragrant with its early aroma. Just awakened from a midday nap, the spring day is long. Pressed upon, my entire body is nothing but eyes;
half a window of sparse shadows turns with the slanting sun (Xueyan Qin).
In the spring mountains, the bamboo shoots and bracken are lush and thick; you should grind the yellow millet through the night.
Do not say that the West has no such intent—the Patriarch is entirely within the alms bowl. (Daming Ying)
In the stillness of the mountains, bees labor with heavy thighs over the flowers; in the emptiness of the woods, the bamboo shoots reveal their smooth, pale skin within their sheaths.
Leaning against the railing, I unconsciously become dazed and motionless, only to be called once more by the yellow oriole. (Shílín Gǒng)

Purple ferns stretch out their fists as bamboo shoots break through the tips. The willow flowers have flown away, and the green shadows interlace. Clearly, this is the single-line transmission verse of the Western Patriarch:
the oriole calls out, and the swallows chatter in their nests. (From *Bátángyǎ*).
He built a dwelling by binding reeds to trees and lived there; he gathered thorny branches to weave his walls and opened a path beside the stream.
It was because this Lazy Zan lacked spiritual efficacy that he provoked the Celestial Writings to come thundering from the earth (Buna Yong).
Cold winds and sparse rain mark the beginning of the new year. In solitude, by the frozen ice of an ancient stream, In a warm chamber, a brazier roasts chestnuts;
To drive away poverty, there is no need to burn more paper money. (By Binggu Yan)
The thatched hall in autumn is like the Palace of Broad Cold. Golden flowers bloom amidst emerald thickets. Sitting for long, one does not realize that the mortal bones have been transformed;
the celestial fragrance wafts clearly within the bright moonlight. (By Tian Zhenze, No. 2)
After finishing tea, I sit alone burning incense; the golden lotus drips as the water-clock ticks slowly. Deep in the night, wishing to sleep, I ask the lad:
"On which branch of the plum tree has the moon risen?"
In the mountain hut of non-action, the door remains unopened; on the earthen steps, spring rains cause green moss to grow.
This mind was thought to be entrusted to no one—whence comes the cry of a solitary bird? (Dawei Lun)
Weaving reeds among the bamboos, leaning against the stone roots; through the gaps in the bamboo stalks, one sees the village ahead. Sleeping idly all day long, no one comes;
the pure breeze itself sweeps the gate (by Hyeon-jung).
Boiling vegetables without salt, too lazy to go begging; the mendicant on his alms-round has not yet returned home. Holding up this single hundred-patch robe to look at it:
last night the frost added flowers upon the roof-tiles. (Dai’an Zhuang San)
The buckwheat flowers bloom as the morning sun shines bright. I call the lad to hear my instructions:
"Gather the purple yams well, then take your long spade and dig for茯苓 (fúlíng)."
Living in the world, my heart is like ice in the twelfth month; dwelling in the mountains, I laugh at myself for being utterly incapable. Let us not waste oil on our vegetable soup;
save some to light the Buddha-lamp before the hall.
Puffing my belly as I wander—what day is this? With nothing to do, I take advantage of the leisure moment to stand by the stream. The mountain breeze arises at evening;
the trees by the stream are cold. Fallen blossoms on the stream rise a foot high. (Fagao, No. 4)
I purchased a mountain and cleared the land to establish a separate home; through mist and winding clouds, the narrow path slants away.
Whether human tracks reach here now or not, one sees only purple moss flowers creeping up the steps.

Clothed in garments of hemp, I dwell in a hut woven of grass. It is people who distance themselves from me first; I do not distance myself from them. Whether one gains a carriage or loses a horse, let it all be left unasked.
In all matters, I have now begun the practice of facing the wall.
The mountains are crimson and the grasses are verdant, with ten thousand points of fireflies; amidst the trees stand scattered yellow reed huts. A gentle breeze blows upon my seat and blows upon me;
the bright moon illuminates the person and illuminates the sutras.
Last night the autumn wind suddenly displayed its power; white clouds and leaves flew back at dawn.
For the recluse there is no need to sweep so often, for in these deep mountains guests arrive but rarely. (From *Huanyou Chuan*)
Is it that with old age I have less time for climbing and gazing? Rather, it is because after my illness I have gained much leisure. I call the boy to wash the inkstone;
having no other business, I shall rewrite the "Song of the Ruined Monastery" from those years. (Xuejian)
Within the world, only Wutai is permitted to be high; the True Man of No Rank keeps silent company. Let the winds from all quarters blow as they may;
with eyes ever empty, I gaze at the clouds and the sky. (By Guyue Chengwu)
Content with poverty beneath the forest trees, my thoughts wander far and wide. On a bamboo mat I sleep soundly, my head resting on a stone pillow.
My life beyond the ordinary is sufficient for its lot; it is all because within my breast there is no seeking at all.
Dwelling by myself beside the red cliffs and green waters, there is utterly no honor or disgrace, nor leisure or haste. This old monk does not understand the principle of returning to the source;
let the green mountains be green and then yellow as they will.
Deeply hidden in mountain caves for years beyond reckoning, the tether of fame and the chain of profit could not pull him.
His seven-pound robe, patched together layer upon layer, grows ever more fresh as it is scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind.
The whistling spring breeze mingles with the lament of birds; their clear notes reach right to my ears.
As I sit upright by the incense burner burning cypress seeds, I unfold once more the incomplete sutra before the moon.

Gazing intently all day at the green mountains, the incense smoke from the stone table and burner speaks of a mind naturally at ease. For long, the hanging mat has lacked the carriage of a high-minded scholar;
with a sudden, long啸 (shout of joy), the white clouds remain in their leisurely stillness. (By Tianyin Xiu)
The great trichiliocosm is but a single thatched hut; good and evil both dwell within it. The long is long and the short is short;
where one gains advantage, there one loses it.
The mountains and waters of Yangxian in Jingxi are truly exquisite; yet, lacking the merit to enjoy them, they are difficult to inhabit.
Amidst tens of thousands of acres of verdant bamboo and ancient pines, the dust of the mortal world cannot fly even to the courtyard gates (Junsui).
In the mountains there dwell those beneath the *bìluó* vines; among them are men so emaciated they seem to have come from a painting. O people, return home and do not linger for long!
Do not let the shade of the vines fade away with the passing seasons. (Xueqiao Xin, 15)
A spring cloud parts as a bird calls out; seven fragments, five pieces of flowers drift upon the pond.
Cool and clear, the moss covers the crumbling stones; fresh ivy pierces through the treetops.

A decrepit old man supports himself against the cold, his tattered robes providing scant protection. He falls asleep at dusk, only to wake with the crows at the fifth watch. His entire body is racked with pain, a malady difficult for even a physician to cure.
Sharing this same ailment, who can truly offer compassion? Who can act as his kinsman?
The spring breeze lifts the curtains as the crows cry at dawn; In leisurely sentiment, nothing surpasses my own home.
Each mountain peak stretches its neck to gaze, Watching me in my hut drinking bitter tea.
The autumn light, once bright, is now nearly spent. Wild chrysanthemums lack fragrance, and the tree leaves are dry. A cold rain passes through half the window, piercing to the bone;
yet for the sorrowful person, it is not the thinness of the clothed robe that matters.
Half the sky is red as the sun shines upon the green peaks; the thatched door is sealed, and my sleep is deep. Do not say that this old monk is truly lazy;
I have risen to blow the fire for fear of the wind and cold.
Green mountains and thatched huts, where mountain mists gather; On stone walls and through misty vines, birds nest together. Who would say I am thirty-five years old?
My body is sick with Zen, as listless as mud.
Last night I returned from a dream; the thatched cottage was cold. Sprouts grew upon the stone bed, and moss sprouted upon the hearth. With provisions exhausted, I sought a kindred spirit;
A single fleecy cloud drifted down from the mountain stream.
How can one who dwells on the mountain path explain it? The sky is cloudless at its edge as the moon climbs the pole; the old hare steals vegetables to eat by the earth’s rim.
Its teeth are cold as it chews and chews—look, look again!
A single dilapidated hut has clouds for its curtain; half a withered plum tree has snow for its blossoms. Warm by the brazier, one does not know that others have fallen asleep;
waking from a dream at dawn, the crows are in the bamboo grove.
A few li past the bridge, I reached a man’s dwelling; wild white bean flowers bloomed through the sparse fence. Leaning on my staff with my hair tied back, I gazed at the clouds until arriving;
incense was burned, we pressed our knees together, and drank a cup of tea.
Having built my dwelling among the green mountains, my body finds peace. Yellow hair curls like snow as the hearth-fire grows cold. I add a few antiquities to simmer some porridge;
the clouds reach the wooden gate as the moon has already waned.
One-third moonlight, seven-tenths autumn; sparse yellow leaves flow together with the current. Do not say that the cold radiance has entirely faded away;
it still leaves behind mist and rain upon the branches.
Suited for flowers, suited for rain, the grasses divide the fragrance. The singing voice breaks off and starts again; the mountain dreams are long. Spring grows old and does not weep;
the woodcutter’s path is late. Separated and winding, the realm of water and clouds.
From beginning to end, there is nothing at all to grasp; an old monk before a withered tree by a cliff. Taking a casual step, he carries a basket to seek wild vegetables;
climbing the creepers, he ascends yet another steep ridge.
Dwelling high beyond the world, he cuts off all human seeking; having deeply planted the good field, there will naturally be harvest in autumn.
When a Chan guest knocks at the door, there is nothing to wait for—strike him with a single blow across the spine. (Stone Cart)
My eyes feel as if intoxicated after reading the scriptures; there is no secret remedy to drive away the demon of sleep.
Only when I rest upon my pillow in the mountain hall do I find true stability, while outside the door a thousand bamboo stalks deliver the coolness of jade. (Lingxi Yu)
Village smoke rises on the long path of begging for alms; By fire-tending and hoe-farming, one’s gourd-bowl hangs sufficient.
If only one could escape the two characters "pān-yuán" (clinging to conditions), Then amidst the red dust, no dream would reach the clouds and sky. (Zhuan’an Wei)

Turning the soil and parting the clouds to drive away passersby; watering the vegetables and leading the water to instruct my children. Do not disdain this livelihood as being the same as that of the common world;
for in the Buddha-dharma, there has never been even a single hair’s breadth of it for many years.
He delights in chanting pure verses in long and short meters; as his attendants, he keeps only the Great and Small Emptinesses.
Living on the mountain in this singular way is truly a joy, where neither the bright moon nor the clear breeze can be distinguished.
The path of love traverses the summit of the thousand sages; with joy, I speak of the remaining Chan of all quarters. My body is old and now often fails to rise;
when people come, I am too weary to raise my coarse fists.
Ten li along Hengtang, reeds and rushes conceal the way; red trees in every village enter the painted scroll. I hear it said that my old friend’s autumnal inspiration is fine;
last night his small boat must have stayed by West Lake.
The lion roams without companion; white clouds drift slowly over lofty peaks. The patriarch’s livelihood is buried in fragrant grass;
how often has he cast even a glance upon the three realms?
When feelings and righteousness unite, glue is joined with lacquer; when conditions and causes part, fire turns them to ash.
When the mechanisms of the wooden man and the flowering birds are severed, how could there be even a single thread of resentment or gratitude?
Clearly observing the crows, one knows two months have passed; amidst green clouds and fragrant grass, the springtime lingers on. In old age, I weary of speaking words that forget the passions;
the new bamboo fills the grove and flowers cover every branch.
Where is the pure autumn deep in the night? The moon shines over green mountains as the clouds have just withdrawn. Sitting leaning against my rope-cot, I open the door and window;
toward the western horizon, where heaven ends, I gaze at my native land.
Wild clouds carry the fragrance of roasted tea smoke; The voice of the cuckoo sounds repeatedly before the Grain Rain Festival.
If one realizes that a single flower is equally pure and wondrous, There is no hindrance to the leisurely life of dwelling in the mountains.

A guest with nothing to do in the great cities of the three realms; a monk in an age of the five turbidities enjoying a time of peace. On the tip of his nose, a blazing fire has vanished into nothingness;
within his belly, cold ashes remain for several liters. (Daiweng’s Joy in Five)
Torn old robes are mended and patched again; a sagging thatched hut is propped up and supported once more.
Unable to join the assembly like Han and Shi, I shall spend my life tending the fire and passing through the midday meal.
In deep mountains and vast marshes, the family atmosphere is cool; by the wheat-rice meal at the thatched gate, the fragrance of laughter lingers.
Strolling leisurely on a clear snowy day while riding a lean donkey, an old villager braving the cold offers me a jar of gruel.
The moonlight fills the sky, white as a bowl of tea; ten plum trees bring clarity to the thatched cottage.
At this moment, thinking of one who might share in this enjoyment, I look repeatedly at the tripod-legged cauldron before my bed.
Sleeping little, I often smile at Xiang as he folds his hands; frequently ill, I once sighed for Can with his red head.
Having resolved to change my ways in recent years, I have come to identify with these two as they flow together.
Mowing the weeds and burning the fields enriches the soil; rows upon rows of mugwort and mallow fill the thatched gate. The mountain kitchen is sufficient for pure offerings;
when guests arrive, there is no need to gather more *wei* sprouts. (Yin, Ming, Lun, Er)
Thorn-apple sandals tread upon the colors of the cold forest; fragrant blossoms fall everywhere like scattered plum petals. Wild birds, having finished their meal, have the scent filling their beaks;
these notes of *gong* and *shang* do not come from mere chance.
A single mat of pines and wind comes upon the pillow; coolness arising from behind is most fitting.
For this old fellow, there is a singular joy of natural truth; ten thousand taels of gold cannot rival it. (Zhutang Pu)

The dawn sun is faintly bright amidst the misty clusters of trees; A seeker of *zhi* fungi stands upon the wooden bridge to the east. Stone sprouts emerge level with the rain of the Flower Festival morning;
Thin river clouds unroll in the breeze at the mouth of the valley. (Dongming and Zhuo)
The stone pillar stands firm as the rain clears and the moonlight shines bright; I smile at myself, for in recent years dreams have not arisen.
Before my eyes, the affairs of past and present are already empty; my breast is as clear as a jade pool.

Dwelling in the market district amidst the dense throngs, one must maintain constant mindfulness. The gate is closed against the spring breeze as the sun sinks low. At times, in a moment of clarity, one hears it clearly:
the sound of flower-sellers comes from the painted tower to the west. (Shuntian)
The patriarch’s verse, once adhering to the wall by the water, has been blown down by the wind; Cobwebs cling to the eaves, opened wide by the rain.
Green shade fills the paths where all the flowers have fallen; Not a single bird has ever come to the gate. (Nanshi Xu)
Dwelling upon the boat, a thousand feet of silk line hang straight down. A single ripple stirs and ten thousand waves follow. At night’s quiet, the waters are cold and the fish do not bite;
the boat returns under the bright moon, empty-handed. (The Boatman’s Second Truth)
For thirty years I have wandered upon the sea; when the waters are clear, the fish appear but do not swallow the hook. When my fishing rods are worn out, I plant new bamboo;
regardless of the time or effort spent, I rest as soon as I find the opportunity.
When Ye Neihan selected the day and gathered his guests to welcome me with exceptional courtesy, I composed this verse to decline their invitation:
Yesterday I already set the date for today; Leaving the gate, leaning on my staff, I pondered once more: As a monk, I ought to dwell among crags and valleys;
In the midst of a banquet for a state guest, it is truly inappropriate. (Wei Zheng)
Ten Verses on the Universal Radiance Cowherd:

Before being herded, the fierce beast runs wild, its horns tossing as it bellows; It gallops along the mountain paths and streams, growing ever more distant. A single mass of black clouds stretches across the valley.
Who knows that with every step one treads upon the fine sprouts?

(Puming) Letting loose one’s will by the waterside of the mountain stream, the tip of the nose wanders far and free. Who knows that wherever one steps within the universe, it is all the King’s transformation?
(Shanziji) Treading wildly through clouds and mountains, one offends the ripening crops. (Shanziji)
South of Xiang, north of Tan, his head and horns are distinct; he strikes east and strikes west (Yulin Xi).
At first, I adjusted him with a sharp rope through his nose; once he began to bolt in competition, I lashed him with a heavy whip. From the start, this inferior nature has been difficult to tame.
